- Root: ر-ب-ط (r-b-ṭ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Binding, tying firmly; a bond or ligament that connects parts into a coherent whole.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Relational dependence among ontological realities; here, the ordered linkage of psychic faculties (quwā) as a divinely instituted hierarchy.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for physical tying; metaphorical (majāz) for causal and teleological connection among non-physical entities.
- Sībawayh Rule: ʾIḍāfah (Genitive Construction) — The phrase «ارتباط قوى النفس» uses a chain of annexations (muḍāf ilayh) to express inseparable ontological relation, not mere juxtaposition.
chapters.translation: I say: Now follows the exposition of how the soul’s faculties (quwā al-nafs) are bound one to another — a binding that is not accidental or arbitrary, but rooted in the very order of creation, whereby each faculty serves as a means (wasīlah) for the next, and the lowest is subservient to the highest, until the whole converges upon the rational soul (al-nafs al-nāṭiqah) as its final end and governing principle.

chapters.title_en: The Hierarchy of Faculties and the Rank of the Intellect
chapters.arabic_text:
اعلم أن هذه القوى متفاوتة الرتب، فإن بعضها أريدت لنفسها، وبعضها أريدت
لغيرها، وبعضها خادمة، وبعضها مخدومة. والرئيس المطلق منها هي التي تراد
لنفسها، ويراد غيرها لها، وليس ذلك إلا الرتبة الأخيرة، وفيها تفاوت رتب
الأولياء والأنبياء. فإن الإنسان لم يخلق إلا لما هو من خاصيته، وما عدا
القوى المخصومة بالنفس الإنسانية يشاركها فيها الحيوانات، فإن الإنسان خلق
على رتبة بين البهيمية والملك، وفيه جملة من القوى والصفات. فهو من حيث
يتغذى وينسل فنبات،
ومن حيث يحس ويتحرك فحيوان، ومن حيث صورته وقامته فكالصورة المنقوشة على
حائط. وإنما خاصته التي لأجلها خلق قوة العقل، ودرك حقائق الأشياء. فمن
استعمل جميع قواه على وجه التوصل بها إلى العلم والعمل، فقد تشبه
بالملائكة، فحقيق بأن يلحق بهم وجدير بأن يسمى ملكا وربانيا، كما قال: (إن
هذا إلا ملك كريم) ومن صرف همته إلى اتباع اللذات البدنية، يأكل كما يأكل
الأنعام، فقد نزل إلى أفق البهائم، فيصير إما غمرا كثور، وإما شرها كخنزير،
وإما صرعة ككلب، وأما حقودا كجمل، أو متكبرا كنمر، أو ذا روغان كثعلب. أو
يجمع ذلك كله كشيطان مريد.
وبالجملة من تصفح القوى التي ذكرناها، عرف أن مقتضيات العقل أرفعها
وأعلاها، فينظر بعين التعجب كيف يخدم بعضها لبعض خدمة ضرورية عليها فطرت،
ولا تستطيع مخالفة أمر الله تعالى فيها.
فإن العقل هو الرئيس المخدوم، ويخدمه وزيره وهو أقرب الأشياء إليه، وهو
العقل العملي، الذي سميناه قوة عاملة بحسب مراسم العقل. لأن العقل العملي
لأجل تدبير البدن، والبدن آلة النفس ومركبها، تقتنص به بواسطة الحواس مبادئ
العلوم التي تستنبط منها حقائق الأمور.
ثم العقل العملي يخدمه الوهم، والوهم يخدمه قوتان: قوة بعده وقوة قبله.
فالقوة التي بعده هي القوة الحافظة لما  أدركه وأداه إليه، والقوة التي قبله
هي جميع القوى الحيوانية على الترتيب الذي سنذكره، ومن جملتها المتخيلة،
أعني المفكرة، ويخدمها قوتان مختلفتا المأخذ، فالقوة الرغبية الشوقية
تخدمها بالانبعاث، لأن انبعاثها إلى الحركة، بالتخيل والفكر. والقوة
الحافظة للصور التي في الحس المشترك تخدمها بقبول التركيب والتفصيل، فيما
فيها من الصور. ثم هذان رئيسان لطائفتين،
أما الحافظة للصور فيخدمها (الحس) المشترك، برفع االصور إليها حتى تحفظ.
وأما القوة النزوعية فتخدمها الشهوة والغضب، والشهوة والغضب تخدمهما القوة
الحركة للعضل، وعندها تنتهي القوى الحيوانية.
والقوى الحيوانية بالجملة يخدمها النباتية، والنباتية ثلاث، المولدة
والمربية والغاذية، ورأسها المولدة، وتخدمها المربية والغاذية تخدمها. ثم
يخدم هذه قوى أربع، وهي الجاذبة والماسكة والهاضمة والدافعة، إذ لا بد في
النبات من قوة جاذبة للغذاء إليه، ثم ماسكة، ثم هاضمة تهضم ما أمسكته
الماسكة، ثم دافعة تدفع فضله،
والدافعة هي الخادمة التي لا خادم لها، وكأنها كالكناس في نظام أمر
البلد، ثم الحرارة والبرودة والرطوبة واليبوسة تخدم القوى الهاضمة والجاذبة
والماسكة والدافعة، وهذه آخر درجات القوى في الأجسام. وقد ضرب للقوى
المذكورة مثال يقربها إلى إفهام العوام، فقيل القوة المفكرة مسكنها وسط
الدماغ بمنزلة الملك، يسكن وسط المملكة. والخيالية مسكنها مقدم الدماغ،
جارية مجرى صاحب بريدة، أو مجتمع الأخبار عنده. والحافظة التي مسكنها مؤخر
الدماغ، جارية مجرى خادمه، والقوى الناطقة جارية مجرى ترجمانه، والعاملة
جارية مجرى كاتبه، والحواس جارية مجرى الجواسيس وأصحاب الأخبار الصادقة
اللهجة، فيما يرفعونه من الأخبار، فيلتقط كل واحد الخبر من الصق الذي وكل
به، إذ البصر موكل بعالم الألوان والسمع بالأصوات، وهكذا الجميع. فيرفعون
هذه الأخبار إلى صاحب البريد وصاحب البريد يسقط ما يراه حشوا، ويرفع الباقي
صافيا إلى حضرة الملك،
فيميزه ويعرف منافعه ومضاره، ويسلمه لخادمه إلى وقت الحاجة، فحينئذ يتقدم
بإخراجه، وكما أن الأعمال التي يتولاها الملك بنفسه أشرف مما يستعمل فيه
غيره، فكذلك ما تتولاه النفس التي هي الملك بالحقيقة، بواسطة المفكرة، من
الروية والاعتبار والقياس والفراسة واستنباط المجهول، أشرف مما تستعمل فيه
الخدم. وهذا المثال قريب مما روي أن حبر الأمة قال: " دخلت على عائشة،
فقالت: الإنسان عيناه مهاد، وأذناه قمع، ولسانه ترجمان، ويداه جناحان،
ورجلاه بريدان، والقلب ملك. فإذا طاب طاب جنوده ". فقالت: " هكذا سمعت رسول
الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول ".
فهذه جمل من أحوال النفس تلوناها عليك على سبيل الاقتصار، وإنها بعض
عجائب النفس. ولو نظرت في تشريح الأعضاء، وفحصت عن عدد العروق والأعصاب
والعضل والعظام والشرايين والأوردة،
ثم إلى الأعضاء الآلية التي أعدت للنفس، ولجذب الطعام ثم لهضمه ثم لدفعه،
وإلى الآلات التي خلقت للتناسل، ورأيت العجائب في خدمة بعضها بعضا
بالضرورة، ثم بعد فراغك من تشريح الأجسام نظرت في تفصيل قوى تلك الأجسام،
واستقصيته بمعرفة حقائق العلوم الطبيعية، لقضيت منها آخر العجب. فتعسا لمن
كفر بالله وغفل عن قوله: (وفي الأرض آيات للموقنين، وفي أنفسكم أفلا
تبصرون) ، بل في كل شيء دليل على أنه واحد. ومن لم يؤمن بالله على الجملة،
فليس من العقلاء، وهو أخس من أن يخاطب بمثل هذه الكلمات. وإنما كلامنا مع
من صدق بالجملة، فندعوه إلى البحث عن صنع الله، ليزداد بسببه يقينه
وإيمانه، ويتفاقم به تعظيمه وإجلاله. فكل ما لا يدرك بالحواس، وإنما يدرك
بالعقل بواسطة آثاره، فسبيل استقصاء معرفته استقصاء النظر في آثاره. بل
نضرب مثالا يقرب من فهم الخلق كافة، فما من فقيه إلا وقد اعتقد في
المذكورين من العلماء مثل أبي حنيفة والشافعي وغيرهما، رتبة تتقاضاه
التعظيم. وهذا يشترك فيه الخلق، ولكن ليس من يتصفح تصنيف مصنف، فيرى فيه من
عجائب صنعه وبدائع حذقه، يبقى اعتقاده في التعظيم على ما كان عليه قبل
معرفته، بل لا يزال يطلع على صفة غريبة له في كلامه وتصنيفه أو شعره،
وتزداد نفسه له تعظيما وتوقيرا واعتقادا
فمن عرف أن الله صانع العالم، كمن عرف أن زيدا متميز عن غيره، بكونه ناظم
ديوان، ومصنف كتاب. وأين هذا من اعتقاد من تصفح الشعر، فرأى فيه غرائبه؟
فهذا يعتقد عظمته ورتبته اعتقادا راسخا عن تحقيق  وبصيرة والآخر يعتقد
اعتقادا مجملا ضعيفا، غير مدرك بالبصيرة والتحقيق. وهذا فرق بين رتبة
العوام وذوي البصائر في هذا الأمر الواحد.
والعالم بما فيه من العجائب تصنيف الله وتأليفه وإبداعه واختراعه، والنفس
جزء من أجزاء العالم، وكل جزء من أجزاء العالم مشحون بالعجائب، فلا يزال
الباحث عنها مستفيدا زيادة اعتقاد، وتأكيد إيمان، ولذلك حث الله على التفكر
في الأنفس والآفاق وملكوت السموات والأرض.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ر-ت-ب (r-t-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Ordering, gradation, station; a thing's fixed rank in a sequence.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ontological station assigned by divine wisdom; the graded scale of being from plant to angel.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical elevation; metaphorical for spiritual degree (martabah) of proximity to God.
- Root: خ-د-م (kh-d-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To serve, to attend upon; a servant subordinate to a master.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Teleological subordination—a faculty exists for the sake of another's perfection.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in social hierarchy; metaphorical for the cosmic order of faculties serving the rational soul.
- Root: ع-ق-ل (ʿ-q-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Restraint, understanding; the faculty that binds one from error.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The noetic principle (al-ʿaql) by which man apprehends universals and is distinguished from beasts.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for intellectual grasp; metaphorical for the "king" (malik) ruling the soul's domain.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Taqdīm wa Taʾkhīr (Fronting for emphasis) — The predicate "هي التي تراد لنفسها" is fronted to highlight the intellect's unique end; also the conditional "فمن استعمل..." employs protasis-apodosis structure for universal moral classification.
chapters.translation:
Know that these faculties are of differing ranks: some are intended for their own sake, some for the sake of another, some are servants, and some are served. The absolute chief among them is that which is intended for itself, and for whose sake all else is intended—and this is none other than the final rank, in which the stations of the saints and prophets differ. For man was not created except for that which is his specific property, and whatever lies beyond the faculties distinguished by the human soul, the animals share with him in it. For man was created upon a rank between beastliness and angelhood, and in him is a host of faculties and attributes. Thus, inasmuch as he is nourished and reproduces, he is a plant; inasmuch as he senses and moves, he is an animal; and inasmuch as his form and stature, he is like an image painted upon a wall. His specific property, for which he was created, is the faculty of reason and the apprehension of the realities of things. Whoever employs all his faculties as a means to attain knowledge and action has become like the angels, and is worthy of being joined to them and deserving of being called an angel and a lordly one (rabbānī), as He said: {«إِنْ هَٰذَا إِلَّا مَلَكٌ كَرِيمٌ»} ("This is none other than a noble angel"). And whoever turns his aspiration to the pursuit of bodily pleasures, eating as cattle eat, has descended to the horizon of beasts, becoming either a dullard like an ox, or a glutton like a swine, or a predator like a dog, or spiteful like a camel, or arrogant like a leopard, or cunning like a fox—or he gathers all of that together like a rebellious devil.

In sum, whoever examines the faculties we have mentioned knows that the dictates of the intellect are the loftiest and highest of them. He then beholds with the eye of wonder how some serve others with a necessary service upon which they were naturally constituted, unable to oppose the command of God, exalted be He, therein.

For the intellect is the served chief, and it is served by its vizier, which is the closest of things to it—namely, the practical intellect, which we have called the operative faculty according to the ordinances of the intellect. For the practical intellect exists for the governance of the body, and the body is the soul's instrument and its mount, by which it hunts, through the senses, the principles of the sciences from which the realities of things are derived.

Then the practical intellect is served by the estimative faculty (al-wahm), and the estimative faculty is served by two faculties: one after it and one before it. The faculty after it is the retentive faculty, which preserves what it has apprehended and conveyed to it; and the faculty before it is all the animal faculties in the order we shall mention, among them the imaginative—I mean the cogitative—which is served by two faculties of differing provenance. The appetitive, desiderative faculty serves it by way of incitement, for its incitement to motion occurs through imagination and thought. And the retentive faculty of the forms in the common sense serves it by accepting composition and division regarding the forms contained therein. Then these two are chiefs over two companies.

As for the retentive of forms, it is served by the common sense, which raises the forms up to it so that it may preserve them. As for the appetitive faculty, it is served by desire and anger; and desire and anger are served by the motive faculty of the muscles—and at this point the animal faculties come to an end.

The animal faculties, in sum, are served by the plant faculties; and the plant faculties are three: the generative, the nutritive, and the augmentative. Their head is the generative, and it is served by the augmentative and the nutritive. Then these are served by four faculties: the attractive, the retentive, the digestive, and the expulsive. For in the plant there must be a faculty attracting nourishment to it, then one retaining it, then one digesting what the retentive has held, then one expelling its surplus. The expulsive is the servant that has no servant, and it is like the street-sweeper in the order of the city. Then heat, cold, moisture, and dryness serve the digestive, attractive, retentive, and expulsive faculties—and these are the last degrees of faculties in bodies.

An example has been struck for the aforementioned faculties to bring them near to the understanding of the common folk. It was said: The cogitative faculty, whose seat is the middle of the brain, is like the king dwelling in the midst of his kingdom. The imaginative faculty, whose seat is the front of the brain, holds the station of the postmaster, or the collector of reports. The retentive faculty, whose seat is the back of the brain, holds the station of his servant. The rational faculties hold the station of his interpreter, the operative faculty his scribe, and the senses his spies and bearers of truthful reports, in what they convey of news. Each one picks up the report from the quarter entrusted to it—for sight is entrusted with the world of colors, hearing with sounds, and so on for all of them. They raise these reports to the postmaster, and the postmaster drops what he deems superfluous and raises the rest, purified, to the presence of the king, who discriminates it, knows its benefits and harms, and hands it to his servant until the time of need, whereupon he commands its bringing forth.

And just as the works that the king undertakes himself are nobler than those in which he employs others, so too what the soul—which is the king in truth—undertakes through the cogitative faculty, of reflection, consideration, analogy, discernment, and the derivation of the unknown, is nobler than what it employs its servants in. This example is close to what is related that the scholar of the community (ḥibr al-ummah) said: "I entered upon ʿĀʾishah, and she said: 'Man's two eyes are his carpet, his two ears are his funnels, his tongue is his interpreter, his two hands are his wings, his two feet are his couriers, and the heart is the king. When the king is good, his troops are good.'" She said: "Thus I heard the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, say."

These are summaries of the states of the soul that we have recited to you by way of brevity, and they are but some of the wonders of the soul. Were you to look into the dissection of the limbs, and investigate the number of veins, nerves, muscles, bones, arteries, and veins; then into the instrumental organs prepared for the soul—for drawing food, then digesting it, then expelling it—and into the instruments created for reproduction, and you saw the wonders in their serving one another by necessity; then, after finishing the dissection of bodies, you looked into the detailed faculties of those bodies and pursued it to completion through knowledge of the realities of natural science, you would derive from it the utmost wonder. So perdition to him who disbelieves in God and is heedless of His saying: {«وَفِي الْأَرْضِ آيَاتٌ لِلْمُوقِنِينَ، وَفِي أَنْفُسِكُمْ أَفَلَا تُبْصِرُونَ»} ("And in the earth are signs for those who are certain, and in yourselves—do you not then see?"). Rather, in everything is a proof that He is One. And whoever does not believe in God in general is not among the rational, and is too base to be addressed with such words. Our discourse is only with him who affirms in general, and we call him to investigate the making of God, so that his certainty and faith may increase thereby, and his veneration and reverence may grow greater.

For everything that is not perceived by the senses, but is perceived by the intellect through its effects, the way to exhaustively know it is to exhaustively examine its effects. Rather, let us strike an example that draws near to the understanding of all people. There is no jurist who has not held, regarding the renowned scholars such as Abū Ḥanīfah, al-Shāfiʿī, and others, a rank that demands veneration. This is shared by all people. But there is none who examines the composition of a composed work, and sees in it the wonders of its making and the marvels of its skill, whose veneration remains as it was before knowing it. Rather, he continually discovers a strange quality in his speech, composition, or poetry, and his soul increases in veneration, reverence, and conviction for him.

So whoever knows that God is the Maker of the world is like one who knows that Zayd is distinguished from others by being the arranger of a collection and the author of a book. But where is this compared to the conviction of one who examines the poetry and sees its marvels? For this one holds his greatness and rank with a firm conviction based on verification and insight, while the other holds a general, weak conviction, not grasped by insight and verification. And this is the difference between the rank of the common folk and those of insight in this single matter.

The world, with all its wonders, is God's composition, His arrangement, His origination, and His invention. And the soul is a part of the parts of the world, and every part of the parts of the world is filled with wonders. So the seeker never ceases to gain increase of conviction and confirmation of faith thereby. For this reason, God urged reflection upon the souls, the horizons, and the dominion of the heavens and the earth.

chapters.title_en: Exposition of the Relation of Action to Knowledge and Its Production
chapters.arabic_text: ### | بيان نسبة العمل من العلم وإنتاجه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ن-س-ب (n-s-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of relation, attribution, or linkage (nisbah) — establishing a connection between two entities.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological discourse, nisbah denotes the ontological or causal dependency of one thing upon another, often used for the relation of created acts to divine or human agency.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage (ḥaqīqah) refers to genealogical or logical attribution; metaphorical (majāz) extends to conceptual or causal ties, as here between ʿamal and ʿilm.
- Root: ع-ل-م (ʿ-l-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of knowledge, perception, or cognizance — the firm grasp of a thing as it is.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): ʿIlm as the stable, certain comprehension of reality, distinct from mere opinion (ẓann) or imitation (taqlīd); in ethics, it is the foundational cognitive act that precedes volition and action.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: direct awareness; metaphorical: the "root" or "seed" from which action sprouts, as in the phrase "knowledge is the tree of action."
- Root: ن-ت-ج (n-t-j)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of producing, yielding, or generating — originally used for the bearing of fruit or the outcome of a process.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Intāj (production) as the necessary causal emergence of a result from its principle, akin to the conclusion (natījah) from premises in logic.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: fruition of a tree; metaphorical: the intellectual or moral "fruit" that action bears from knowledge.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of ʾiḍāfah (Construct State) — The phrase "نسبة العمل من العلم" employs a genitive construction where the relation (nisbah) is specified by its two terms, and the preposition "من" (min) indicates the source or origin, governing a partitive or causal reading. The verbal noun "إنتاجه" (intājuhu) is annexed to its object, implying a transitive production whose agent is implicit in the preceding context.
chapters.translation: I say: Know that the relation of action to knowledge is that of a branch to its root, and of a fruit to its tree. For action is produced (intāj) from knowledge, just as the effect is produced from its cause, and the conclusion from its premise. Thus, every action that issues from a human being, whether praiseworthy or blameworthy, is necessarily preceded by a corresponding knowledge — either of the benefit in performing it, or of the harm in abandoning it. For the soul does not move toward any particular action except after a conception (taṣawwur) of its end and a judgment (taṣdīq) concerning its desirability. Hence, knowledge is the origin (aṣl) and the foundation (miqdād), while action is the branch (farʿ) and the fruit (thamrah). And since the fruit is perfected only by the perfection of the tree, so too is action perfected only by the perfection of knowledge. Therefore, whoever seeks to rectify his action must first rectify his knowledge, for the rectification of the branch is dependent upon the rectification of the root, and the soundness of the fruit upon the soundness of the seed.

chapters.title_en: The Criterion of Moral Action — Section 8: The True Meaning of Action as Purification for Felicity
chapters.arabic_text:
السعادة التي اتفق عليها المحققون من الصوفية بأجمعهم، وساعدهم من النظار
طوائف سواهم: إن تأثير العمل لإزالة ما لا ينبغي، والسعي في العلم، سعي في
تحصيل ما ينبغي وإزالة ما لا ينبغي، شرط لتفريغ المحل لما ينبغي، والمشروط
هو المقصود، وهو أشرف من الشرط. ومثاله من أراد استيلاد إمرأة بها علة،
تمنع العلوق، فعليه وظيفتان: إحداهما إماطة العلة المفسدة للحمل، المانعة
من العلوق، والأخرى إيداع النطفة بعد إزالة العلة المانعة. فالأولى شرط
للثانية، والثانية هي الغاية المطلوبة. وإذا فرضت دارا بنيت لملك، رتبة تلك
الدار نزول الملك فيها، وقد اغتصبها القردة والخنازير، فجمال تلك الدار
وكمالها موقوف على أمرين: أحدهما إزعاج القردة النازلين فيها بغير حق
والآخر نزول المستحق.
وإذا فرضنا مرآة صدئة قد ستر الخبث صفاها، ومنع انطباع صورنا فيها، فكمال
المرآة أن تستعد لقبول الصور، فتحكيها كما هي عليها، وعلى مكملها وظيفتان:
إحداهما الجلاء والثقل، وهي إزالة الخبث الذي ينبغي أن لا يكون، والثانية
أن يحاذي بها نحو المطلوب حكاية صورته. فكذلك نفس الآدمي مستعدة لأن تصير
مرآة، يحاذي بها شطر الحق في كل شيء، فتنطبع به كأنها هو من وجه، وإن كانت
غيره من وجه آخر، كما في الصورة والمرآة. وكمالها في مثل هذه الدرجة وهذه
الخاصة التي فارقت بها ما تحتها من الحيوانات، إذ هذا الاستعداد مسلوب عن
الحيوانات كلها، سوى الآدمي بالقوة والفعل جميعا، كما انسلب عن التراب
والخشب الاستعداد لحكاية الصور، وأن يكون مرآة لها، وهو موجود بالفعل أبدا
للملائكة، لا يفارقها، كما أنه موجود  للماء الصافي، فإنه يحكي الصورة بطبعه
حكاية مخصوصة، وهو موجود للآدمي بالقوة لا بالفعل. فإن جاهد نفسه التحق
بأفق الملائكة، وإن استمر على الأسباب الموجبة لتراكم الخبث على مرآة
النفس، باتباع الشهوات، اسود قلبه وتراكمت ظلمته، وبطل بالكلية استعداده،
والتحق بأفق البهائم، وحرم سعادته وكماله حرمانا أبديا، لا تدارك له.
فإذن العمل معناه كسر الشهوات بصرف النفس عن
صوبها، إلى الجنبة العالية الآلهية، ليمحي عن النفس الهيئات الخبيثة،
والعلائق الردية التي ربطتها بالجنبة السافلة. حتى إذا محقت تلك العلائق،
أو ضعفت حوذي بها نحو النظر في الحقائق الآلهية، ففاضت عليه من جهة الله
تعالى تلك الأمور الشريفة، كما فاضت على الأولياء والأنبياء والصديقين.
وذلك صيد ينفق على قدر الرزق، وبأحكام الأصل فيه يزيد الاسترزاق، كما يعرضن
من زيادة الاسترزاق بالأسباب في اقتناص الصيد، بل في اقتناص الربح
والتجارة، بل في اقتناص فقه النفس. فإن القليل بالاجتهاد قد يجاوز حد
المجتهدين بمزيد ذكاء فطري، فكذا طهارة النفس عن هذه العلائق في أول الفطرة
في غاية الاختلاف. ثم الجهد أيضا يختلف وينشأ من ذلك تفاوت لا ينحصر، فكذا
سعادة الآخرة. ففيضان هذه الرحمة من الله عز وجل على النفس غاية المطلوب،
وهو عين السعادة التي للنفس بعد الموت، ولكنها مشروطة بإزالة العلائق ومحو
الصفات الردية التي تأكدت للنفس باتباع الشهوات.
فإذن العمل يرجع إلى مجاهدة النفس بإزالة ما لا ينبغي. وإذا نسب إلى
اتباع الشهوات ظهرت فضيلتها، وإذا نسب إلى تحصيل ما ينبغي كانت رتبتها منه
مرتبة
الشرط من المشروط، والخادم من المخدوم، وما أريد لغيره بالنسبة إلى ما
أريد لنفسه، وعليه نبه النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا قال: " الإيمان بضع
وسبعون بابا، أدناها إماطة الأذى من الطريق. والمجاهدة بالعبادات أكثر
أغراضها إماطة الأذى عن الطريق.
ولقائل أن يقول المراد بالحديث التقاط الزجاج العظم والحجارة من الشوارع،
وأن هذا هو السابق إلى فهم الأكثرين. ولقائل آخر: أن يقول إن الناس
يتفاوتون في فهم معاني الألفاظ، على حسب تفاوت رتبهم، ولذلك قال  عليه
السلام: " نضر الله أمرا سمع مقالتي فوعاها، ثم أداها كما سمعها، فرب حامل
فقه غير فقيه ورب حامل فقه إلى من هو أفقه منه ". فلولا أن في ألفاظه ما
يسبق إلى فهم غير الفقيه خلاف ما يسبق إلى فهم الفقيه، لما أكد الوصية
بذلك. ثم ليت شعري إذا فهم غير الفقيه خلاف ما يسبق إلى فهم الفقيه، لما
أكد الوصية بذلك. ثم ليت شعري إذا فهم غير الفقيه خلاف ما يسبق إلى فهم
الفقيه أو الأفقه أو في جانب غيرهم؟ ولا شك أن هذا عزيز نادر، والغالب
خلافه. فالسابق إلى فهم الجماهير يكاد الحق يجانبه، وينحاز إلى ما يفهمه
الفقيه والأفقه، ولا سيما في لفظ لا يصرح بالتخصيص. فإن لفظ الأذى عام،
ولفظ الطريق عام. ولو أريد الخاص لذكر الزجاج أو المدر ونبه على أمثاله.
وذلك الظاهر أيضا مندرج تحت العموم، فإنه بذلك العمل
أيضا مصلح نفسه، ومهذب خلقه، ومميط عن النفس رذيلة الغفلة والغشاوة، وقلة
الشفقة، على ما سنذكره في تفصيل سوء الأخلاق وحسنها.
فقد عرفت أن سعادة النفس وكمالها أن تنتقش بحقائق الأمور الآلهية وتتحد
بها حتى كأنها هي، وأن ذلك لا يكون إلا بتطهير النفس عن هيئات ردية تقتضيها
الشهوة والغضب، وذلك بالمجاهدة والعمل. فالعمل للطهارة، والطهارة شرط ذلك
الكمال. ولذلك قال عليه السلام: " بني الدين على النظافة ".
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ط-ه-ر (ṭ-h-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is cleanliness and purity, both physical and spiritual; removal of filth (khabath) and defilement.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, ṭahārah signifies purification of the soul from vicious traits (akhlaq radhiyyah) and base attachments, a prerequisite for receptivity to divine truths.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) refers to physical cleansing; metaphorical (majāz) extends to moral and spiritual purification, as in the soul's polishing (tajallī) for the imprint of divine realities.
- Root: ج-ل-ا (j-l-ā)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Polishing, burnishing, clearing away rust or tarnish; making something shine.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Used for the soul's refinement, removing the rust (ṣada’) of sin and heedlessness to restore its original reflective capacity.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for mirrors and metals; metaphorical for the heart's purification, as in the prophetic tradition about polishing the heart.
- Root: ع-ل-ق (ʿ-l-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Attachment, clinging, suspension; a bond that ties one thing to another.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the soul's context, ʿalā’iq are the worldly attachments that bind it to the lower realm (jihah sāfilah), impeding ascent to the divine.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical clinging; metaphorical for spiritual dependencies that must be severed for liberation.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Construction (al-sharṭ wa al-jawāb) — The text repeatedly employs conditional structures (e.g., "in jāhada... ilḥaqa" and "in istamarra... i'swadda") to express causal necessity: the protasis (condition) is the means, the apodosis (result) is the end, mirroring the logical priority of the condition over the conditioned.
chapters.translation:
I say: The felicity (saʿādah) upon which the verifiers (muḥaqqiqūn) among the Sufis have unanimously agreed, and in which they were seconded by groups of speculative theologians (nuẓẓār) besides them, is this: The effect of action (ʿamal) is the removal of what ought not to be (mā lā yanbaghī), and striving in knowledge is striving to acquire what ought to be (mā yanbaghī) and to remove what ought not to be — this being a condition (sharṭ) for emptying the locus (maḥall) for what ought to be. And the conditioned (mashrūṭ) is the intended goal, and it is nobler than the condition. Its parable: one who desires to beget a child from a woman who has an ailment preventing conception — upon him are two duties: one is the removal of the ailment that corrupts pregnancy and prevents conception, and the other is the deposition of the seed after the removal of the preventing ailment. The first is a condition for the second, and the second is the sought-after end (ghāyah maṭlūbah). And if you suppose a house built for a king, the rank of that house being the king's descent into it, and it has been usurped by apes and swine — then the beauty and perfection of that house are contingent upon two matters: one is the expulsion of the apes dwelling in it without right, and the other is the descent of the rightful one.

And if we suppose a rusted mirror whose impurity has veiled its clarity and prevented the imprint of our forms in it — then the perfection of the mirror is that it becomes prepared to receive forms and to depict them as they are in themselves. Upon its perfecter are two duties: one is the polishing and cleansing (al-jalā’ wa al-thaqal), which is the removal of the impurity that ought not to be, and the second is that he direct it toward the sought object to depict its form. Likewise, the human soul (nafs) is prepared to become a mirror, directed toward the direction (shiṭr) of the Truth (al-Ḥaqq) in all things, so that it is imprinted with Him as if it were He in one respect, though it is other than He in another respect — as in the case of the image and the mirror. And its perfection lies in such a degree and such a property by which it has been distinguished from the animals beneath it, for this preparedness (istiʿdād) is stripped from all animals, save the human being, both in potentiality (bi-al-quwwah) and actuality (bi-al-fiʿl) — just as the preparedness to depict forms and to be a mirror for them is stripped from dust and wood, while it exists in actuality perpetually for the angels, never departing from them — as it exists for clear water, for it depicts the form by its very nature in a specific depiction — and it exists for the human being in potentiality, not in actuality. If he strives against his soul (jāhada nafsahu), he joins the horizon of the angels (ufq al-malā’ikah); but if he persists in the causes that necessitate the accumulation of rust upon the mirror of the soul, by following the appetites (shahawāt), his heart blackens, its darkness accumulates, his preparedness is nullified entirely, and he joins the horizon of the beasts (ufq al-bahā’im), being deprived of his felicity and perfection with an eternal deprivation that admits no remedy.

Thus, the meaning of action is the breaking of the appetites by diverting the soul from their direction toward the lofty divine side (al-jihah al-ʿāliyah al-ilāhiyyah), so that the vicious traits (hay’āt khabīthah) and base attachments (ʿalā’iq radiyyah) that bound it to the lower side (al-jihah al-sāfilah) are effaced from the soul. Until, when those attachments are effaced or weakened, it is directed toward the contemplation of divine realities (al-naẓar fī al-ḥaqā’iq al-ilāhiyyah), and those noble matters overflow upon it from the side of God Most High — just as they overflowed upon the saints (awliyā’), the prophets (anbiyā’), and the veracious (ṣiddīqīn). And that is a hunt (ṣayd) that is expended according to the measure of provision (rizq), and by the soundness of the root therein, the seeking of provision (istirzāq) increases — just as occurs in the increase of provision through means in the hunting of game, nay, in the hunting of profit and trade, nay, in the hunting of self-understanding (fiqh al-nafs). For the little one, by exertion, may surpass the limit of the exerting ones by an excess of innate intelligence; likewise, the purification of the soul from these attachments at the beginning of the primordial nature (fiṭrah) is at the utmost degree of variation. Then exertion also varies, and from that arises a difference that is not limited — and so too the felicity of the Hereafter. Thus, the overflowing of this mercy from God, Mighty and Majestic, upon the soul is the utmost object of desire, and it is the very felicity of the soul after death — but it is conditioned upon the removal of attachments and the effacement of the vicious traits that were confirmed in the soul by following the appetites.

Thus, action reduces to striving against the soul (mujāhadat al-nafs) by removing what ought not to be. When it is attributed to the following of appetites, its virtue appears; and when it is attributed to the acquisition of what ought to be, its rank relative to it is the rank of the condition to the conditioned, and the servant (khādim) to the served (makhdūm), and what is desired for another's sake relative to what is desired for its own sake. And upon this the Prophet, peace be upon him, alerted when he said: «الإيمان بضع وسبعون بابا، أدناها إماطة الأذى من الطريق» — "Faith has seventy-odd branches; the lowest of them is the removal of harm from the road." And striving through acts of worship — most of its purposes is the removal of harm from the road.

Now, one might say: The intended meaning of the hadith is the picking up of glass, bone, and stones from the streets, and that this is what springs first to the understanding of the majority. And another might say: People vary in their understanding of the meanings of words according to the variation of their ranks. For this reason, he, peace be upon him, said: «نضر الله أمرا سمع مقالتي فوعاها، ثم أداها كما سمعها، فرب حامل فقه غير فقيه ورب حامل فقه إلى من هو أفقه منه» — "May God brighten a man who hears my saying, comprehends it, then conveys it as he heard it; for perhaps a carrier of understanding (fiqh) is not himself a jurist (faqīh), and perhaps a carrier of understanding conveys it to one more juristic than he." Were it not that in his words there is what springs to the understanding of the non-jurist differently from what springs to the understanding of the jurist, he would not have emphasized the injunction thereby. Then, would that I knew — if the non-jurist understands something different from what springs to the understanding of the jurist, or the more juristic, or in a direction other than theirs? And there is no doubt that this is rare and uncommon, and the predominant is the contrary. So what springs to the understanding of the masses — the truth nearly shuns it, and inclines toward what the jurist and the more juristic understand, especially in a word that does not specify particularization. For the word "harm" (adhā) is general, and the word "road" (ṭarīq) is general. Had the specific been intended, he would have mentioned glass or clay and alerted to its likes. And that apparent meaning is also included under the generality, for by that very act one also reforms oneself, refines one's character, and removes from the soul the vice of heedlessness (ghaflah), the veil (ghishāwah), and the lack of compassion (qillat al-shafaqah) — as we shall mention in the detailing of evil and good traits of character.

You have thus known that the felicity of the soul and its perfection is that it be engraved with the divine realities of things (ḥaqā’iq al-umūr al-ilāhiyyah) and become united with them until it is as if it were they — and that this occurs only by the purification of the soul from vicious traits necessitated by appetite and anger, and that is through striving and action. So action is for purification, and purification is the condition of that perfection. For this reason, he, peace be upon him, said: «بني الدين على النظافة» — "Religion is built upon cleanliness."

chapters.title_en: Clarifying the Divergence of the Sufi Path from Others in the Domain of Knowledge
chapters.arabic_text:
### | بيان مفارقة طريق الصوفية

### | في جانب العلم طريق غيرهم:
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ف-ر-ق (f-r-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Separation, division, or distinction between two things; the act of parting or differentiating.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, denotes a categorical distinction in method or essence, not mere superficial difference.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — physical separation; metaphorical (majāz) — divergence in doctrine or practice.
- Root: ص-و-ف (ṣ-w-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Wool (ṣūf); by extension, the wearer of wool — the ascetic.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The Sufi path (ṭarīqah) as a disciplined spiritual method, distinct from speculative theology.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — wool garment; metaphorical — the inner purification and renunciation signified by it.
- Root: ع-ل-م (ʿ-l-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Knowledge, perception, or cognition; the act of knowing.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Kalām, ʿilm is certain cognition (yaqīn) as opposed to conjecture (ẓann); here, the theoretical knowledge of the scholastic theologians.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — acquired knowledge; metaphorical — the path of discursive reasoning (naẓar) as opposed to direct spiritual unveiling (kashf).
- Sībawayh Rule: **Bayān al-Tamyīz** (Clarification of Distinction) — The construction "بيان مفارقة" (bayān mufāraqah) functions as a genitive annexation (iḍāfah) where the first term (bayān) governs the second (mufāraqah), indicating an explanatory exposition of a separation, with the following prepositional phrase (fī jānib al-ʿilm) specifying the domain of that separation.
chapters.translation: I say: Now we must clarify the manner in which the path of the Sufis diverges from the path of others — namely, in the domain of knowledge (ʿilm). For the Sufis do not traverse the road of discursive reasoning (naẓar) and speculative theology (kalām), nor do they rely upon the acquired sciences of the scholastics. Rather, their way in knowledge is distinct and separate, as will be made evident.

chapters.title_en: The Divergence Between the Sufi Path and the Path of the Theologians (Mīzān al-ʿAmal, Section 10)
chapters.arabic_text:
اعلم أن جانب العمل متفق عليه، وأنه مقصود لمحو الصفات الردية، وتطهير
النفس من الأخلاق السيئة. ولكن جانب العلم مختلف فيه، وتباين فيه طرق
الصوفية طرق النظار، من أهل العلم. فإن الصوفية لم يحرضوا على تحصيل العلوم
ودراستها، وتحصيل ما صنفه المصنفون في البحث عن حقائق الأمور،
بل قالوا: الطريق تقديم المجاهدة بمحو الصفات المذمومة وقطع العلائق
كلها، والإقبال بكل الهمة على الله تعالى. ومهما حصل ذلك فاضت عليه الرحمة،
وانكشف له سر الملكوت، وظهرت له الحقائق. وليس عليه إلا الاستعداد بالتصفية
المجردة، وإحضار النية، مع الإرادة الصادقة والتعطش  التام، والترصد
بالانتظار لما يفتحه الله تعالى من الرحمة. إذ الأولياء والأنبياء انكشفت
لهم الأمور، وسعدت نفوسهم بنيل كمالها الممكن لها، لا بالتعلم بل بالزهد في
الدنيا والإعراض والتبري عن علائقها، والاقبال بكل الهمة على الله تعالى.
فمن كان لله كان الله له، حتى أن في الوقت الذي صدقت فيه رغبتي لسلوك هذا
الطريق، شاورت متبوعا مقدما من الصوفية في المواظبة على تلاوة القرآن،
فمنعني وقال: السيل أن تقطع علائقك من الدنيا بالكلية، بحيث لا يلتفت قلبك
إلى أهل وولد ومال ووطن وعلم وولاية، بل تصير إلى حالة يستوي عندك وجودها
وعدمها، ثم تخلو بنفسك في زاوية تقتصر من العبادة على الفرائض والرواتب،
وتجلس فارغ القلب مجموع الهم، مقبلا بذكرك على الله تعالى.
وذلك في أول الأمر، بأن تواظب باللسان على ذكر الله تعالى، فلا تزال
تقول: الله الله، مع حضور القلب وإدراكه، إلى أن تنتهي إلى حالة لو تركت
تحريك اللسان، لرأيت كأن الكلمة جارية على لسانك، لكثرة اعتياده. ثم تصير
مواظبا عليه إلى أن يمحى أثر اللسان، فتصادف نفسك وقلبك مواظبين على هذا
الذكر، من غير حركة اللسان. ثم تواظب إلى أن لا يبقى في قلبك إلا معنى
اللفظ، ولا يخطر ببالك حروف اللفظ، وهيئات الكلمة، بل يبقى المعنى المجرد
حاضرا في قلبك على اللزوم والدوام. ولك اختيار إلى هذا الحد فقط، ولا
اختيار بعده لك، إلا في استدامة لدفع الوساوس الصارفة. ثم ينقطع اختيارك،
فلا يبقى لك إلا الانتظار لما يظهر من فتوح، ظهر مثله للأولياء، وهو بعض ما
يظهر للأنبياء، قد يكون أمرا كالبرق الخاطف لا يثبت ثم يعود، وقد يتأخر.
فإن عاد فقد يتظاهر أمثاله على التلاحق، وقد لا يقتصر على فن واحد، ومنازل
أولياء الله فيه لا تحصى، لتفاوت خلقهم وأخلاقهم.
فهذا منهج الصوفية، وقد ردوا الأمر إلى تطهير محض من جانبك، وتصفية
وجلاء، ثم استعداد وانتظار فقط. وأما النظار فلم ينكروا وجود هذا الطريق،
وافضاءه إلى
المقصد، وهو أكبر أحوال الأولياء والأنبياء، ولكن  استوعروا هذا الطريق،
واستبعدوا فضاءه إلى المقصود، وزعموا أن محو العلائق إلى ذلك الحد
بالاجتهاد كالممتنع، وإن حصل في حالة، فثباته أبعد منه، وأدنى إلى ذلك الحد
بالاجتهاد كالممتنع، وإن حصل في حالة، فثباته أبعد منه، وأدنى وسواس وخاطر
يشوش. وفي أثناء هذه المجاهدة قد يفسد المزاج، ويختلط العقل ويمرض البدن،
ويفضي إلى الماليخوليا.
فإذا لم تكن النفس قد ارتاضت بالعلوم الحقيقة البرهانية، اكتسبت بالخاطر
خيالات تظنها حقائق تنزل عليها. فكم من صوفي بقي في خيال واحد عشر سنين،
إلى أن تخلص عنه. ولو كان قد أتقن العلوم أولا، لتخلص منه على البديهة.
فالاشتغال بتحصيل العلوم بمعرفة معيار العلم، وتحصيل براهين العلوم المفصلة
أولى، فإنه يسوق إلى المقصود سياقة موثوقا بها، كما يوثق بالاجتهاد، في أن
يحصل فقه النفس. وقد كان، عليه السلام، فقيه النفس من غير اجتهاد، لكن لو
أراد مريد أن ينال رتبته بمجرد الرياضة، فقد توقع بعيدا، فيجب تحصيل نفس
العلوم الحقيقة في النفس، بطريق البحث والنظر على غاية الإمكان، وذلك
بتحصيل ما حصله الأولون أولا. ثم لا بأس بعد ذلك بالانتظار لما لم ينكشف
للعلماء
الباحثين عن الأمور الآلهية، فما لم ينكشف للخلق أكثر مما انكشف. وهذا
تباين الفريقين. وقد خطر لي مثال لا يبعد أن يكون منبها للافهام الضعيفة،
المفتقرة إلى الأمثلة المحسوسة، في درك الحقائق العقلية، ومعرفا لوجه الفرق
بين الفريقين. فقد حكي أن أهل الصين والروم تباهوا بحسن صناعة النقش
والتصوير، بين يدي بعض الملوك، فاستقر رأي الملك على أن يسلم إليهم صفة
ينقش أهل الصين منها جانبا، وأهل الروم جانبا، ويرخي بينهم حجاب، بحيث لا
يطلع كل فريق على صاحبه، فإذا فرغوا رفع الحجاب، ونظر إلى الجانبن، وعرف
رجحان من رجح من الفريقين، ففعل ذلك، فجمع أهل الروم من الأصباغ الغريبة ما
لا ينحصر، ودخل أهل الصين وراء الحجاب من غير صبغ، وهم يجلون جانبهم
ويصقلونه، والناس يتعجبون من توانيهم في طلب الصبغ. فلما فرغ أهل الروم
ادعى أهل الصين أننا أيضا  قد فرغنا. فقيل لهم: كيف فرغتم ولم يكن معكم صبغ،
ولا اشتغلتم بنقش؟ فقالوا: ما عليكم ارفعوا الحجاب، وعلينا تصحيح دعوانا.
فرفعوا الحجاب، وإذا بجانبهم وقد تلألأ فيه جميع الأصباغ الرومية الغريبة،
إذ قد صار كالمرآة لكثرة التصفية
والجلاء، فازداد حسن جانبهم بمزيد الصفاء، وظهر فيه ما سعى من تحصيله
غيرهم. فقدر كأن النفس محل نقش العلوم الآلهية، ولك في تحصيله طريقان:
أحدهما تحصيل عين النقش، كطريق أهل الروم والثاني الاستعداد لقبول النقش من
خارج. والخارج ههنا اللوح المحفوظ، ونفوس الملائكة، فإنها منقوشة بالعلوم
الحقيقية نقشا بالفعل على الدوام، كما أن دماغك منقوش بالقرآن كله، إن كنت
حافظا له، وكذلك جملة علومك، لا نقشا يحس ويبصر، ولكن نوعا من الانتقاش
عقليا، ينكره من اقتصرت به خساسة نفسه على المحسوسات ولم يترق عنها.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ج-ه-د (j-h-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Exertion of effort to the utmost degree; striving against hardship.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Spiritual warfare against the lower self (nafs) and its blameworthy traits; the practical counterpart to theoretical knowledge (ʿilm).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in the sense of physical/military exertion; metaphorical here for the soul's struggle against its own attributes.
- Root: ص-ف-و (ṣ-f-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Purity, clarity, being free from admixture; the essence of something after refinement.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Purification of the heart from all attachments save God; the precondition for divine disclosure (kashf).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for strained liquids; metaphorical for the soul's refinement to mirror-like transparency.
- Root: ك-ش-ف (k-sh-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Removal of a covering; unveiling.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The unveiling of metaphysical realities (ḥaqāʾiq) granted to saints and prophets as divine gift, not acquired merit.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for lifting a veil; metaphorical for intellectual/spiritual disclosure.
- Root: ن-ظ-ر (n-ẓ-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Gazing, examining, deliberating.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Rational inquiry and demonstrative reasoning (naẓar) as the method of the theologians (mutakallimūn).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for visual sight; metaphorical for intellectual contemplation.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text employs intricate conditional chains (e.g., "if... then... until...") and exceptions ("no choice except...") to delineate the stages of spiritual progress, requiring careful parsing of the apodosis and protasis.
chapters.translation:
Know that the aspect of action [in the religious life] is agreed upon [by all parties], and that it is intended for the erasure of blameworthy attributes and the purification of the soul from evil character traits. But the aspect of knowledge is disputed, and therein the paths of the Sufis diverge from the paths of the speculative theologians (al-nuẓẓār) among the people of learning. For the Sufis did not urge the acquisition of the sciences and their study, nor the mastery of what the authors have composed in the investigation of the realities of things. Rather, they said: The way is the prioritization of spiritual striving (mujāhadah) through the erasure of blameworthy attributes and the severance of all attachments, and the turning with one's entire resolve toward God, exalted be He. And whenever that is attained, mercy pours down upon him, the secret of the dominion (malakūt) is unveiled to him, and the realities appear to him. And upon him is nothing but readiness through pure purification, the presence of intention, with sincere will and complete thirst, and the watchful waiting for what God, exalted be He, opens up of mercy. For the saints and the prophets — the matters were unveiled to them, and their souls were blessed with the attainment of their possible perfection, not through learning, but through renunciation of this world, turning away from it, and disavowal of its attachments, and the turning with one's entire resolve toward God, exalted be He. So whoever is for God, God is for him — to the point that at the very time when my desire became sincere to tread this path, I consulted a leading master (mutabbaʿ) among the Sufis regarding persevering in the recitation of the Qurʾān, and he forbade me, saying: The proper course is that you sever your attachments from this world entirely, such that your heart pays no heed to family, child, wealth, homeland, learning, or rank; rather, you reach a state where their existence and non-existence are equal to you. Then you seclude yourself in a corner, restricting your worship to the obligatory acts and the supererogatory routines (rawātib), and you sit with an empty heart, gathered in resolve, turning your remembrance toward God, exalted be He.

And that is at the beginning of the matter: that you persevere with the tongue in the remembrance of God, exalted be He, and you do not cease saying: "Allāh, Allāh," with the heart's presence and its awareness, until you reach a state where, if you were to abandon the movement of the tongue, you would see as though the word were flowing upon your tongue, due to the frequency of its habituation. Then you persevere upon it until the trace of the tongue is effaced, and you find your self and your heart persevering upon this remembrance, without the movement of the tongue. Then you persevere until there remains not in your heart but the meaning of the word, and the letters of the word and the forms of the utterance do not occur to your mind; rather, the bare meaning remains present in your heart with constancy and permanence. And you have choice only up to this limit; and there is no choice for you after it, except in the continuation of repelling the distracting whisperings (wasāwis). Then your choice is cut off, and there remains for you nothing but the waiting for what appears of the openings (futūḥ), the like of which appeared to the saints — and it is a portion of what appears to the prophets. It may be a thing like the flashing lightning that does not abide, then returns; and it may be delayed. And if it returns, then its likes may follow in succession; and it may not be confined to a single domain. And the stations of the saints of God therein are beyond enumeration, due to the disparity of their natures and their character traits.

So this is the method of the Sufis, and they have reduced the matter to pure purification on your side, and refinement and polishing, then readiness and waiting only. As for the speculative theologians, they did not deny the existence of this path, nor its leading to the goal — for it is the greatest of the states of the saints and the prophets — but they deemed this path arduous, and deemed it far-fetched that it should lead to the intended end. And they claimed that the erasure of attachments to that limit through striving is as though impossible; and if it occurs in some state, its persistence is even more remote than it. And the least whisper or passing thought disturbs it. And in the midst of this striving, the temperament may be corrupted, the intellect may become disordered, the body may fall ill, and it may lead to melancholia (mālīkhūliyā).

So if the soul has not been disciplined by the true demonstrative sciences, it acquires, through the passing thought, fancies that it supposes to be realities, and it descends upon them. How many a Sufi has remained in a single fancy for ten years, until he was delivered from it. And had he mastered the sciences first, he would have been delivered from it by immediate intuition (badīhah). So the occupation with the acquisition of the sciences — through knowledge of the criterion of knowledge, and the acquisition of the detailed demonstrations of the sciences — is more fitting, for it drives one to the intended end with a trustworthy driving, just as one trusts in striving, in that the jurisprudence of the soul (fiqh al-nafs) is attained. And he, peace be upon him, was a jurist of the soul without striving; but if a seeker wished to attain his rank through mere spiritual exercise alone, he would have hoped for something remote. So it is obligatory to acquire the true sciences themselves in the soul, by way of investigation and contemplation, to the utmost of possibility — and that is through the acquisition of what the predecessors acquired first. Then, after that, there is no harm in waiting for what was not unveiled to the scholars who investigate the divine matters — for what was not unveiled to creation is more than what was unveiled. And this is the divergence of the two parties.

And there has occurred to me an example that is not unlikely to be an alert for weak intellects, which are in need of sensible examples for grasping intellectual realities, and a means of recognizing the manner of the difference between the two parties. For it has been related that the people of China and the people of Rūm boasted of the excellence of the craft of engraving and painting before a certain king. So the king's opinion settled upon handing over to them a chamber: the people of China would engrave one side of it, and the people of Rūm the other side, and a curtain would be let down between them, such that neither party could see the other. And when they finished, the curtain would be raised, and he would look at both sides, and recognize the superiority of whichever of the two parties was superior. So he did that. The people of Rūm gathered an incalculable array of rare pigments, while the people of China entered behind the curtain without any pigment, and they were polishing their side and burnishing it, while the people marveled at their negligence in seeking pigments. And when the people of Rūm finished, the people of China claimed: "We too have finished." So it was said to them: "How have you finished, when you had no pigment with you, nor did you occupy yourselves with engraving?" They said: "It is not upon you — raise the curtain, and upon us is the verification of our claim." So they raised the curtain, and lo, their side was gleaming with all the rare pigments of Rūm, for it had become like a mirror through the abundance of polishing and burnishing. So the beauty of their side increased by the excess of clarity, and there appeared in it what the others had striven to produce. So consider: as though the soul is the locus of the engraving of the divine sciences, and you have two ways in its acquisition: one is the acquisition of the very engraving itself, like the way of the people of Rūm; and the second is the readiness to receive the engraving from without. And "without" here is the Preserved Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ) and the souls of the angels, for they are engraved with the true sciences with an actual engraving perpetually — just as your brain is engraved with the entire Qurʾān, if you are a memorizer of it, and likewise the totality of your sciences — not an engraving that is sensed and seen, but a kind of intellectual impression, which is denied by one whose base nature has confined him to the sensible things and has not risen above them.

chapters.title_en: Clarifying the Preferable of the Two Paths
chapters.arabic_text:
### | بيان الأولى من الطريقين

فإن قلت: فقد مهدت للسعادة طريقين متباينين، فأيهما أولى عندك؟ فاعلم أن
الحكم في مثل هذه الأمور بحسب الاجتهاد الذي يقتضيه حال المجتهد، ومقامه
الذي هو فيه. والحق الذي يلوح لي، والعلم عند الله فيه، إن الحكم بالنفي أو
الإثبات في هذا على الإطلاق خطأ، بل يختلف بالإضافة إلى الأشخاص والأحوال.
فكل من رغب في السلوك، فقد كبر شأنه، فالأولى به أن يقتنع بطريق الصوفية،
وهو المواظبة على العبادة، وقطع العلائق. فإن البحث عن العلوم الكسبية
لتحصل ملكة كتابته في النفس شديد، ولا يتيسر إلا في عنفوان العمر، والتعلم
في الصغر كالنقش على الحجر. ومن العناء رياضة الهرم.
وقيل لأحد الأكابر: من أراد أن يتعلم شيخا، ما يفعل؟ فقال: إغسل مسخا
فعساه يبيض. وقد خرج من هذا أن الأولى بأكثر الخلق الاشتغال بالعمل
والاقتصاد من العلم على القدر الذي يعرف به العمل. فإن الأكثر لا ينتبهون
لهذا الأمر في عنفوان الشباب، وإن تنبه في عنفوان شبابه، نظر إلى طبعه
وذكائه. فإن علم أنه لا يستعد لفهم الحقائق العقلية الدقيقة، وجب عليه أن
يشتغل بالعمل أيضا، فلا فائدة في اشتغاله بالعلوم النظرية، وهم الأكثرون من
الأقل، الذي تتبعناه. فإن ذكيا قابلا للعلوم، فإن لم يكن في بلده أو في
العصر مستقل بالعلوم النظرية، مترق عن رتبة تقليد من سبقه، فالأولى به
العمل. فإن هذه لا يمكن تحصيلها إلا بمعلم، فليس في القوة البشرية، في شخص
واحد، الوصول إليها إلا قليل بطول الزمن. ولذلك لو لم يكن علم الطب مثلا
صار متقنا بالخواطر المتعاونة، في الأزمنة المتطاولة، لافتقر أذكى الناس
إلى عمر طويل، في معرفة علاج علة واحدة، فضلا عن الجميع. والغالب في البلاد
الخلو عن مثل هذا العالم المستقل.
فإذن لم يبق إلا قليل من قليل وهو ذكي تنبه في عنفوان عمره لهذا الأمر،
وهو مستعد لفهم العلوم، وصادف عالما مستقلا بالعلوم تحقيقا لا إسما، وحسبة
لا رسما، كما ترى أكثر العلماء، فهم إما مقلدون في أعيان المذاهب، أو في
أعيان المذاهب وأدلة تلك المذاهب جميعا، على الوجه الذي تلقوه من أرباب
المذاهب. ومن قلد أعمى، فلا خير في متابعة العميان وأتباعهم أو شاب نشأ في
طلب العلم وهو زكي في نفسه، وتنبه له بعد الارتياض بأنواع العلوم، ولكن
بهذا النوع من العلم الذي تنبه له، فمثل هذا الشخص مستعد للطريقين جميعا.
فالأولى به أن يقدم طريق التعلم، فيحصل من العلوم البرهانية ما للقوة
البشرية إدراكه بالجهد والتعلم، فقد كفى المؤنة فيه تعب من قبله، فإذا حصل
ذلك على قدر إمكانه، حتى لم يبق علم من جنس هذه العلوم، إلا وقد حصله، فلا
بأس بعده أن يؤثر الاعتزال عن هذا الخلق، والإعراض عن الدنيا، والتجرد لله
وأن ينتظر، فعساه ينفتح له بذلك الطريق ما التبس على سالكي هذا الطريق. هذا
ما أراه، والعلم عند الله.
وقد يخرج منه أن الصواب لأكثر الاشتغال بالعمل،
ومن العمل العلم العملي أعني ما يعرف به كيفيته. فإن العلم العملي ليس
بأشرف من العمل، بل هو دونه، فإن مراد له دون العلم الذي يراد منه المعلوم،
كالعلم بالله وملائكته وكتبه ورسله والعلم بالنفس وصفاتها. والعلم بملكوت
السموات والأرض وغيره. فهذه  العلوم نظرية، وليست بعملية وإن كان قد ينتفع
بها في العمل، على سبيل العرض، لا على سبيل القصد، ولكون الصواب في العمل
لأكثر الخلق استقصاء النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم، تفصيلا وتأصيلا، حتى علم
الخلق الاستنجاء وكيفيته، ولما آل الأمر إلى العلوم النظرية أجمل ولم يفصل،
ولم يذكر من صفات الله إلا أنه ليس كمثله شيء وهو السميع البصير. نعم بعد
إجمال العلم، ذكر من تعظيمه وتشريفه وتقديمه على العمل ما لا يكاد يحصى
كقوله: " تفكر ساعة خير من عبادة سنة " وكقوله: " فضل العالم على العابد،
كفضل القمر ليلة البدر " إلى غير ذلك مما ورد فيه. ثم ذلك العلم المقدم على
العمل لا يخلو أما أن يكون هو العلم بكيفية العمل وهو الفقه وعلم العبادات
وأما أن يكون علما سواه. وباطل أن يكون الأول هو المراد لوجهين:
أحدهما أنه فضل العالم على العابد، والعابد هو الذي له العلم بالعبادة
وإلا فهو عابد فاسق. والثاني: أن العلم بالعمل لا يكون أشرف من العمل لأن
العلم العملي لا يراد لنفسه، وإنما يراد للعمل. وما يراد لغيره يستحيل أن
يكون أشرف منه.

### | بيان جنس العلم والعمل الموصلين إلى جنة المأوى
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ق-ص-د (qaṣada)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Intentional aiming, directing one's course toward a goal; the middle way.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The deliberate orientation of the soul's striving (irādah) toward an end, distinguishing essential from accidental aims.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical heading; metaphorical: the soul's purposive pursuit of felicity (saʿādah).
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional-Responsive Construction (al-sharṭ wa-l-jawāb) — the protasis "fa-in qulta" governs the apodosis with "fa-aʿlam," marking a dialectical turn requiring the reader's assent before the author's verdict.
chapters.translation:
I say: If you say, "You have laid out two divergent paths to felicity—which of the two is preferable in your view?"—then know that the judgment in such matters depends upon the personal exertion of judgment (ijtihād) warranted by the state of the one who exercises it, and the station in which he finds himself. The truth that appears to me—and knowledge of it rests with God—is that an unqualified verdict of negation or affirmation here is an error; rather, it varies relative to persons and circumstances.

Whoever has earnestly desired to tread the path, his matter has become grave. For such a one, the preferable course is to content himself with the way of the Sufis—namely, persevering in worship and severing worldly attachments. For the pursuit of the acquired sciences, so as to engender a firm disposition (malakah) of them in the soul, is arduous, and it is not facilitated except in the prime of youth; learning in childhood is like engraving upon stone, while disciplining the decrepit is sheer toil. It was said to one of the great masters: "If a man wishes to learn in his old age, what should he do?" He replied: "Wash a black garment—perhaps it will turn white."

From this it emerges that the preferable course for most creatures is to occupy themselves with action, and to take from knowledge only so much as suffices to know how to act. For most do not awaken to this matter in the prime of their youth; and if one does awaken in his prime, he must then look to his natural temperament and his intelligence. If he knows that he is not disposed to grasp the subtle rational verities, then he too is obliged to occupy himself with action—there is no benefit in his engaging in theoretical sciences. Such are the majority of that minority which we have been tracing.

But if he is intelligent and receptive to the sciences, yet in his land or in his age there is no one independent in the theoretical sciences, rising above the rank of mere imitation (taqlīd) of those before him, then action is preferable for him. For these sciences cannot be acquired except through a teacher; it is not within human power, for a single individual, to reach them except in small measure over a long span of time. For this reason, had the science of medicine, for example, not been perfected through the cooperating reflections of many across protracted ages, the most intelligent of men would need a lifetime merely to know the treatment of a single ailment—let alone all of them. And the common state of the lands is to be devoid of such an independent scholar.

Thus there remains only a rare few of the rare—one who is intelligent, awakened in the prime of his life to this matter, disposed to grasp the sciences, and who encounters a scholar truly independent in the sciences—in reality, not merely in name; in earnestness, not in form—as you see most scholars are: either imitators regarding the very doctrines of the schools, or imitators regarding both the doctrines and all their proofs, exactly as they received them from the school authorities. Whoever imitates blindly—there is no good in following the blind and their followers.

Or [there is] a youth who grew up seeking knowledge, himself intelligent, and awakened to this matter after having been disciplined in various sciences—but not in this particular kind of science to which he has now awakened. Such a person is disposed to both paths alike. For him, the preferable course is to advance along the path of learning, acquiring from the demonstrative sciences (al-ʿulūm al-burhāniyyah) whatever human power can grasp through effort and study; for the burden of that has been borne by the toil of those before him. When he has attained that to the extent of his capacity, until no science of that kind remains unmastered, then there is no harm thereafter in his choosing seclusion from mankind, turning away from the world, devoting himself wholly to God, and waiting—perhaps that path will open to him which remained obscure to those who trod it. This is what I see; and knowledge rests with God.

From this it may also be derived that the correct course for most is to occupy themselves with action—and from action, with practical knowledge (al-ʿilm al-ʿamalī), that is, knowledge by which one learns its modality. For practical knowledge is not nobler than action; rather, it is beneath it, since it is sought for the sake of action—unlike that knowledge which is sought for the sake of the known object itself, such as knowledge of God, His angels, His books, His messengers, knowledge of the soul and its attributes, and knowledge of the dominion (malakūt) of the heavens and the earth and other such things. These are theoretical sciences, not practical—even though one may benefit from them in action incidentally, not as a primary intent.

And because the correct course for most creatures lies in action, the Prophet (peace be upon him) was exhaustive in detailing and grounding it—to the point that he taught people the manner of cleansing after relieving oneself. But when it came to the theoretical sciences, he was concise and did not elaborate; he mentioned of God's attributes only that {«لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ وَهُوَ السَّمِيعُ الْبَصِيرُ»} ("there is nothing like unto Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing") {Q 42:11}. Indeed, after this concision regarding knowledge, he mentioned of its glorification, honor, and precedence over action what can scarcely be enumerated—such as his saying: "An hour of reflection is better than a year of worship," and his saying: "The superiority of the scholar over the worshiper is like the superiority of the moon on the night of the full moon," and other such reports.

Now, that knowledge which is preferred over action must be either: (a) knowledge of the modality of action—namely jurisprudence (fiqh) and the science of devotional acts—or (b) knowledge other than that. It is false that the first is intended, for two reasons:

First: he extolled the scholar over the worshiper—yet the worshiper is precisely one who possesses knowledge of worship; otherwise he would be a sinful worshiper.

Second: knowledge of action cannot be nobler than action itself, because practical knowledge is not sought for its own sake, but only for the sake of action. And that which is sought for the sake of something else cannot possibly be nobler than that for which it is sought.

### | Clarifying the Kind of Knowledge and Action That Lead to the Garden of Refuge
