And just as the body in its beginning is not created complete, but only becomes complete through growth and nurture by food, so likewise the soul is created deficient, and only becomes complete through purification (tazkiyah), refinement of character (tahdhīb al-akhlāq), and nourishment by knowledge. And just as the body — if it is healthy, the physician’s task is to lay down the regimen that preserves health, but if it is sick, his task is to bring health back to it — so likewise, O soul, if you are pure, clean, and refined in character, you ought to strive to preserve your health and to bring to yourself increased strength and clarity. And just as the ailment that alters equilibrium and necessitates sickness is not treated except by its opposite — if it be from heat, then by cold, and vice versa — so likewise the vice that necessitates the soul’s deficiency is treated by its opposite, as previously mentioned: ignorance by learning, miserliness by deliberate generosity (tasakhkhī takallufan), pride by deliberate humility (tawāḍuʿ takallufan), and gluttony by abstaining from the desired thing deliberately. And just as not every cooling agent suffices for an ailment caused by heat, unless it be in a specific measure, and this varies by intensity and weakness, by continuity and its absence, and by abundance and scarcity — and there must be a standard (miʿyār) by which the beneficial amount is measured, for if its standard is not preserved, corruption increases — so likewise the opposite trait by which character is treated must have a standard. And just as the standard of the medicine is derived from the standard of the ailment — so that the physician does not treat until he knows whether the ailment is from heat or cold, and if it be heat, what its degree is, whether weak or strong — and when he knows this, he then attends to the conditions of the body, the conditions of the time, and the occupation the patient is engaged in, and treats accordingly — so likewise the revered elder (al-shaykh al-matbūʿ), who seeks the souls of aspirants (murīdīn) and seekers of guidance, ought not to rush upon them with spiritual exercises (riyāḍāt) and obligations in a particular discipline until he knows their characters. When he knows what dominates the aspirant of evil character, and knows its measure, and observes his condition and age, and what he can bear of treatment, he then prescribes for him the path. For this reason, you see the elder directing some aspirants to go out to the marketplace to beg — this is because he discerns in him a kind of love of leadership and pride, so he treats him with what he sees as humiliation, which is the opposite of his trait, so that his pride is broken by it. And he directs some of them to attend to the latrine and prepare the stones for cleansing — this is when he sees his soul inclining toward vanity in cleanliness that exceeds the limit of moderation. And he may direct him to fasting and command him to fast continuously (wiṣāl), except to the extent that would fall under the prohibition — this is when he sees him as a young man of strong appetite, addicted to the pleasures of the belly and the private parts. And so on with other methods of refinement.

And it is related of some of them that he treated the power of anger and deliberately cultivated the trait of forbearance (ḥilm): he would pay fools a wage to insult him in gatherings, so that he would become accustomed to enduring it, until he became a proverb in forbearance. Another trained himself in courage by riding the sea in winter. Another would prepare delicious foods and feed them to others in his presence while he confined himself to barley bread, to break his gluttony. And the worshippers of India treat laziness in worship by standing the entire night on one leg without shifting from it. Another treated his love of wealth by selling all his possessions and throwing their price into the sea.

This, then, is a general path in the refinement of character; the detailed discussion of it would be lengthy. The purpose is that you, O aspirant to the purification of your soul, should examine your own character traits. If they are refined, preserve them; if they are inclined [toward excess or deficiency], rectify them by returning them to the limit of moderation, as will be detailed hereafter. For the purpose of attaining moderation is the removal of the two extremes, since the goal is to purify the soul of those attributes that attach it to the accidents of the body, so that after separation [from the body] it does not turn toward them, loving and regretting its strength, and prevented by occupation and pain with them from the felicities befitting its essence. And whenever we wish water to be neither hot nor cold, we seek in it moderation, and lukewarm is neither hot nor cold — so likewise are these attributes.

If you say: “By what means do I know that what I have attained is the beautiful character (al-khulq al-jamīl), which is the moderate mean between the two extremes of excess and deficiency?” — Then your way is to examine the actions that this character, which you are struggling over, necessitates. If you take delight in its action, then know that the character necessitating it is firmly rooted in your soul. If that action is ugly, then know that the character is ugly — for example, if you delight in hoarding and accumulating wealth, its necessitating cause is the trait of miserliness (bukhl); so accustom your soul to its opposite. The good and evil character traits have been detailed by the Sacred Law (al-sharʿ), and what encompasses them is what has been compiled on the etiquette (ādāb) of the Prophet, peace be upon him; these are well-known, and we shall indicate their general principles.

And by moderation (iʿtidāl) I mean: if you were to delight in extravagance in dispersing wealth, know that this too is blameworthy — it is what is called prodigality (tabdhīr). The praiseworthy moderate trait is generosity (sakhāʾ), which lies between parsimony (taḥarruq) and prodigality — namely, that spending what the Sacred Law and reason require to be spent becomes easy for you, willingly and with desire. And likewise for all other traits; a single example suffices. And when you know that the standard of actions is derived from the measure of traits and characters, it will not be hidden from you that the path in this matter varies with the variation of persons, and varies for a single person with the variation of circumstances. Whoever is granted insight (baṣīrah) follows the cause and treats it by its proper way. And since most people are incapable of this, and it was difficult for the Sacred Law to provide a detailed prescription covering all persons in all ages, the Sacred Law confined its detailed prescriptions to the common principles (al-qawānīn al-mushtarakah) whose benefit is general — namely, acts of obedience and abstention from forbidden sins. Then it discouraged the permissible indulgences (mubāḥāt) sought for delight in beautiful things, as in his saying, peace be upon him: “Love of the world is the head of every sin,” and similar sayings. Then it acquainted the people of insight with the ultimate goal and its path, and the ultimate danger and its path, and stopped them at the detailed prescriptions, and guided to them whoever was granted success in following them. Thus they became deputies (nuwwāb) of the prophets in detailing what the prophets summarized and explaining what they established. For this reason, he said, peace be upon him: {«العلماء ورثة الأنبياء»} (“The scholars are the heirs of the prophets”).

chapters.title_en: Exposition of the Mother Virtues
chapters.arabic_text: ### | بيان أمهات الفضائل
chapters.anchors:
- Root: أ-م-م (ʾ-m-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: "Mother" (umm) as origin, source, or principal foundation; that to which all else returns and from which branches derive.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, "ummahāt" (mothers) denotes primary principles or archetypes—here, the cardinal virtues from which all subsidiary moral excellences (faḍāʾil) are generated.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is maternal lineage; metaphorical (majāz) extension applies to foundational, generative roots—not mere examples but causal origins.
- Sībawayh Rule: ʾIḍāfah (Construct State) — "Ummahāt al-faḍāʾil" is a genitive annexation where the first term (ummahāt) is grammatically indefinite but semantically definite through the second term (al-faḍāʾil), indicating a fixed, exhaustive set of principles.
chapters.translation: I say: Know that the virtues (al-faḍāʾil) are many in their branches, but their roots are few. For every praiseworthy trait (khulq maḥmūd) traces back to one of four mother virtues (ummahāt al-faḍāʾil), which are the sources of all moral excellences. These are: wisdom (ḥikmah), courage (shajāʿah), temperance (ʿiffah), and justice (ʿadālah). From these four, all other virtues branch forth, just as all acts of worship and habits of excellence derive from them. Whoever attains these four has attained the perfection of moral character, and whoever is deprived of them is deprived of the foundation of all goodness.

chapters.title_en: The Four Cardinal Virtues and Their Extremes
chapters.arabic_text:
الفضائل، وإن كانت كثيرة فتجمعها أربعة تشمل شعبها وأنواعها، وهي الحكمة،
والشجاعة، والعفة، والعدالة. فالحكمة فضيلة القوة العقلية، والشجاعة فضيلة
القوة الغضبية، والعفة فضيلة القوة الشهوانية، والعدالة عبارة عن وقوع هذه
القوى على الترتيب الواجب فيها تتم جميع الأمور، ولذلك قيل: بالعدل قامت
السموات والأرض.
فلنشرح آحاد هذه الأمهات، ثم لنشرح بيانها وما ينطوي من الأنواع تحتها.
فأما الحكمة فنعني  بها مع عظم الله تعالى في قوله: (ومن يؤت الحكمة فقد
أوتي خيرا كثيرا) .
وما أراده رسول الله حيث قال: " الحكمة ضالة المؤمن ". وهي منسوبة إلى
القوة العقلية، وقد عرفت فيما سبق، أن للنفس قوتين: إحداهما تلي جهة فوق،
وهي التي بها تتلقى حقائق العلوم الكلية الضرورية والنظرية من الملأ
الأعلى، وهي العلوم اليقينية الصادقة أزلا وأبدا، لا تختلف باختلاف الأعصار
والأمم، كالعلم بالله تعالى وصفاته وملائكته وكتبه ورسله، وأضاف خلقه في
العالم. بل من جملة العلم أن النفي والاثبات لا يصدقان على شيء واحد في حال
واحدة، وكذلك العلوم الحقيقية. فهذه العلوم هي الحكمة الحقيقية. والقوة
الثانية هي التي تلي جهة تحت، أعني جهة البدن وتدبيره وسياسته، وبها تدرك
النفس الخيرات في الأعمال وتسمى العقل العملي، وبها يسوس قوى نفسه ويسوس
أهل بلده ومنزله، واسم الحكمة لها من وجه كالمجاز لأن معلوماتها كالزيبق
تتقلب ولا تثبت، فمن معلوماتها أن بذل المال فضيلة، وقد يصير رذيلة في بعض
الأوقات، وفي حق بعض الأشخاص. فلذلك كان اسم الحكمة بالأول أحق، وهذا
الثاني كالكمال والتتمة للأول، وهذه هي الحكمة الخلقية،
والأولى هي الحكمة العلمية النظرية، ونعني بالحكمة الخلقية حالة وفضيلة
للنفس العاقلة، بها تسوس القوة الغضبية والشهوانية، وتقدر حركاتها بالقدر
الواجب في الانقباض والانبساط، وهي العلم بصواب الأفعال. وهذه الفضيلة
تكتنفها رذيلتان، وهما الخب والبله، فهما طرفا إفراطها وتفريطها، أما الحب
فهو طرف إفراطها، وهو حالة يكون بها الإنسان ذا مكر وحيلة، بإطلاق الغضبية
والشهوانية يتحركان إلى المطلوب حركة زائدة على الواجب. وأما البله، فهو
طرف تفريطها ونقصانها عن الاعتدال. وهي حالة للنفس، تقصر بالغضبية
والشهوانية عن القدر الواجب، ومنشأه بطؤ الفهم، وقلة الاحاطة بصوب الأفعال.
وأما الشجاعة فهي فضيلة للقوة الغضبية، لكونها قوية، ومع قوة الحمية،
منقادة للعقل المتأدب بالشرع، في إقدامها وإحجامها، وهي وسط بين رذيلتيها
المطيفتين بها، وهما التهور والجبن. فالتهور لطرف الزيادة عن الاعتدال، وهي
الحالة التي بها يقدم الإنسان على الأمور المحظورة، التي يجب في العقل
الاحجام  عنها، وأما الجبن فلطرف النقصان، وهي حالة بها تنقص حركة
الغضبية عن القدر الواجب، فتصرف عن الإقدام حيث يجب الإقدام. ومهما حصلت
هذه الأخلاق، صدرت منها هذه الأفعال، أي يصدر من خلق الشجاعة الإقدام حيث
يجب وكما يجب، وهو الخلق الحسن المحمود، وإياه أريد بقوله تعالى: (أشداء
على الكفار رحماء بينهم) ، فلا الشدة في كل مقام محمودة، ولا الرحمة، بل
المحمود ما يوافق معيار العقل والشرع. فمن حصل له ذلك، فليحفظه بالمواظبة
على أفعاله. ومن لم يحصل له، فلينظر، فإن كان طبعه مائلا إلى النقصان الذي
هو الجبن، فليتعاط أفعال الشجعان، متكلفا مواظبا عليه، حتى يصير له
الاعتياد طبعا وخلقا، فيفيظ منه أفعال الشجعان بعد ذلك طبعا، وإن كان مائلا
إلى طرف الزيادة، وهو التهور، فليشعر نفسه بعواقب الأمور، وليعظم أخطارها،
وليتكلف الإحجام إلى الاعتدال، أو ما يقرب منه. فإن الوقوف على حد الاعتدال
شديد، ولو تصور ذلك، لارتحلت النفس عن البدن، وليس معها علاقة منه، فكانت
لا تتعذب أصلا بالتأسف على ما يفوتها منه،
وكان لا يتكدر عليها ابتهاجها بما يتجلى لها من جمال الحق وجلاله. ولكن
لما عسر ذلك قيل: (وإن منكم إلا واردها) . وقد رأى بعض المشايخ رسول الله
في المنام فقال: ما الذي أردت بقولك " شيبتني سورة هود "، فقال: قوله
(استقم كما أمرت) ، يعني الاستمرار على الصراط المستقيم. وطلب الوسط بين
هذه الأطراف شديد، وهو أدق من الشعر وأحد من السيف، كما وصف من حال الصراط
في الدار الآخرة، ومن استقام على الصراط في الدار الدنيا، استقام على
الصراط في الآخرة مستقيما، إذ يموت المرء على ما عاش عليه، ويحشر على ما
مات عليه. ولذلك وجب في كل ركعة من الصلاة قراءة الفاتحة المشتملة على
قوله: (إهدنا الصراط المستقيم) ، فإنه أعقد الأمور وأعصاها على الطالب. ولو
كلف ذلك في خلق واحد لطال العناء فيه. وقد كلفنا ذلك في جميع الأخلاق، مع
خروجها عن
الحصر، كما سيأتي. ولا مخلص عن هذه المحظورات إلا بتوفيق الله ورحمته
ولذلك  قال عليه السلام: " الناس كلهم موتى إلا العالمون! والعالمون كلهم
موتى إلا العاملون، والعاملون كلهم موتى إلا المخلصون، والمخلصون على خطر
عظيم "، فنسأل الله تعالى أن يمدنا بتوفيقه لنجاوز الأخطار في هذه الدار،
ولا ننخدع بدواعي الاغترار.
وأما العفة، فهي فضيلة القوة الشهوانية، وهي انقيادها على تيسر وسهولة
للقوة العقلية، حتى يكون انقباضها وانبساطها بحسب إشارتها، ويكتنفها
رذيلتان: الشره والخمود، فالشره هو إفراط الشهوة، إلى المبالغة في اللذات
التي تستقبحها القوة العقلية وتنهي عنها، والخمود هو خمود الشهوة عن
الانبعاث إلى ما يقتضي العقل نيله وتحصيله، وهما مذمومان، كما أن العفة
التي هي الوسط محمودة، وعلى الإنسان أن يراقب شهوته، والغالب عليها الإفراط
لا سيما إلى منقضى الفرج والبطن، وإلى المال والرياسة وحب الثناء، والإفراط
والتفريط في كل ذلك نقصان،
وإنما الكمال في الاعتدال، ومعيار الاعتدال العقل والشرع، وذلك أن يعلم
الغاية المطلوبة من خلق الشهوة والغضب، مثلا بأن يعلم أن شهوة الطعام، إنما
خلقت لتبعث على تناول الغذاء الذي يسد خلل ما ينحل من أجزائه بالحرارة
الغريزية، حتى يبقى البدن حيا والحواس سليمة، ليتوصل بالبدن إلى نيل
العلوم، ودرك حقائق الأمور، ويتشبه بالطبقة العليا بالإضافة إليه، وهي رتبة
الملائكة، وبها كمالها وسعادتها. ومن عرف هذا كان قصده من الطعام التقوى
على العبادة، دون التلذذ به، فيقتصر ويقتصد لا محالة، ولا يشتد إليه شرهه،
ويعلم أن شهوة الجماع خلقت فيه لتكون باعثة على الجماع الذي هو سبب بقاء
النوع محفوظا ليطلب النكاح للولد والتحصن، لا للعب والتمتع، وإن تمتع ولعب
كان باعثه عليه الآلف والاستمالة الباعثة على حسن الصحبة ودوام النكاح،
ويقتصر من الأنكحة على القدر الذي لا يعجزه عن القيام بحقوقه. ومن عرف ذلك
سهل عليه الاقتصار، وعند ذلك لا يقيس نفسه بصاحب الشرع عليه السلام، إذ كان
لا يشغله كثرة الأنكحة عن ذكر الله تعالى، ولا يلزمه طلب الدنيا لأجل
الأزواج. ومن ظن أن ما لا يضر صاحب الشرع لا يضره، كان كمن ظن أن ما لا
يغير  البحر الخضم من النجاسات، لا يغير كوزا مغترفا من البحر، وأن ما لا
يضر الشخص القوي البنية
السي من الأطعمة اللذيذة، لا يضر الصبي الرضيع السخيف البنية. وكم من
أحمق يتكايس، فيقيس نفسه بصاحب الشرع، مقايسة الملائكة بالحدادين، فيهلك من
حيث لا يدري. نعوذ بالله من عمش البصيرة، فإنه يكاد يكون أردى من العمى، إذ
الأعمى يعتقد عجزه فيقلد فيهديه غيره، والأعمش ينفتح من بصيرته بقدر ما
يستنكف به من الاتباع ثم لا يكمل نوره بحيث يستكمل مستمرا في سواء السبيل،
ومن هذه حاله لا يبالي الله في أي واد هلك.
ولقد رأيت جماعة من الحمقى العوام يتكايسون في التصوف بآرائهم ويزعمون أن
هذه الشهوات لم خلقت إن كان اتباعها مذموما ومهلكا، ولم يعلموا أن تحت خلق
الشهوتين، أعني شهوة الفرج والبطن، حكمتين عظيمتين: إحداهما إبقاء الشخص
بالغذاء والنوع بالحرث، فإنهما ضروريتان في الوجود بحكم إجراء الله سنته
بمشيئة الله الأزلية التي لا يجد لها تبديلا ولا تحويلا، والثانية ترغيب
الخلق في السعادات الآخروية، فإنهم ما لم يحسوا بهذه اللذات والآلام لم
يرغبوا في الجنة ولم يحذروا النار، ولو وعدوا بما لا عين رأت ولا أذن سمعت،
ولا خطر
على قلب بشر، لما أثر ذلك بمجرده في نفوسهم، هذا حد العفة.
وأما العدل فهو حالة للقوى الثلاث في انتظامها على التناسب، بحسب الترتيب
الواجب في الاستعلاء والانقياد، فليس هو جزءا من الفضائل، بل هو عبارة عن
جملة من الفضائل، فإنه مهما كان بين الملك وجنده ورعيته ترتيب محمود، بكون
الملك بصيرا قاهرا، وكون الجند ذوي قوة وطاعة، وكون الرعية ضعفاء سلسي
الانقياد، قيل: إن العدل قائم في البلد. ولن ينتظم العدل بأن يكون بعضهم
بهذه الصفات دون كلهم، وكذلك العدل في مملكة البدن بين هذه الصفات. والعدل
في أخلاق النفس يتبعه لا محالة العدل في المعاملة والسياسة، ويكون كالمتفرع
منه. ومعنى العدل الترتيب المستحب، إما في الأخلاق، وإما في حقوق
المعاملات، وإما في أجزاء ما به قوام البلد. والعدل في  المعاملة وسط بين
رزيلتي الغبن أن
يأخذ ما ليس له، والتغابن أن يعطي في المعاملة ما ليس عليه حمد وأجر.
والعد في السياسة أن ترتب أجزاء المدينة الترتيب المشاكل لترتيب أجزاء
النفس، حتى يكون المدينة في ائتلافها وتناسب أجزائها، وتعاون أركانها على
الغرض المطلوب من الاجتماع، كالشخص الواحد، فيوضع كل شيء موضعه، وينقسم
سكانه إلى مخدوم لا يخدم وإلى خادم ليس بمخدوم، وغلى طبقة يخدمون من وجه،
ويخدمون من وجه آخر، كما ذكرناه في قوى النفس. ولا يكتنف العدل رذيلتان، بل
رذيلة الجور المقابلة له، إذ ليس بين الترتيب وعدم الترتيب وسط، وبمثل هذا
الترتيب والعدل قامت السموات والأرض حتى صار العالم كله كالشخص الواحد،
متعاون القوى والأجزاء، وإذ قد ذكرنا جملة هذه الأمهات فلنذكر تفصيل ما
يندرج تحت كل فضيلة ورذيلة من أنواع الفضائل والرذائل، مبتدئين فيه بالقوة
العقلية، ثم الغضبية، ثم الشهوانية، ليكون ذلك أشفى في البيان.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح-ك-م (ḥ-k-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Firm judgment, preventing corruption; wisdom as putting things in their proper place
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The knowledge of realities through intellection; in Qur'anic usage, prophetic wisdom and sound judgment
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Ḥaqīqah — wisdom as genuine knowledge of eternal verities; majāz — practical wisdom whose objects are mutable
- Root: ع-د-ل (ʿ-d-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Straightness, equity, balancing; the mean between excess and deficiency
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The state of the soul's faculties in due proportion; cosmic order as divine justice
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Ḥaqīqah — proportional ordering; majāz — justice in transactions as derived from inner moral justice
- Root: ش-ج-ع (sh-j-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Strength of heart in confronting danger
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The irascible faculty's obedience to reason in both advance and retreat
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Ḥaqīqah — courage as the mean; majāz — recklessness and cowardice as its corrupt extremes
- Root: ع-ف-ف (ʿ-f-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Abstention from what is unlawful; contentment with the permissible
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The appetitive faculty's easy compliance with rational command
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Ḥaqīqah — continence as the mean; majāz — gluttony and torpor as its deviations
- Sībawayh Rule: Al-ʿAṭf ʿalā al-Sabab (Coordination on Causal Grounds) — The four virtues are coordinated as causes encompassing their species, with each virtue's definition following its faculty in ordered sequence.
chapters.translation:
I say: The virtues, though numerous, are gathered into four that encompass all their branches and kinds: wisdom (ḥikmah), courage (shajāʿah), temperance (ʿiffah), and justice (ʿadālah). Wisdom is the virtue of the rational faculty; courage is the virtue of the irascible faculty; temperance is the virtue of the appetitive faculty; and justice is an expression for these faculties falling into their obligatory order, whereby all affairs are accomplished. For this reason it was said: "By justice the heavens and the earth stand."

Let us then explain each of these mothers [of virtues], then clarify their natures and what kinds lie hidden beneath them.

As for wisdom (ḥikmah), we mean by it what God—may He be exalted—meant in His saying: {«And whoever is given wisdom has been given abundant good»} (Q 2:269). And what the Messenger of God—peace be upon him—meant when he said: "Wisdom is the lost property of the believer." It is attributed to the rational faculty. You have already learned in what preceded that the soul has two faculties: one facing the direction above—that by which it receives the realities of universal sciences, both necessary and theoretical, from the highest assembly (al-malaʾ al-aʿlā)—namely, the certain and true sciences, eternal and everlasting, not varying with the variation of epochs and nations, such as knowledge of God—may He be exalted—His attributes, His angels, His books, His messengers, and His creation's disposition in the world. Nay, among the sciences is that negation and affirmation cannot both be true of one thing in one state, and likewise the real sciences. These sciences are the true wisdom. The second faculty is that which faces the direction below—namely, the direction of the body, its governance, and its management—and by it the soul perceives the goods in actions; it is called the practical intellect (al-ʿaql al-ʿamalī), and by it one governs the faculties of one's soul and governs the people of one's land and household. The name "wisdom" applies to it only in a manner akin to metaphor (majāz), because its objects are like quicksilver, shifting and unstable. Among its objects is that spending wealth is a virtue—yet it may become a vice at certain times and with respect to certain persons. Therefore, the name "wisdom" belongs more properly to the first; this second is like a perfection and completion of the first. This is the moral wisdom (al-ḥikmah al-khuluqiyyah), while the first is the scientific, contemplative wisdom (al-ḥikmah al-ʿilmiyyah al-naẓariyyah).

By moral wisdom we mean a state and virtue of the rational soul by which it governs the irascible and appetitive faculties, and measures their movements to the obligatory degree in contraction and expansion—and it is knowledge of the correctness of actions. This virtue is flanked by two vices: cunning (al-khubth) and dullness (al-balah). These are the two extremes of its excess and deficiency. As for cunning, it is the extreme of excess—a state by which a man possesses deceit and stratagem, such that the irascible and appetitive faculties are unleashed and move toward the desired object with a movement exceeding what is obligatory. As for dullness, it is the extreme of deficiency and its falling short of moderation—a state of the soul by which the irascible and appetitive faculties fall short of the obligatory degree; its source is slowness of understanding and lack of comprehension of the correctness of actions.

As for courage (shajāʿah), it is a virtue of the irascible faculty, in that it is strong, and with the strength of protective zeal (ḥamiyyah), it is submissive to the intellect disciplined by the Sacred Law in its advance and retreat. It is the mean between its two encompassing vices: recklessness (tahawwur) and cowardice (jubn). Recklessness is the extreme of excess beyond moderation—the state by which a man advances upon forbidden matters from which reason obliges retreat. As for cowardice, it is the extreme of deficiency—a state by which the movement of the irascible faculty falls short of the obligatory degree, so that it turns away from advance where advance is obligatory. Whenever these moral traits are attained, these actions issue from them—that is, from the trait of courage issues advance where obligatory and as obligatory. This is the good, praiseworthy trait, and it is what is meant by His saying—may He be exalted: {«Harsh against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves»} (Q 48:29). Neither harshness in every station is praiseworthy, nor mercy; rather, what is praiseworthy is what conforms to the standard (miʿyār) of intellect and Sacred Law. Whoever attains this, let him preserve it by persisting in its actions. And whoever has not attained it, let him examine: if his nature inclines toward the deficiency that is cowardice, let him practice the actions of the courageous, with effort and persistence, until habit becomes for him nature and character, and the actions of the courageous then flow from him naturally. If he inclines toward the extreme of excess—recklessness—let him make his soul aware of the consequences of affairs, magnify their perils, and undertake retreat toward moderation or what approaches it.

For standing upon the limit of moderation is severe. Were one to conceive this truly, the soul would depart from the body, having no attachment to it, and would suffer no torment at all from regret over what eludes it of the body, nor would its delight in what is unveiled to it of the beauty of the Truth and His majesty be clouded. But since that is difficult, it was said: {«And there is none of you but will enter it»} (Q 19:71). Some masters saw the Messenger of God—peace be upon him—in a dream and asked: "What did you mean by your saying, 'Sūrat Hūd has aged me'?" He replied: "His saying {«So stand firm as you have been commanded»} (Q 11:112)"—meaning persistence upon the straight path (al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm). Seeking the mean between these extremes is severe—finer than a hair and sharper than a sword, as described of the state of the Bridge (al-ṣirāṭ) in the Hereafter. Whoever stands firm upon the Bridge in this world will stand firm upon the Bridge in the Hereafter, for a man dies upon what he lived, and is resurrected upon what he died. For this reason, reciting the Fātiḥah—which contains His saying: {«Guide us to the straight path»} (Q 1:6)—is obligatory in every unit of prayer, for it is the most knotty and most difficult of matters for the seeker. Were this required in a single trait, the toil would be long; yet we have been charged with it in all moral traits, beyond enumeration, as will follow. And there is no deliverance from these perils except by God's success (tawfīq) and mercy. Therefore he—peace be upon him—said: "All people are dead except the learned! And the learned are all dead except the doers! And the doers are all dead except the sincere! And the sincere are upon a great peril." We ask God—may He be exalted—to extend to us His success that we may cross the perils in this abode, and not be deceived by the promptings of self-delusion.

As for temperance (ʿiffah), it is the virtue of the appetitive faculty—namely, its easy and smooth submission to the rational faculty, so that its contraction and expansion follow its indication. It is flanked by two vices: gluttony (al-sharah) and torpor (al-khumūd). Gluttony is the excess of appetite toward exaggeration in the pleasures that the rational faculty deems repugnant and forbids. Torpor is the dulling of appetite from being roused toward what reason deems worthy of attainment and acquisition. Both are blameworthy, just as temperance—which is the mean—is praiseworthy. A man must watch over his appetite, for excess prevails over it—especially toward the gratification of the loins and belly, toward wealth, position, and love of praise. Excess and deficiency in all these are deficiency; perfection lies only in moderation, and the standard of moderation is intellect and Sacred Law.

That is, one should know the purpose sought from the creation of appetite and anger. For example, one should know that the appetite for food was created only to prompt the intake of nourishment that repairs the dissolution of one's parts by innate heat, so that the body remains alive and the senses sound—so that through the body one may attain the sciences, apprehend the realities of things, and become assimilated to the highest stratum relative to oneself—namely, the rank of the angels—in which lies one's perfection and felicity. Whoever knows this, his aim in food is strength for worship, not pleasure in it; so he will inevitably be frugal and moderate, and his gluttony will not rage against him. He knows that the sexual appetite was created in him to be a motive for intercourse, which is the cause of the preservation of the species—so that he seeks marriage for offspring and self-restraint, not for play and pleasure. And if he does enjoy and play, its motive is the familiarity and attraction that foster good companionship and the continuance of marriage—and he limits his marriages to what does not incapacitate him from fulfilling their rights. Whoever knows this, frugality becomes easy for him. At that point, he does not measure himself against the possessor of the Sacred Law—peace be upon him—for numerous marriages did not distract him from the remembrance of God, nor did he need to seek the world for the sake of spouses. Whoever supposes that what does not harm the possessor of the Sacred Law does not harm him is like one who supposes that what does not alter the vast sea of impurities does not alter a small cup scooped from the sea—and that what does not harm a strong-bodied man of delicious foods does not harm a suckling infant of frail constitution. How many a fool plays the clever one, measuring himself against the possessor of the Sacred Law—the measuring of angels against blacksmiths—and perishes without knowing whence! We seek refuge in God from dimness of insight (ʿamash al-baṣīrah), for it is nearly worse than blindness. The blind man acknowledges his incapacity, so he follows and another guides him; but the dim-sighted one has opened from his insight just enough to disdain following, yet his light does not complete so that he might continue upon the middle way. Whoever is in this state, God cares not in which valley he perishes.

I have seen a company of foolish commoners playing the clever ones in Sufism with their own opinions, claiming: "Why were these appetites created, if following them is blameworthy and destructive?" They did not know that beneath the creation of the two appetites—namely, those of the loins and belly—lie two great wisdoms: the first is the preservation of the person through nourishment and of the species through procreation, for both are necessary in existence by the decree of God's running His sunnah through His eternal will, for which one finds neither alteration nor change. The second is to incline creation toward the felicities of the Hereafter—for were they not to feel these pleasures and pains, they would not desire Paradise nor fear the Fire. Even if they were promised what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and has never crossed the heart of any mortal, that alone would have no effect upon their souls. This is the limit of temperance.

As for justice (ʿadl), it is a state of the three faculties in their harmonious ordering according to the obligatory rank in dominance and submission. It is not a part of the virtues, but rather an expression for the totality of the virtues. For whenever there is a praiseworthy order between a king, his army, and his subjects—the king being insightful and forceful, the army possessing strength and obedience, and the subjects being weak and pliant in submission—it is said that justice prevails in the land. Justice is not established by some of them possessing these qualities without all of them. Likewise is justice in the kingdom of the body among these qualities. Justice in the soul's moral traits is inevitably followed by justice in dealings and governance, being as it were a branch thereof. The meaning of justice is the commendable ordering—whether in moral traits, in the rights of transactions, or in the parts by which the polity stands. Justice in transactions is the mean between two vices: fraud (al-ghubn)—that one take what is not one's due—and mutual defrauding (al-taghābun)—that one give in a transaction what brings neither praise nor reward. Justice in governance is that one order the parts of the city according to an order corresponding to the order of the parts of the soul—so that the city, in its harmony, the proportionality of its parts, and the mutual aid of its pillars toward the purpose sought from association, is like a single person. Everything is placed in its proper position, and its inhabitants are divided into the served who do not serve, the servant who is not served, and a stratum who serve in one respect and are served in another—as we mentioned regarding the faculties of the soul. Justice is not flanked by two vices, but rather by the single vice of tyranny (al-jawr) opposing it, for there is no mean between order and disorder. By such order and justice the heavens and the earth stand, until the entire world becomes like a single person, its forces and parts mutually aiding. Now that we have mentioned the summary of these mothers [of virtues], let us mention in detail what falls under each virtue and vice of the kinds of virtues and vices—beginning with the rational faculty, then the irascible, then the appetitive—that this may be more curative in exposition.

chapters.title_en: Exposition of What Falls Under the Virtue of Wisdom and Its Two Vices: Cunning and Dullness
chapters.arabic_text:
### | بيان ما يندرج تحت فضيلة الحكمة

### | ورذيلتيها من الخب والبله:

أما الحكمة فيندرج تحت فضيلتها حسن التدبير وجودة الذهن وثقابة الرأي
وصواب الظن. أما حسن التدبير فهو جودة الروية في استنباط ما هو الأصلح
والأفضل في تحصيل الخيرات العظيمة والغايات الشريفة مما يتعلق بك أو تشير
به على غيرك في تدبير منزل أو مدينة أو مقاومة عدو ودفع شر، وبالجملة في كل
أمر متفاقم خطير، فإن كان الأمر هينا حقيرا سمي كيسا ولم يسمى تدبيرا. وأما
جودة الذهن فهو القدرة على صواب الحكم عند اشتباه الآراء وثوران النزاع
فيها. وأما نقابة الرأي فهو سرعة الوقوف على الأسباب الموصلة في الأمول إلى
العواقب المحمودة، وأما صواب الظن فهو موافقة الحق لما تقتضيه المشاهدات من
غير استعانة بتأمل الأدلة.
وأما رذيلة الخب فيندرج تحتها الدهاء والجربزة، فالدهاء هو جودة استنباط
ما هو أبلغ في إتمام ما يظن صاحبه أنه خير، وليس بخير في الحقيقة، ولكن فيه
ربح خطير، فإن كان الربح خسيسا سمي جربزة، فالفرق بين الدهاء والجربزة،
يرجع إلى الحقارة والشرف. وأما  رذيلة البله، فتندرج تحتها الغمارة والحمق
والجنون. فأما الغمارة فهي قلة التجربة بالجملة في الأمور العملية، مع
سلامة التخيل. وقد يكون الإنسان غمرا في شيء، بحسب التجربة، والغمر بالجملة
هو الذي لم تحنكه التجارب. وأما الحمق فهو فساد أول الرؤية فيما يؤدي إلى
الغاية المطلوبة، حتى ينهج غير السبيل الموصل، فإن كان خلقه، سمي حمقا
طبيعيا ولا يقبل العلاج. وقد يحدث عند مرض، فيزول بزوال المرض.
وأما الجنون فهو فساد التخيل في انتقاء ما ينبغي أن يؤثر، حتى يتجه إلى
إيثار غير المؤثر، فالفاسد من الجنون غرضه، ومن الأحمق سلوكه، إذ غرض
الأحمق كغرض العاقل، ولذلك لا يعرف في أول الأمر إلا بالسلوك إلى تحصيل
الغرض، والجنون هو فساد الغرض، ولذلك يعرف في أول الأمر.

### | بيان ما يندرج تحت فضيلة الشجاعة

وهو الكرم، والنجدة، وكبر النفس، والاحتمال، والحلم، والثبات والنبل،
والشهامة، والوقار.
أما الكرم فهو وسط بين البذخ والنذالة، وهو طيب النفس بالاتفاق في الأمور
الجليلة القدر، العظيمة النفع وقد يسمى حرية. وأما النجدة، فهو وسط بين
الجسارة والانخذال، وهو ثقة النفس عند استرسالها إلى الموت، مهما وجب ذلك
من غير خوف. وأما كبر النفس فهو وسط بين التكبر وصغر النفس، وهو فضيلة يقدر
بها الإنسان أن يؤهل نفسه للأمور الجليلة، مع استحقاره لها وقلة مبالاته
بها، ابتهاجا منه بقدر نفسه وجلالتها. وأثره أن يقل شروره بالإكرام الكبير
من العلماء، ولا يسر بإكرام الأوغال، ولا بالأمور الصغار، ولا بما يجري
مجرى البخت والاتفاق من السعادات. وأما الاحتمال فهو وسط بين الجسارة
والهلع، وهو حبس النفس عن مسايرة المؤذيات. وأما الحلم فهو وسط بين
الاستشاطة والانفراك، وهي حالة تكسب النفس الوقار. وأما الثبات فهو شدة
النفس، وبعدها من الخور. وأما الشهامة، فهو الحرص على الأعمال توقعا
للجمال. وأما النبل فهو سرور النفس بالأفعال العظام. وأما الوقار فهو وسط
بين الكبر والتواضع، وهو أن يضع
نفسه موضع استحقاقها لمعرفته بقدرها.
وأما رذيلتا الشجاعة، وهما التهور والجبن، فيندرج تحتهما البذخ،
والنذالة، والجسارة، والنكول،  والتبجح، وصغر النفس، والهلع، والاستشاطة،
والانفراك، والتكبر، والتخاسس، والتعجب، والمهانة، فما يميل منها إلى جانب
الزيادة، فهو تحت التهور. وما يميل إلى جانب النقصان، فهو تحت الجبن. فأما
البذخ فهو الانفاق فيما لا يجب من الزينة، وغيرها طلبا للصلب. وأما النذالة
فهي الدنائة وترك الانفاق فيما يجب، والافتخار بالأشياء الصغار. وأما
الجسارة، فالاستهانة بالموت، حيث لا تجب الاستهانة،
وأما النكول، فهو الانقباض فيما لا يجب عنه الانقباض، خوفا من الهلاك،
وأما التبجح فهو تأهيل النفس للأمور الكبار، من غير استحقاق. وأما صغر
النفس، فهو تأهيل النفس لما دون الاستحقاق. وأما الجسارة، فهو قلة التأثر
بأسباب الهلاك، من غير أثر جميل تقتضيه، وأما الهلع، فهو سوء احتمال الآلام
والمؤذيات، وأما الاستشاطة فهو سرعة الغضب وحدته، وأما الانفراك، فهو بطؤ
الغضب وبلادته، وأما التكبر فهو رفع النفس فوق قدرها، وأما التخاسس، فحط
النفس في الكرامة والتوقير إلى ما دون قدرها، فإن كان على الوجه الواجب سمي
تواضعا محمودا، والمولد للكبر هو العجب، وذلك جهل الإنسان بمقدار نفسه،
وظنه أنها على رتبة عالية من غير أن تكون كذلك. وذم الناس للتكبر والبخل
أشد من ذمهم للتخاسس والتبذير، فإنهما في غاية القبح، وهذان وإن كانا
مذمومين، فهما شبيهان بالسخاء والتواضع، وربما يدق الفرق بينهما، فيظن
أنهما محمودان، وهما رذيلتان بالحقيقة، ومائلتان عن الوسط. ولذلك قال عليه
السلام: " طوبى لمن تواضع من غير منقصة، وذل في نفسه من غير مسكنة ".

### | بيان ما يندرج تحت فضيلة العفة ورذيلتها
chapters.anchors:
- Root: د-ب-ر (d-b-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: "To consider the end/outcome of a matter; to manage affairs with foresight toward their consequences."
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): "Tadbīr is the intellectual ordering of means toward a praiseworthy end, distinct from mere wishful planning."
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): "Literal: turning something over (taqlīb); metaphorical: governance of affairs (siyāsat al-amr)."
- Root: خ-ب-ث (kh-b-th) [for khabath, though here خِبّ (khubb)]
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: "Khubb: deceitfulness and corruption of intention concealed beneath a fair exterior."
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): "The vice opposed to ḥikmah; it is the employment of acumen toward what is apparent good but real evil."
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): "Literal: rottenness (fasād); metaphorical: moral corruption of the inward (fasād al-bāṭin)."
- Root: ب-ل-ه (b-l-h)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: "Balāh: dullness of perception; the opposite of sharpness (kayyās)."
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): "A deficiency in the rational faculty (nuqṣān fī al-quwwah al-nāṭiqah), whether congenital or acquired."
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): "Literal: being soaked/softened; metaphorical: softness of intellect (rakākat al-ʿaql)."
- Sībawayh Rule: "Al-ʿAṭf ʿalā al-Sabab" (Coordination of causes): In enumerating sub-virtues and sub-vices, the conjunction (wa) links items sharing a single governing principle (al-aṣl al-jāmiʿ), requiring the reader to parse each as a distinct species under one genus.
chapters.translation:
I say: As for wisdom (al-ḥikmah), there fall under its virtue: excellence of management (ḥusn al-tadbīr), soundness of intellect (jawdat al-dhihn), penetrativeness of opinion (thaqābat al-raʾy), and correctness of conjecture (ṣawāb al-ẓann). As for excellence of management, it is the quality of deliberation (jawdat al-rawiyyah) in eliciting what is most fitting and most excellent in the attainment of great goods and noble ends—whether pertaining to yourself or that which you advise another in managing a household, a city, resisting an enemy, repelling evil, and in sum, in every grave and momentous affair. If the matter be trivial and paltry, it is called shrewdness (kays) and is not termed management (tadbīr). As for soundness of intellect, it is the capacity for correct judgment when opinions are confounded and dispute surges concerning them. As for penetrativeness of opinion, it is swiftness in discerning the means that lead, in affairs, to praiseworthy outcomes. As for correctness of conjecture, it is the agreement of truth with what immediate observations dictate, without recourse to reflection upon proofs.

As for the vice of cunning (al-khubb), there fall under it: deceitfulness (al-dahāʾ) and sharp-witted roguery (al-jarbazah). Deceitfulness is the excellence of eliciting what is more efficacious in completing what its possessor supposes to be good—though it is not good in reality—but therein lies a momentous gain. If the gain be base, it is called jarbazah. Thus the difference between dahāʾ and jarbazah reduces to baseness versus nobility. As for the vice of dullness (al-balāh), there fall under it: inexperience (al-ghamārah), foolishness (al-ḥumq), and madness (al-junūn). As for inexperience, it is the general lack of trial (qillat al-tajribah) in practical affairs, while imagination remains sound. A man may be inexperienced in one thing according to his trial; and the inexperienced one (al-ghamr) in general is he whom trials have not seasoned (lam taḥnukhu al-tajārib). As for foolishness, it is the corruption of the initial vision (fasād awwal al-ruʾyah) concerning what leads to the sought end, such that he pursues other than the path that arrives. If this be his innate disposition, it is called natural foolishness (ḥumq ṭabīʿī) and admits no cure. It may also arise from illness, and then vanishes with the vanishing of the illness. As for madness, it is the corruption of imagination (fasād al-takhayyul) in selecting what ought to be preferred, such that he inclines toward preferring what is not preferable. Thus the corrupted element in the madman is his aim (gharaḍ), while in the fool it is his conduct (sulūk)—for the fool's aim is like the sane man's aim, and therefore he is not recognized at first except by his conduct toward attaining the aim; whereas madness is the corruption of the aim itself, and therefore it is recognized at first glance.

---

### | Exposition of What Falls Under the Virtue of Courage

And it is: generosity (al-karam), valor (al-najdah), greatness of soul (kibr al-nafs), forbearance (al-iḥtimāl), clemency (al-ḥilm), steadfastness (al-thabāt), nobility (al-nubl), zeal (al-shahāmah), and dignity (al-waqār).

As for generosity, it is the mean between prodigality (al-badhdhakh) and baseness (al-nadhālah); it is the soul's being at ease in expending upon matters of great import and vast benefit, and it may be called liberality (al-ḥurriyyah). As for valor, it is the mean between recklessness (al-jasārah) and cowardly retreat (al-inkhidhāl); it is the soul's confidence when it launches itself toward death, whenever that is obligatory, without fear. As for greatness of soul, it is the mean between arrogance (al-takabbur) and abasement of soul (ṣighar al-nafs); it is a virtue by which a man deems himself worthy of great matters, while holding them in contempt and paying them little heed—taking delight in his own worth and majesty. Its effect is that his evils diminish: he is not honored by the great honor of scholars, nor pleased by the honor of the rabble, nor by petty things, nor by those felicities that come by way of luck and chance. As for forbearance, it is the mean between recklessness and panic (al-halaʿ); it is the restraint of the soul from keeping company with harmful things. As for clemency, it is the mean between fury (al-ishtiyāṭah) and dullness (al-infirāk); it is a state that clothes the soul with dignity. As for steadfastness, it is the firmness of the soul and its distance from flaccidity (al-khawar). As for zeal, it is eagerness for deeds in anticipation of beauty (tawaqquʿan lil-jamāl). As for nobility, it is the soul's delight in great acts. As for dignity, it is the mean between arrogance and humility (al-tawāḍuʿ); it is that one places oneself in the station one deserves, by virtue of one's knowledge of one's own measure.

As for the two vices of courage—namely recklessness (al-tahawwur) and cowardice (al-jubn)—there fall under them: prodigality, baseness, rashness (al-jasārah), shrinking (al-nukūl), vainglory (al-tabajjuh), abasement of soul, panic, fury, dullness, arrogance, self-debasement (al-takhāsus), self-amazement (al-taʿajjub), and contemptibility (al-mahānah). Whatever of these inclines toward the side of excess falls under recklessness; whatever inclines toward the side of deficiency falls under cowardice. As for prodigality, it is spending upon what is not obligatory—of adornment and the like—seeking praise. As for baseness, it is vileness and abandoning expenditure upon what is obligatory, and taking pride in petty things. As for rashness, it is making light of death where making light is not obligatory. As for shrinking, it is drawing back where drawing back is not obligatory, out of fear of destruction. As for vainglory, it is deeming oneself worthy of great matters without deserving them. As for abasement of soul, it is deeming oneself worthy of less than one deserves. As for rashness (again), it is being little affected by causes of destruction, with no beautiful effect that demands it. As for panic, it is the evil endurance of pains and harms. As for fury, it is the swiftness and sharpness of anger. As for dullness, it is the slowness and torpor of anger. As for arrogance, it is raising oneself above one's measure. As for self-debasement, it is lowering oneself in honor and veneration to below one's measure—and if this be done in the obligatory manner, it is called praiseworthy humility. What generates arrogance is self-amazement (al-ʿujb), which is a man's ignorance of his own measure, supposing himself to be upon a lofty rank when he is not so. The people's censure of arrogance and miserliness is more severe than their censure of self-debasement and prodigality—for the former two are at the extreme of ugliness, while the latter two, though blameworthy, resemble generosity and humility; and perhaps the distinction between them is subtle, so that they are thought praiseworthy, while in truth they are vices, inclining away from the mean. Therefore the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: {«طُوبَى لِمَنْ تَوَاضَعَ مِنْ غَيْرِ مَنْقَصَةٍ، وَذَلَّ فِي نَفْسِهِ مِنْ غَيْرِ مَسْكَنَةٍ»} "Blessed is he who humbles himself without deficiency, and abases himself in his own sight without wretchedness."

---

### | Exposition of What Falls Under the Virtue of Chastity and Its Vice

chapters.title_en: The Virtues of Temperance and Their Vices — Section 22 of The Criterion of Moral Action
chapters.arabic_text:
أما فضائل العفة فهي الحياء، والخجل، والمسامحة، والصبر، والسخاء، وحسن
التقدير، والانبساط، والدماثة، والانتظام، وحسن الهيئة، والقناعة، والهدوء،
والورع، والطلاقة، والمساعدة، والتسخط،
والظرف. أما الحياء فهو وسطبينقاحة والخنوثة، وقيل في حده أنه ألم يعرض
للنفس عند الفزع من النقيصة. وقيل: إنه خوف الإنسان من تقصير، يقع فيه عند
من هو أفضل منه، وقيل أنه رقة الوجه عند إتيان القبائح، وتحفظ النفس عن
مذمومة يتوجه عليها الحق فيها. وبالجملة، فإنه يستعمل في الانقباض عن القبح
ويستعمل في الانقباض عما  يظنه المستحي قبحا. وهذا الأخير يليق بالصبيان
والنساء وهو مذموم من العقلاء.
والأول جميل من كل أحد والمراد بقوله: " إن الله يستحي من ذي شيبة في
الإسلام أن يعذبه "، أنه يترك تعذيبه. وأما الخجل، فهو فترة النفس لفرط
الحياء، وإنما يحمد في الصبيان والنساء، دون الرجال. وإنما يستحي الإنسان
ممن يكبر في نفسه. فأما من يستحي من الناس، فنفسه أخس عنده من غيره، ومن لا
يستحي من الله فلعدم معرفته لجلاله، ولذلك قال عليه السلام: " استحيوا من
الله حق الحياء ". ولذلك قال تعالى:
(ألم يعلم بأن الله يرى) ، فإنه مهما أحس في نفسه أن الله يراه، فيستحي
لا محالة إن كان متدينا معظما، كما قال عليه السلام: " لا إيمان لمن لا
حياء له " لأن الحياء للإنسان، هو أول إمارات العقل، والإيمان آخر مراتب
العقل، وكيف ينال المرتبة الأخيرة من لم يجاوز الأولى؟.
وأما المسامحة، فهو التجافي عن بعض الاستحقاق باختيار وطيب نفس، وهو وسط
بين المنافسة والإهمال. وأما الصبر، فهو مقاومة النفس للهوى، واحتماؤها عن
اللذات القبيحة. وأما السخاء فهو وسط بين التبذير والتقتير، وهو سهولة
الانفاق وتجنب اكتساب الشيء من غير وجهه. وأما حسن التقدير، فهو الاعتدال
في النفقات احترازا عن طرفي التقتير والتبذير. وأما الدماثة، فهو حسن هيئة
النفس الشهوانية في الاشتياق إلى المشتهيات. وأما الانتظام، فهو حال للنفس
يدعوها إلى نظر ما يقدره من النفقات حتى يناسب بعضها بعضا. وأما حسن الهيئة
فمحبة الزينة الواجبة التي لا رعونة فيها. وأما القناعة، فحسن تدبير
المعاش، من غير خب. وأما الهدوء، فسكون النفس فيما تناله من اللذات
الجميلة. وأما الورع، فوسط بين الرياء والهتكة، وهو تزيين النفس
بالأعمال الصالحة الفاضلة طلبا لكمال النفس، وتقربا إلى الله دون الرياء
والسمعة. وأما الطلاقة فهو المزاج بالأدب من غير فحش وافتراء، وهو وسط بين
الإفراط والتفريط في الجد والهزل، وأما الظرف، فهو وسط بين التقطيب الذي هو
الإفراط في التحاشي وبين الهزل، وهو أن يعرف الإنسان طبقات الجلساء، ويحفظ
أوقات الأنس ويعطي  كلا ما هو أهله من المباسطة في الوقت معه.
ولما كان الإنسان مفتقرا إلى استراحة ضرورية ترويحا للقلب، لم يكن بد من
نوع من العشرة. والدعابة مستطابة غير مترقية إلى الهزل، لكن بمقدار ما
يفارق به الإنسان حد التوحش وسيرة الجفاء غير مجاوز إلى دأب المساخر في
المضحكات. وقد نقل من دعابة رسول الله وأصحابه ما ينبه على جنسه، ولسنا
نطول به، وأما المساعدة، فهو وسط بين الشكاسة والملق، وهو ترك الخلاف،
والإنكار على المعاشرين في الأمور الاعتيادية إيثارا للتلذذ بالمخاطبة.
وأما التسخط، فهو وسط بين الحسد والشماتة، وهو الاغتمام بالخيرات الواصلة
إلى من لم يستحقها، والشرور التي تلحق من لا يستحقها.
وأما الرذائل المندرجة تحت رذيلتي العفة، فهي الشره،
وكلال الشهوة، والوقاحة، والتخنث، والتبذير، والتقتير، والرياء، والهتكة،
والكزازة، والمجانة، والعبث، والتحاشي، والشكاسة، والملق، والحسد،
والشماتة. فأما الوقاحة، فلجاج النفس في تعاطي القبيح، من غير احتزاز من
الذم. وأما التخنث، فحال يعتري النفس من إفراط الحياء، يقبض النفس عن
الانبساط قولا وفعلا. وأما التبذير فإفناء المال، فيما لا يجب وفي الوقت
الذي لا يجب فيه، وأكثر مما يجب. وأما التقتير، فهو الامتناع من إنفاق ما
يجب، وسببه البخل والشح واللؤم. ولكل واحد من هذه الثلاثة رتبة، وأما
التقتير، فهو الامتناع من إنفاق ما يجب، وسببه البخل والشح واللؤم. ولكل
واحد من هذه الثلاثة رتبة.
أما البخيل، فهو الذي يفرط ويقصر في الإنفاق، خوفا من أن تضطره الفاقة
إلى المسئلة، والتذلل للأعداء، وكأن سبب البخل هو الجبن عند البحث. وأما
الشحيح فهو الذي يجمع إلى ما ذكرناه أن يكره حسن حال غيره، طمعا في أن
يضطره إلى الحاجة إليه، فينال به الجاه والرفعة، ومنشأ هذا ضرب من الجهل.
وأما اللئيم، فهو الذي يجمع إلى هذه الصفات احتمال العار في الشيء الحقير،
وسببه نوع من الخبث، وذلك مثل المتلصص والديوث. وأما الرياء فهو التشبه
بذوي الأعمال الفاضلة، طلبا للسمعة والمفاخرة. وأما الهتكة، فالإعراض عن
تزيين النفس بالأعمال الفاضلة، والمجاهرة بأضدادها، وأما الكزازة،  فاإفراط
في الجد. وأما المجانة فالإفراط في الهزل، وأما العبث فالإفراط في الإعجاب
بلقاء الجليس والأنيس. وأما التحاشي، فإفراط في التبرم بالجليس. وأما
الشكاسة، فمخالفة المعاشرين، في شرائط الأنس، وأما الملق فالتحبب إلى
المعاشرين، مع التغافل عما يلحقه من عار الاستخفاف.
وأما الحسد، فالاغتمام بالخير الواصل إلى المستحق، الذي يعرفه الحاسد.
وأما الشماتة، فالفرح بالشر الواصل إلى غير المستحق، ممن يعرفه الشامت.
وأما العدالة، فجامعة لجميع الفضائل والجور المقابل لها، فجامع لجميع
الرذائل، وما من خلق من هذه الأخلاق، إلا وقد ورد في فضائله أخبار باعثة
عليه، وفي رذائله زواجر عنه، ولم نر تطويل الكتاب بها، فليطلب ذلك من آداب
النبي عليه السلام، وغيره من الكتب، وإنما الغرض بيان أن الإنسان بسبب هذه
القوى الثلاث يحصل هذه الأخلاق كلها. ولكل واحد طرفان وواسطة، وهو مأمور
بالتوسط والاستقامة بين طرفي الإفراط والتفريط في جملة ذلك. حتى إذا حصل
ذلك كله، كمل كمالا بقربه إلى الله تقريبا، بالرتبة لا بالمكان، بحسب قرب
الملائكة المقربين من الله عز وجل. فلله البهاء الأعظم، والكمال الأتم. وكل
موجود فمشتاق إلى الكمال الممكن له، وهو غايته المطلوبة منه، فإن ناله
التحق بأفق العالم الذي فوقه،
وإن حرم عنه انحط إلى الحضيض الذي تحته، فالإنسان بين أن ينال الكمال،
فليلتحق في القرب من الله بأفق الملائكة، وذلك سعادته، أو يقبل على ما هو
مشترك بينه وبين البهائم، من رذائل الشهوة والغضب، فينحط إلى درجة البهائم،
ويملك هلاكا مؤبدا، وهو شقاوته، ومثاله الفرس الجواد الذي كماله في شدة
عدوه، فإن عجز عن ذلك حط إلى رتبة ما دونه، فاتخذ حمولة وأكولة. ومراتب
الكمال للإنسان بحسب هذه الأخلاق وبحسب العلوم غير منحصرة، ولذلك تتفاوت
درجات الخلق في الآخرة، كما تتفاوت في الدنيا في الخلق والأخلاق، والثورة
واليسار وسائر الأحوال.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح-ي-ا (ḥayāʾ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Root denotes life and, derivatively, the recoiling of the soul from base acts; ḥayāʾ is the state of restraint born of self-respect.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ḥayāʾ is a moral faculty (malakah) restraining the soul from the ugly (qabīḥ), tied to consciousness of divine oversight.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally for bodily shrinking; metaphorically (majāz) for the soul's contraction from vice.
- Root: ع-ف-ف (ʿiffah)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Abstention from what is unlawful or excessive; the mean of restraint.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A cardinal virtue (faḍīlah) governing the appetitive faculty (al-quwwah al-shahwāniyyah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: refraining; metaphorical: the soul's temperance as a stable trait.
- Root: س-خ-ا (sakhāʾ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Generosity, ease of giving.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The mean between squandering (tabdhīr) and stinginess (taqtīr).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: liberality; metaphorical: spiritual magnanimity.
- Sībawayh Rule: ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Coordination) — The enumeration of virtues and vices uses coordinated nouns (e.g., "al-ḥayāʾ, wa-l-khajal...") requiring the translator to preserve the serial structure without inserting causal links absent from the original.
chapters.translation:
I say: As for the virtues of temperance (ʿiffah), they are: modesty (ḥayāʾ), bashfulness (khajal), forbearance (musāmaḥah), patience (ṣabr), generosity (sakhāʾ), sound estimation (ḥusn al-taqdīr), expansiveness (inbisāṭ), gentleness (damāthah), orderliness (intiẓām), comeliness of bearing (ḥusn al-hayʾah), contentment (qanāʿah), tranquility (hudūʾ), scrupulousness (waraʿ), cheerfulness (ṭalāqah), helpfulness (musāʿadah), indignation (tasakhkhuṭ), and refinement (ẓarf).

As for modesty (ḥayāʾ), it is the mean between shamelessness (wiqāḥah) and effeminacy (khunūthah). It has been said in its definition that it is a pain that befalls the soul at the moment of fearing a deficiency (naqīṣah). And it has been said: it is a man's fear of a shortcoming that occurs in him in the presence of one who is more excellent than he. And it has been said: it is the softening of the face upon committing base deeds, and the soul's guarding itself against that which is blameworthy, upon which the truth has a claim. In sum, it is used for the contraction from ugliness, and it is also used for the contraction from what the modest person merely supposes to be ugly. This latter kind befits boys and women, and it is blameworthy in the rational (ʿuqalāʾ). The former is beautiful from everyone. The meaning of his saying — peace be upon him — {«إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَسْتَحْيِي مِنْ ذِي شَيْبَةٍ فِي الْإِسْلَامِ أَنْ يُعَذِّبَهُ»} ("Verily Allah is too modest to chastise an aged man in Islam") is that He leaves off chastising him.

As for bashfulness (khajal), it is a languor of the soul due to excess of modesty. It is only praised in boys and women, not in men. A man is only modest before one who is great in his estimation. As for him who is modest before people [generally], his own self is meaner in his sight than others. And he who does not feel modesty before Allah — that is due to his lack of knowledge of His Majesty. For this reason he — peace be upon him — said: "Be modest before Allah with true modesty." And for this reason the Exalted said: {«أَلَمْ يَعْلَمْ بِأَنَّ اللَّهَ يَرَى»} ("Does he not know that Allah sees?"). For whenever a man senses in himself that Allah sees him, he will inevitably feel modesty — if he is religious and reverent — as he — peace be upon him — said: "There is no faith for him who has no modesty," because modesty in a man is the first mark of intellect (ʿaql), and faith is the last station of intellect. How can one attain the final station who has not passed the first?

As for forbearance (musāmaḥah), it is the relinquishing of part of one's due, by choice and with a contented soul. It is the mean between contentiousness (munāfasah) and negligence (ihmāl).

As for patience (ṣabr), it is the soul's resistance to passion (hawā) and its guarding itself against base pleasures.

As for generosity (sakhāʾ), it is the mean between squandering (tabdhīr) and stinginess (taqtīr). It is the ease of expenditure and the avoidance of acquiring a thing from other than its proper source.

As for sound estimation (ḥusn al-taqdīr), it is moderation in expenditures, guarding against the two extremes of stinginess and squandering.

As for gentleness (damāthah), it is the comeliness of the appetitive soul's state in its yearning toward desired things.

As for orderliness (intiẓām), it is a state of the soul that calls it to consider what it estimates of expenditures, so that some of them correspond to others.

As for comeliness of bearing (ḥusn al-hayʾah), it is the love of the obligatory adornment (zīnah) in which there is no vanity (raʿūnah).

As for contentment (qanāʿah), it is the sound management of livelihood, without cunning (khubb).

As for tranquility (hudūʾ), it is the soul's stillness in what it attains of beautiful pleasures.

As for scrupulousness (waraʿ), it is the mean between ostentation (riyāʾ) and shameless exposure (hatk). It is the adorning of the soul with righteous, virtuous deeds, seeking the perfection of the soul and drawing near to Allah — not for ostentation or reputation (sumʿah).

As for cheerfulness (ṭalāqah), it is the blending with courtesy (adab), without obscenity (fuḥsh) or calumny (iftirāʾ). It is the mean between excess and deficiency in seriousness (jidd) and jest (hazl).

As for refinement (ẓarf), it is the mean between frowning (taqṭīb) — which is excess in aloofness (taḥāshī) — and jesting. It is that a man knows the ranks of his companions, preserves the times of intimacy (uns), and gives each one what he deserves of cheerfulness (mubāsatah) at the proper time with him.

And since man is in need of necessary rest to refresh the heart, there is no escape from a kind of sociability (ʿishrah). Pleasantry (duʿābah) is agreeable, not rising to jest (hazl), but to the extent by which a man departs from the limit of wildness (tawaḥḥush) and the way of harshness (jafāʾ), without overstepping into the habit of buffoons (masākhir) in laughable matters. Reports have been transmitted of the pleasantry of the Messenger of Allah — peace be upon him — and his Companions that indicate its kind, and we shall not prolong [the book] with them.

As for helpfulness (musāʿadah), it is the mean between harshness (shakāsah) and flattery (malaq). It is the abandonment of opposition and censure of one's associates in customary matters, preferring the delight of conversation.

As for indignation (tasakhkhuṭ), it is the mean between envy (ḥasad) and gloating (shamātah). It is grief over the goods that reach one who does not deserve them, and over the evils that befall one who does not deserve them.

As for the vices subsumed under the two vices [opposed to] temperance, they are: greed (sharah), languor of appetite (kalāl al-shahwah), shamelessness (wiqāḥah), effeminacy (takhnuth), squandering (tabdhīr), stinginess (taqtīr), ostentation (riyāʾ), shameless exposure (hatk), excessive seriousness (kazāzah), buffoonery (majānah), frivolity (ʿabath), aloofness (taḥāshī), harshness (shakāsah), flattery (malaq), envy (ḥasad), and gloating (shamātah).

As for shamelessness (wiqāḥah), it is the soul's persistence in committing the ugly, without guarding against blame.

As for effeminacy (takhnuth), it is a state that befalls the soul from excess of modesty, contracting the soul from expansiveness in word and deed.

As for squandering (tabdhīr), it is the destruction of wealth in what is not obligatory, at a time when it is not obligatory, and more than what is obligatory.

As for stinginess (taqtīr), it is the refusal to spend what is obligatory. Its cause is miserliness (bukhl), avarice (shuḥḥ), and baseness (luʾm). Each of these three has a rank.

As for the miser (bakhīl), he is one who exceeds and falls short in expenditure, out of fear that poverty will compel him to begging and humiliation before enemies. It is as if the cause of miserliness is cowardice (jubn), upon examination.

As for the avaricious (shaḥīḥ), he is one who adds to what we have mentioned that he dislikes the good state of others, hoping that it will compel them to need of him, so that he attains through that prestige (jāh) and elevation. The origin of this is a kind of ignorance (jahl).

As for the base (laʾīm), he is one who adds to these traits the endurance of disgrace (ʿār) for a paltry thing. Its cause is a kind of malice (khubth) — such as the thief and the cuckold (dayyūth).

As for ostentation (riyāʾ), it is the imitation of those possessed of virtuous deeds, seeking reputation and vainglory (mufākharah).

As for shameless exposure (hatk), it is the turning away from adorning the soul with virtuous deeds, and the open commission of their opposites.

As for excessive seriousness (kazāzah), it is excess in gravity (jidd).

As for buffoonery (majānah), it is excess in jest (hazl).

As for frivolity (ʿabath), it is excess in delighting in the meeting of the companion and intimate.

As for aloofness (taḥāshī), it is excess in being vexed with the companion.

As for harshness (shakāsah), it is opposing one's associates in the conditions of intimacy (uns).

As for flattery (malaq), it is seeking affection from one's associates while feigning ignorance of the disgrace of being held in contempt that attaches to one.

As for envy (ḥasad), it is grief over the good that reaches one who deserves it, whom the envier knows [to deserve it].

As for gloating (shamātah), it is rejoicing over the evil that reaches one who does not deserve it, from among those whom the gloater knows.

As for justice (ʿadālah), it encompasses all the virtues; and the injustice (jawr) opposed to it encompasses all the vices. There is no trait among these traits but that reports have come concerning its virtues that incite toward it, and concerning its vices that deter from it. We have not seen fit to lengthen the book with them; let that be sought from the books of the manners (ādāb) of the Prophet — peace be upon him — and other books. The purpose here is only to show that through these three faculties [the intellective, the appetitive, and the irascible] all these traits are acquired. Each has two extremes and a mean, and man is commanded to pursue the mean and uprightness between the two extremes of excess and deficiency in all of that — until, when all of that is attained, he is perfected with a perfection that draws him near to Allah — a drawing near by rank (ruthah), not by place (makān) — in accordance with the nearness of the angels brought nigh (al-malāʾikah al-muqarrabūn) to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. To Allah belongs the greatest glory (bahāʾ) and the most complete perfection (kamāl). Every existent thing yearns for the perfection possible to it, and that is its sought end (ghāyah). If it attains it, it joins the horizon (ufq) of the world above it; and if it is deprived of it, it sinks to the lowest depth (ḥaḍīḍ) beneath it.

Man, then, is between two states: either he attains perfection and so joins, in nearness to Allah, the horizon of the angels — and that is his felicity (saʿādah) — or he turns toward what is shared between him and the beasts — the vices of appetite and anger — and so sinks to the rank of beasts, and earns an everlasting ruin — and that is his misery (shaqāwah). Its parable is the swift horse (al-faras al-jawād) whose perfection lies in the intensity of its running; if it falls short of that, it is lowered to the rank of what is beneath it, and is taken for carrying loads and for eating. The ranks of perfection for man, according to these traits and according to the sciences, are not limited (munḥaṣirah). For this reason the degrees of creatures differ in the Hereafter, just as they differ in this world in creation (khalq), character (akhlāq), wealth (tharwah), ease (yasār), and all other states.

chapters.title_en: Exposition of the Motives Impelling the Pursuit of Goods and the Deterrents Diverting from Them
chapters.arabic_text: ### | بيان البواعث على تحري الخيرات والصوارف عنها
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ب-ع-ث (ba-ʿ-th)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To rouse, stir up, or incite from a state of rest; the act of sending forth or prompting an agent toward action.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, denotes the divine or natural impetus that moves the soul toward an end—distinct from mere inclination (mayl), as it implies an active, purposive arousal.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for physical arousal (e.g., raising the dead); metaphorical (majāz) here for internal psychological prompting toward moral ends.
- Root: ح-ر-ي (ḥ-r-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To be worthy, deserving, or fit for something; earnest seeking after what is proper.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In ethical contexts, denotes the deliberate pursuit of what is genuinely good (khayr) as opposed to mere desire (hawā), aligning with rational discernment.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for "deserving" (e.g., a worthy man); metaphorical for the soul's striving toward virtue as its due.
- Root: ص-ر-ف (ṣ-r-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To turn away, divert, or repel; to change the direction of something from its course.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In moral psychology, the active deflection of the soul from good—whether by external temptation or internal vice—contrasting with the passive state of neglect (ghaflah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical turning (e.g., turning a vessel); metaphorical for the heart's aversion from righteousness.
- Sībawayh Rule: Bāb al-Maṣdar al-Muʾawwal (The Substantive Clause) — The construction «بيان البواعث» (bayān al-bawāʿith) functions as a genitive annexation (iḍāfah) where the first term (bayān) is a verbal noun governing the second as its object, yielding a nominal sentence that serves as a section heading, implying an elided copula ("This is an exposition...").
chapters.translation: I say: Now that the path of moral action has been clarified, it behooves us to set forth the motives (bawāʿith) that impel the soul toward the pursuit of goods (khayrāt), and the deterrents (ṣawārif) that divert it therefrom. For the soul does not move toward any end save by a motive that arouses it, nor does it abandon a pursuit save by a deterrent that repels it. And the knowledge of these two is the key to the discipline of the soul, since he who knows not the springs of his own striving, nor the barriers that obstruct his course, remains a captive to his passions, unable to distinguish the true good from the apparent good, nor the wholesome motive from the corrupting one.

chapters.title_en: The Three Ranks of Motivations and Deterrents in Worldly and Otherworldly Goods
chapters.arabic_text:
أما الخيرات الدنيوية، فالبواعث عليها ثلاثة أنواع: الترغيب والترهيب بما
يجري ويخشى في الحال والمال، والثاني رجاء المحمدة وخوف المذمة ممن يعتد
بحمده  وذمه، والثالث طلب الفضيلة وكمال النفس، لأنه كمال وفضيلة، لا لغاية
أخرى وراءها، فالأول مقتضى الشهوة، وهي رتبة العوام،
والثاني من مقتضى الحياء ومبادئ العقل القاصر، وهو من أفعال السلاطين،
وأكابر الدنيا، ودهاتهم المعدودين من جملة العقلاء، بالإضافة إلى العوام.
والثالث مقتضى كمال العقل، وهو فعل الأولياء والحكماء ومحققي العقلاء.
ولتفاوت هذه الرتب قيل: خير ما أعطي الإنسان عقل يردعه، فإن لم يكن فحياء
يمنعه، فإن لم يكن فخوف يزعجه، فإن لم يكن فمال يستره، فإن لم يكن فصاعقة
تحرقه، فيستريح منه العباد والبلاد. وهذا التفاوت يعهد لكل شخص من صباه إلى
كبره، إذ هو في ابتداء صباه لا يمكن زجره وحثه بالحمد والذم بل بمطعوم
حاضر، أو ضرب ناجز يحس به. فإذا صار مميزا مقاربا للبلوغ، أمكن زجره وحثه
بالمحمدة والمذمة. فطريق زجره مذمة المزجور عنه. وتقبيح حال متعاطيه، وطريق
ترغيبه في تعلم الأدب وغيره لكثرة الثناء على آتيه، وكثرة الذم لمجتنبيه،
فيؤثر ذلك تأثيرا ظاهرا. وأكثر الخلق لا يجاوزون هاتين المرتبتين إلى
الرتبة الثالثة، فيكون إقدامهم وإحجامهم صادرا عن هذه البواعث والصوارف.
وأما الرتبة الثالثة، فيعزو وجودها، والخيرات الآخروية أيضا هذا شأنها.
وبهذا الطريق تتفاوت الناس فيها، إذ لا فرق بين الآخروية
والدنيوية، إلا بتأخر وتقدم، وإلا فالخبر مطلوب كل عاقل عاجلا وآجلا.
والبواعث على الطلب لا تعدو هذه الأقسام، فكأن من أطاع الله وترك معصيته
فرتبه ثلاث: الأولى من يرغب في ثوابه الموصوف له في الجنة، أو يخاف من
عقابه الموعود له في النار. وهذه الرتبة للعامة، وهم الأكثرون. والثانية
رجاء حمد الله ومخافة ذمه، أعني حمدا وذما في الحال من جهة الشرع. وهذه
منزلة الصالحين، وهي أقل من الأولى بكثير. والثالثة وهي العزيز الفذ رتبة
من لا يبتغي إلا التقرب إلى الله تعالى وطلب مرضاته، وابتغاء وجهه
والالتحاق بزمرة المقربين إليه، زلفى من ملائكته، وهو درجة الصديقين
والنبيين، ولذلك قال تعالى: (واصبر نفسك مع الذين يدعون ربهم بالغداة
والعشي يريدون وجهه) ، وقيل لرابعة العدوية " ألا تسألين  الله الجنة؟
فقالت: الجار ثم الدار " وقال بعضهم:
من عبد الله لعوض، فهو لئيم. ولما كان العقل الضعيف لا يقف على كنه هذا
المعنى، وأكثر العقول ضعيفة، خلق الله الجنة والنار، ووعد الخلق بهما زجرا
وحثا، وأطنب في وصفهما ولم يتعرض لهذه المعاني إلا بالمرامز، مثل قوله
تعالى: (يريدون وجهه) ، (وأعددت لعبادي الصالحين ما لا عين رأت ولا أذن
سمعت ولا خطر على قلب بشر) .
وأما الصوارف فقصور أو تقصير. أما القصور، فالمرض المانع والشغل الضروري
في طلب قوت النفس والعيال وما يجري مجراه. وهذا معذور غير مذموم، إلا أنه
عن ذروة الكمال محروم، ولا دواء له إلا الفزع إلى الله تعالى، لإماطة هذه
الصوارف بجودة. وأما التقصير، فقسمان: أهل وشهوة غالبة. أما الجهل، فهو أن
لا يعرف الخيرات الآخروية وشرفها وحقارة متاع الدنيا، بالإضافة إليها، وهو
على رتبتين: إحداهما أن يكون عن غفلة وعدم مصادفة مرشد منبه، وهذا علاجه
سهل، ولأجله وجب أن يكون في كل قطر جماعة من العلماء والوعاظ، ينبهون الخلق
عن غفلتهم ويرغبون عن الدنيا
في الآخرة، لا على الوجه الذي ألفه أكثر وعاظ الزمن، فهذا ما يجرأ الخلق
على المعاصي، أو يحقر الدين عندهم. والثاني أن يكون لاعتقادهم أن السعادة
هي اللذات الدنيوية والرياسة الحاضرة، وان أمر الآخرة لا أصل له، أو لأن
الإيمان وحده كاف، وهو مبذول لكل مؤمن كيف كان عمله، أو يظن الاتكال على
عفو الله ينجيه، وأن الله كريم رحيم، لا نقصان له من معصية العصاة، فلا بد
أن يرحمهم. وهذه أنواع من الحماقات فترت خلائق كثيرة عن الطاعات، وجرأتهم
على المعاصي.
فأما من ظن أن الآخرة لا أصل لها، فهو الكفر المحض، والضلال الصرف. ومهما
كان هذا الاعتقاد مصمما، بعدت الإنسانية عن صاحبه والتحق بالهلكي على كل
حال، وأما من ظن أن مجرد الإيمان يكفيه، فهو جهل بحقيقة الإيمان وغفلة عن
قوله: " من قال لا إله إلا الله مخلصا دخل الجنة "، وأن معنى الإخلاص أن
يكون معتقده وفعله موافقا لقوله،  حتى لا يكون منافقا، وأقل درجاته أن لا
يتخذ إلهه هواه، فمن اتبع هواه فهو عبده، وصار إلهه هواه. وذلك يبطل قوله
لا إله إلا الله
وينافي في إخلاصه. ومن ظن أن سعادة الآخرة تنال بمجرد قوله لا إله إلا
الله، دون تحقيقه بالمعاملة، كان كمن ظن أن الطبخ يحلو بقوله طرحت السكر
فيه دون أن يطرحه، أو الولد يخلق بقوله وطأت الجارية، دون أن يطأها، والزرع
ينبت بقوله بذرت البذر، دون أن يبذره. وكما أن هذه المقاصد في الدنيا، لا
تنال إلا بأسبابها، فكذلك أمر الآخرة، فإن أمر الآخرة والدنيا واحد، وإنما
خص باسم الآخرة لتأخره، والخروج لقضاء العالم آخرة، بالإضافة إلى الكون في
بطن الأم، والبلوغ إلى عالم التمييز آخرة بالإضافة إلى ما قبله، والبلوغ
إلى رتبة العقلاء آخرة بالإضافة إلى ما قبلها. وإنما هذه تردد في أطوار
الخلقة. والموت طور آخر من الأطوار، ونوع آخر في الترقي، وضرب آخر من
الولادة، والانتقال من عالم إلى عالم، كما قال عليه السلام: " القبر أما
حفرة من حفر النار أو روضة من رياض الجنة "، أي ليس في الموت إلا تبديل
منزل.
وكما أن من جلس متكلا على رحمة الله ونعمته متعطشا جائعا، لم يسلك الطريق
في شرب الماء وتناول الخبز هلك، ومن اتكل عليه في طلب المال ولم يتجر لم
يحصل له المال وكان شقيا، فكذا من أراد الآخرة وسعا لها سعيها، وهو مؤمن،
فأولئك كان سعيهم مشكورا، ولذلك نبه الله تعالى عليه فقال: (وأن ليس
للإنسان إلا ما سعى) ، ومهما عرف أن البهاء الأكمل لله وإن السعادة القصوى
في القرب منه وأن القرب منه ليس بالمكان وإنما هو باكتساب الكمال على حسب
الإمكان، وأن كمال النفس بالعلم والعمل والاطلاع على حقائق الأمور مع حسن
الأخلاق، فمن لم يكمل كيف يقرب من الله تعالى، ومن أراد أن تقرب رتبته عند
الملك بنوع من العلم لو تعطل في بيته متكلا على كرم الملك ملازما صفة
النقصان غير مجتهد طول الليل في  طاب العلم معولا على فضل الله في أن يبيت
ليله ويصبح أفضل أهل زمانه، فإن فضل الله عز وجل أوسع له وقدرته متسعة
لأضعافه، قيل له: هذا فعل مشحون بالباطل والحماقة مزين الظاهر بكلام يظن
أنه محمود. فكذا من ظن أن الآخرة تنال بالبطالة والعطالة فهذه حاله.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ب-ع-ث (ba-ʿa-tha)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To rouse, incite, or send forth; the core sense is an external stimulus that moves one from quiescence to action.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, the "rousing cause" (bāʿith) is that which impels the soul toward an act, whether appetitive or rational; it is the engine of moral psychology.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally for physical propulsion; metaphorically extended to psychological impulsion, where the "movement" is inward and invisible.
- Root: ح-ي-ا (ḥ-y-ā)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Shame, modesty, self-restraint; from the same root as "life" (ḥayāh), implying that shame is a vital principle that preserves moral life.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A restraining faculty (mānīʿah) implanted in the soul that checks base appetites; it is a precursor to fully developed rationality.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the blush of modesty; metaphorical for the internal deterrent that functions as a "bridle" (lijām) on the self.
- Root: خ-ل-ص (kh-l-ṣ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To be pure, unmixed, sincere; the root denotes clarity from adulteration.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Kalām, ikhlāṣ is the purification of intention such that one's inward belief and outward act are perfectly concordant with one's verbal confession—the condition of true tawḥīd.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for refining gold; metaphorical for the soul's purification from hypocrisy (nifāq) and following caprice (hawā).
- Sībawayh Rule: The Conditional of Equivalence (al-sharṭ al-muʿādil) — In sentences like "فإن لم يكن فحياء يمنعه" (if not, then shame restrains him), the apodosis is a nominal sentence whose predicate is a verbal clause, indicating a graded, substitutive sequence where each rank replaces the prior in absence.
chapters.translation:
I say: As for the worldly goods, the motivations (bawāʿith) toward them are of three types. The first is enticement (targhīb) and intimidation (tarhīb) concerning what occurs and is feared in the present state and in wealth. The second is the hope of praise and the fear of blame from those whose commendation and censure are regarded as weighty. The third is the pursuit of virtue (faḍīlah) and the perfection of the soul (kamāl al-nafs), because it is perfection and virtue, not for any further end beyond itself.

The first is the requirement of appetite (shahwah), and it is the rank of the common folk (al-ʿawāmm). The second is a requirement of shame (ḥayāʾ) and the beginnings of deficient reason (al-ʿaql al-qāṣir), and it is the act of sultans, the great ones of the world, and their shrewd managers who are counted among the rational, relative to the common folk. The third is the requirement of the perfection of reason, and it is the act of the saints (al-awliyāʾ), the sages (al-ḥukamāʾ), and the verifiers among the rational.

Because of the disparity of these ranks, it was said: "The best thing given to a man is a reason that restrains him; if not, then a shame that prevents him; if not, then a fear that agitates him; if not, then wealth that covers him; if not, then a thunderbolt that burns him, so that the servants and the lands are relieved of him."

This disparity is witnessed in every person from his childhood to his maturity. For at the beginning of his childhood, he cannot be deterred or impelled by praise and blame, but only by present food or an immediate blow that he feels. When he becomes discerning (mumayyiz), approaching puberty, he can be deterred and impelled by praise and blame. The way of deterring him is blame of the thing deterred from and the uglification of the state of its practitioner; the way of impelling him toward learning good manners (adab) and other things is the abundance of praise upon its doer and the abundance of blame upon its abandoner. This produces a manifest effect. Most creatures do not surpass these two ranks to the third, so their advance and retreat issue from these motivations and deterrents (ṣawārif).

As for the third rank, its existence is rare. And the otherworldly goods (al-khayrāt al-ākhrawiyyah) are likewise in this matter. By this path, people differ therein, for there is no difference between the otherworldly and the worldly except in delay and precedence. Otherwise, the good is sought by every rational being, both immediately and ultimately. The motivations toward seeking do not exceed these divisions.

Thus, whoever obeys God and abandons disobedience to Him is of three ranks. The first is he who desires His reward described to him in Paradise, or fears His punishment promised to him in the Fire. This rank is for the common folk, and they are the majority. The second is the hope of God's praise and the fear of His blame—I mean praise and blame in the present state, from the direction of the Sacred Law (al-sharʿ). This is the station of the righteous (al-ṣāliḥūn), and it is far fewer than the first. The third—and it is the precious, the singular—is the rank of him who seeks only nearness to God Most High, the pursuit of His good pleasure, the seeking of His Face (wajh), and joining the company of those brought near (al-muqarrabūn) to Him, as a proximity (zulfā) among His angels. This is the degree of the veracious (al-ṣiddīqūn) and the prophets.

Therefore God Most High said: {«وَاصْبِرْ نَفْسَكَ مَعَ الَّذِينَ يَدْعُونَ رَبَّهُم بِالْغَدَاةِ وَالْعَشِيِّ يُرِيدُونَ وَجْهَهُ»} (And restrain yourself with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His Face) [al-Kahf 18:28]. And it was said to Rābiʿah al-ʿAdawiyyah: "Do you not ask God for Paradise?" She replied: "The Neighbor first, then the abode." And one of them said: "Whoever worships God for a recompense is base (laʾīm)."

Since the weak intellect does not stand upon the inner reality (kunnah) of this meaning, and most intellects are weak, God created Paradise and the Fire, and promised creation both of them as deterrence and impulsion. He elaborated extensively in describing them, but did not touch upon these meanings except by allusions (marāmiz), such as His saying: {«يُرِيدُونَ وَجْهَهُ»} (seeking His Face), and {«أَعْدَدْتُ لِعِبَادِيَ الصَّالِحِينَ مَا لَا عَيْنٌ رَأَتْ وَلَا أُذُنٌ سَمِعَتْ وَلَا خَطَرَ عَلَى قَلْبِ بَشَرٍ»} (I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and has never occurred to the heart of a man).

As for the deterrents (ṣawārif), they are either deficiency (quṣūr) or shortcoming (taqṣīr). As for deficiency, it is the preventing illness and the necessary occupation in seeking sustenance for oneself and one's family, and what runs in that course. This one is excused, not blameworthy, except that he is deprived of the summit of perfection. There is no remedy for him except fleeing to God Most High, to remove these deterrents by His bounty.

As for shortcoming (taqṣīr), it is of two kinds: ignorance (jahl) and overwhelming appetite (shahwah ghālibah). As for ignorance, it is that one does not know the otherworldly goods, their honor, and the pettiness of the goods of this world in comparison to them. It is of two ranks. The first is that it arises from heedlessness (ghaflah) and the absence of encountering an awakening guide. This one's cure is easy, and for its sake it is obligatory that in every region there be a group of scholars and preachers who awaken creation from their heedlessness and turn them away from this world toward the Hereafter—not in the manner that most preachers of the age have habituated, for that is what emboldens creation toward disobedience or makes religion contemptible in their eyes.

The second is that it arises from their belief that happiness (saʿādah) is the worldly pleasures and present dominion, and that the matter of the Hereafter has no foundation; or because faith alone is sufficient, and it is available to every believer however his deed may be; or one supposes that relying on God's pardon will save him, and that God is Generous, Merciful—no loss accrues to Him from the disobedience of the disobedient—so He must needs have mercy on them. These are types of foolishness (ḥamāqāt) that have slackened many creatures from acts of obedience and emboldened them toward disobedience.
