As for him who supposes that the Hereafter has no foundation, that is pure unbelief (kufr maḥḍ) and sheer error (ḍalāl ṣirf). Whenever this belief is firmly resolved (muṣammam), humanity is distanced from its possessor, and he joins the perished in every case.

As for him who supposes that mere faith suffices him, that is ignorance of the reality of faith and heedlessness of his saying, upon him be peace: "Whoever says 'There is no god but God' sincerely (mukhliṣan) enters Paradise." The meaning of sincerity (ikhlāṣ) is that his belief and his act conform to his utterance, so that he is not a hypocrite (munāfiq). The least of its degrees is that he not take his caprice (hawā) as his god. Whoever follows his caprice is its slave, and his caprice becomes his god. That nullifies his saying "There is no god but God" and contradicts his sincerity.

And whoever supposes that the happiness of the Hereafter is attained by merely saying "There is no god but God," without verifying it by right action (muʿāmalah), is like one who supposes that cooking becomes sweet by saying "I have thrown sugar into it" without throwing it; or that a child is created by saying "I have lain with the slave-girl" without lying with her; or that the crop grows by saying "I have sown the seed" without sowing it. Just as these purposes in this world are not attained except by their causes, so likewise is the matter of the Hereafter. For the matter of the Hereafter and this world is one; it is only distinguished by the name "Hereafter" (ākhirah) for its delay.

The emergence to the decree of the world is an "after" (ākhirah) relative to being in the mother's womb; and reaching the world of discernment is an "after" relative to what precedes it; and reaching the rank of the rational is an "after" relative to what precedes it. These are but a passage through the stages (aṭwār) of creation. Death is another stage among the stages, another type in ascent, another kind of birth, and a transition from one world to another—as he said, upon him be peace: "The grave is either a pit among the pits of the Fire or a garden among the gardens of Paradise"—that is, in death there is nothing but a change of abode.

Just as one who sits relying on God's mercy and bounty, thirsty and hungry, without taking the path of drinking water and eating bread, perishes; and one who relies on Him in seeking wealth without trading obtains no wealth and is wretched—so likewise, whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it with its due striving, being a believer, "those—their striving is thanked" (fa-ulāʾika kāna saʿyuhum mashkūran). Therefore God Most High alerted to this, saying: {«وَأَن لَّيْسَ لِلْإِنسَانِ إِلَّا مَا سَعَىٰ»} (And that man has nothing but what he strives for) [al-Najm 53:39].

Whenever one knows that the most complete splendor (al-bahāʾ al-akmal) belongs to God, that the utmost happiness (al-saʿādah al-quṣwā) lies in nearness to Him, that nearness to Him is not by place but by acquiring perfection to the extent of possibility (al-imkān), and that the perfection of the soul is by knowledge, action, and insight into the realities of things, along with good character (ḥusn al-akhlāq)—then whoever does not perfect himself, how can he draw near to God Most High?

And whoever desires that his rank be elevated before the King by a type of knowledge, yet if he were to remain idle in his house, relying on the King's generosity, clinging to the attribute of deficiency, not exerting himself through the length of the night in seeking knowledge, depending on God's bounty that he might spend his night and wake as the most excellent of his time—for God's bounty, Glorified and Exalted, is wider for him and His power is capacious for its multiples—it would be said to him: "This is an act filled with falsehood and foolishness, adorning the outward with speech that one supposes to be praiseworthy." So likewise, whoever supposes that the Hereafter is attained by idleness and inactivity—this is his state.

chapters.title_en: Exposition of the Kinds of Goods and Felicities
chapters.arabic_text: ### | بيان أنواع الخيرات والسعادات
chapters.anchors:
- Root: خ-ي-ر (khayr)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of "goodness" as that which is desirable and chosen for its own benefit; also denotes superiority in rank or quality.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, al-khayr is that which leads to ultimate felicity (saʿādah) in the afterlife, encompassing both moral and intellectual virtues.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for intrinsic good; metaphorical (majāz) when applied to means that are good only relative to an end.
- Root: س-ع-د (saʿd)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Root denotes auspiciousness, prosperity, and the state of being favored by fortune; also the star of good omen.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Saʿādah is the ultimate perfection of the rational soul through knowledge and virtuous action, culminating in eternal bliss.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for worldly prosperity; metaphorical for spiritual and eternal felicity, as the latter is the true and enduring form.
- Sībawayh Rule: ʾIḍāfah (Genitive Construction) — The phrase "أنواع الخيرات والسعادات" employs a genitive annexation where the first term (أنواع) is indefinite in meaning but defined by the second (الخيرات والسعادات), indicating a comprehensive enumeration of all kinds.
chapters.translation: I say: Now we shall set forth the kinds of goods and felicities, that the seeker may discern their true natures and distinguish the means from the ends. For the goods are not all of one rank, nor are the felicities of one degree; rather, they are divided into that which is sought for its own sake, and that which is sought for the sake of something else. And the felicity which is ultimate and absolute is that which has no end beyond itself, and to which all other goods are subordinated as means.

chapters.title_en: The Five Categories of Divine Blessings and the Interdependence of the Virtues
chapters.arabic_text:
نعم الله سبحانه، وإن كانت لا تحصى مفصلة، فجملتها منحصرة في خمسة أنواع:
الأول السعادة الآخروية، التي هي بقاء لا فناء له، وسرور لا غم فيه، وعلم
لا جهل معه، وغنى لا فقر معه يخالطه، ولن يتوصل إليه إلا بالله ولا يكمل
إلا بالنوع الثاني، وهو الفضائل النفسية، التي حصرنا جملتها من قبل في
أربعة أمور: العقل وكماله العلم، والعفة وكمالها الورع، والشجاعة وكمالها
المجاهدة، والعدالة وكمالها الانصاف، وهي على التحقيق أصول الدين. وإنما
تتكامل هذه الفضائل بالنوع الثالث، وهي الفضائل البدنية المنحصرة في أربعة
أمور: في الصحة
والقوة والجمال وطول العمر، ويهممها النوع الرابع، وهي الفضائل المطيفة
بالإنسان، المنحصرة في أربعة أمور: وهي المال والأهل والعز وكرم العشيرة.
ولا يتم الانتفاع بشيء من ذلك إلا بالنوع الخامس، وهي الفضائل التوفيقية،
وهي أربعة: هدايا الله ورشده وتسديده وتأييده، فهذه السعادات بعد السعادة
الآخروية، ستة عشر ضربا. ولا مدخل للاجتهاد في اكتساب شيء منها إلا الفضائل
النفسية، على الوجه الذي سبق. فقد عرفت أن هذه الخيرات خمسة: وهي الآخروية
والنفسية والبدنية والخارجة والتوفيقية. والبعض منها يحتاج إلى البعض،
أما حاجة ضرورية، كالفضائل النفسية التي لا مطمح في الوصول إلى نعيم الآخرة
إلا بها، وصحة البدن الذي لا وصول إلى تحصيل الفضائل النفسية إلا به، وإما
حاجة نافعة كحاجة هذه الفضائل الخارجة، فإن المال والأهل والعشيرة، إن
عدمت، تطرق الخلل إلى أسباب هذه الفضائل.
فإن قلت: فما وجه الحاجة إلى الفضائل الخارجة، من المال والأهل والعز
وكرم العشيرة. فاعلم أن هذه الأمور جارية مجرى الجناح المبلغ، والآلة
المسهلة للمقصود. أما المال، فالفقير في طلب الكمال، كساع إلى الهيجاء بغير
سلاح، وكباز  متصيد بلا جناح. ولذلك قال عليه السلام: " نعم المال الصالح
للرجل الصالح ". وقال: " نعم العون على تقوى الله المال ". كيف ومن عدم
المال، صار مستغرق الأوقات
في طلب القوت واللباس والمسكن وضرورات المعيشة، فلا يتفرغ لاقتناء العلم
الذي هو أشرف الفضائل. ثم يحرم عن فضيلة الحج والصدقة والزكاة وإفاضة
الخيرات. وأما الأهل والولد الصالح، فالحاجة إليهما ظاهرة. أما المرأة
الصالحة، فحرث الرجل وحصين دينه. قال عليه السلام: " نعم العون على الدين
المرأة الصالحة "، وقال في الولد: " إذا مات الرجل انقطع عمله إلا من ثلاث:
صدقة جارية، أو علم ينتفع به، أو ولد صالح يدعو له "، ومهما كثر أهل الرجل
وأقاربه وساعدوه، كانوا له بمنزلة الآذان والأعين والأيدي، فيتيسر له
بسببهم من الأمور الدنيوية، ما يطول فيه شغله لو انفرد. وكلما تخففت
الأشغال الضرورية في الدنيا، تفرغ القلب للعبادة والعلم، فهو معين على
الدين.
وأما العز فيه يدفع الإنسان عن نفسه الضيم، ولا يستغني عنه مسلم، فإنه لا
ينفك عن عدوه يؤذيه، وظالم يقصده، فيشوش عليه وقته ويشغل قلبه. ولذلك قيل:
" الدين والسلطان توأمان ".
وقيل: " الدين أس والسلطان حارس وما أس له فمهدوم وما لا حارس له فضايع
". ولذلك قال تعالى: (ولولا دفع الله الناس بعضهم ببعض لفسدت الأرض)
وبالجملة دفع الأذى لا بد منه للفراغ للعبادة، ولا يتم ذلك إلا بنوع من
العز. وكما أن الموصل إلى الخير خير، فدفع الصارف عن الخير خير أيضا. وأما
كرم العشيرة وشرف الآباء، فقد يستهان به ويقال: " المرء بنفسه، والناس
أبناء ما يحسنون، وقيمة كل امرئ ما يحسنه ". ولعمري إذا قوبل شرف الأصل دون
شرف النفس، بشرف النفس دون شرف الأصل استحقر شرف الأصل. أما إذا انضم إليه
لم تنكر فضيلته، " فأين السري إذا سرى أسراهما ". وقد شرط النسب في
الإمامة، وقيل: " الأئمة من قريش ". كيف لا، والأخلاق تتبع الأمزجة، وتسري
من الأصول إلى الفروع، ولذلك قال عليه السلام: " تخيروا لنطفكم "،
وقال: " إياكم وخضراء الدمن "، وهي المرأة الحسناء في المنبت السوء. فهذا
أيضا  من السعادات، ولا نعني به الانتساب إلى بني الدنيا ورؤسها وأمرائها،
ولكن الانتساب إلى النفوس الزكية الطاهرة المزينة بالعلم والعبادة والعقل.
فإن قلت: فما غناء هذه الفضائل الجسمية؟ فنقول: أما الحاجة إلى الصحة
والقوة وطول العمر، فلا شك فيه. وإنما يستحقر أمر الجمال، فيقال: يكفي أن
يكون البدن سليما من الأمراض الشاغلة عن تحري الفضائل. ولعمري أن الجمال
لقليل الغناء، ولكنه من السعادات والخيرات على الجملة. اما في الدنيا فلا
يخفي وجهه. وأما في الآخرة فمن وجهين: أحدهما أن القبح مذموم، والطباع منه
نافرة، وحاجات الجميل إلى الاجابة أقرب، فكأنه جناح مبلغ، مثال المال،
والمعين على قضاء حاجات الدنيا معين على الآخرة، إذ الوصول إلى الآخرة بهذه
الأسباب الدنيوية. والثاني أن الجمال في الأكثر يدل على فضيلة النفس، لأن
نور النفس، إذا تم إشراقه تبدى إلى البدن.
والمنظر والمخبر كثيرا ما يتلازمان. ولذلك عول أصحاب الفراسة على هيئات
البدن واستدلوا بها على الأخلاق الباطنة. والعين والوجه كالمرآة للباطن،
ولذلك يظهر فيهما أثر الغضب والشر. وقيل: " طلاقة الوجه عنوان ما في النفس،
وما في الأرض قبيح إلا وجهه أقبح منه ". واستعرض المأمون جيشا، فعرض عليه
رجل قبيح فاستنطقه، فإذا هو ألكن، فأسقط اسمه.
وقال: " الروح إن أشرقت على الظاهر ففصاحة وهذا ليس له ظاهر ولا باطن ".
وقد قال عليه السلام: " اطلبوا الحاجة عند حسان الوجوه "، وقال: " إذا
بعثتم رسولا، فاطلبوا حسن الوجه وحسن الاسم "، وقال: " الفقهاء إذا تساوت
درجات المصلين، فأحسنهم وجها أولاهم بالإمامة ". وقال تعالى ممتنا به:
(وزاده بسطة في العلم والجسم) ، ولسنا نعني بالجمال ما يحرك الشهوة، فإن
ذلك أنوثة، وإنما نعني به ارتفاع القامة على الاستقامة، مع الاعتدال في
اللحم وتناسب الأعضاء وتناصف خلقة الوجه، بحيث لا تنبو
الطباع عن النظر إليها.
فإن قلت فما معنى الفضائل التوفيقية، التي هي الهداية والرشد والتسديد
والتأييد؟ فاعلم أن التوفيق هو الذي لا يستغني عنه الإنسان في كل حال،
ومعناه موافقة إرادة الإنسان وفعله قضاء الله تعالى وقدره. وهو صالح
للاستعمال  في الخير والشر، ولكن صار متعارفا في الخير والسعادة. ووجه
الحاجة إلى التوفيق بين، ولذلك قيل:
إذا لم يكن عون من الله للفتى ... فأكثر ما يجني عليه اجتهاده
وأما الهداية، فلا سبيل لأحد إلى طلب الفضائل إلا بها فهي مبدأ الخيرات
كما قال تعالى: (أعطى كل خلقه ثم هدى) وقال تعالى: (ولولا فضل الله عليكم
ورحمته ما زكى منكم من أحد أبدا ولكن الله يزكي من يشاء) . وقال عليه
السلام: " ما من أحد يدخل الجنة إلا برحمة الله " أي بهدايته. قيل: " ولا
أنت يا رسول الله " قال: " ولا أنا ".
والهداية ثلاث منازل: الأولى تعريف طريق الخير والشر المشار إليه بقوله
عز وجل: (وهديناه النجدين) ، وقد أنعم الله به على كافة عباده، بعضهم
بالعقل وبعضهم على ألسنة رسله. ولذلك قال تعالى: (وأما ثمود فهديناهم
فاستحبوا العمى على الهدى) . والثانية ما يمد به العبد حالا بعد حال بحسب
ترقيه في العلوم، وزيادته في صالح الأعمال. وإياه عني بقوله تعالى: (والذين
اهتدوا زادهم هدى وآتاهم تقواهم) ، والثالثة هو النور الذي يشرق في عالم
الولاية والنبوة، فيهتدي به إلى ما لا يهتدي إليه، ببضاعة العقل الذي به
يحصل التكليف وإمكان التعلم. وإياه عني بقوله تعالى: (قل إن هدى الله هو
الهدى) ،
فإضافة إلى نفسه وسماه الهدى المطلق. وهو المسمى حياة في قوله: (أو من
كان ميتا فأحييناه وجعلنا له نورا يمشي به في الناسس) ، وقوله تعال: (أفمن
شرح الله صدره للإسلام فهو على نور من ربه) .
وأما الرشد فنعني به العناية الإلهية، التي تعين الإنسان على توجهه إلى
مقاصده، فتوجيه على ما فيه صلاحه، وتفتره عما فيه فساده، ويكون ذلك من
الباطن كما قال تعالى: (ولقد آتينا إبراهيم رشده من قبل وكنا به عالمين) .
وأما التسديد، فهو أن يقوم إرادته وحركاته نحو الغرض المطلوب، ليهجم عليه
في أسرع وقت، فالرشد تنبيه بالتعريف، والتسديد إعانة ونصرة بالتحريك، وأما
التأييد، فهو تقوية أمره بالبصيرة من داخل، وتقوية البطش من خارج، وهو
المراد بقوله تعالى: (إذ أيدتك  بروح القدس) ، ويقرب منه العصمة، وهو فيض
إلهي يقوى به الإنسان
على تحري الخير، وتجنب الشر، حتى يصير كمانع من باطنه غير محسوس. وإياه
عنى بقوله: (ولقد همت به وهم بها لولا أن رأى برهان ربه) ، ولن تستتب هذه
الأمور، إلا بما يمد الله به عبده من الفهم الثاقب الصافي، والسمع المصغي
الواعي، والقلب البصير المراعي، والمعلم الناصح، والمال الزائد، على مقتضى
المهمات لقلة القاصر، لا ما يشغل عن الدين لكثرته، والعشيرة والعز الذي
يصون عن سفه السفهاء، ويرفع ظلم الأعداء. فبهذه الأسباب تكمل السعادات.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح-ص-ر (ḥ-ṣ-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To confine, enclose, restrict within bounds; to enumerate exhaustively.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Used for the exhaustive delimitation of categories (ḥaṣr) in demonstrative reasoning.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of physical enclosure; metaphorically, the logical restriction of a genus to its species.
- Root: ف-ض-ل (f-ḍ-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Excess, surplus; superiority in merit.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The virtue (faḍīlah) as a mean-state (wasat) between two vices — the technical ethical term.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal surplus; metaphorically, moral excellence as an "excess" of good over base inclination.
- Root: و-ف-ق (w-f-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To reconcile, harmonize; success (tawfīq) as divine alignment.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Divine succor (tawfīq) — the concordance of human will with divine decree (qaḍāʾ wa qadar).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal fitting together of parts; metaphorically, the providential fitting of human action to divine purpose.
- Root: س-د-د (s-d-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To set straight, aim correctly; to close a gap.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Tasdīd — divine guidance of one's movements and intentions toward the precise target.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal straightening of an arrow's flight; metaphorically, divine direction of the soul's aim.
- Sībawayh Rule: ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Coordination) — The five categories are enumerated with coordinating particles (fa-, wa-) that mark sequential dependence, each category being grammatically subordinated to the next in a chain of necessary conditions.
chapters.translation:
I say: The blessings of God — Glorified be He — even if they cannot be enumerated in their particulars, are nonetheless confined in their totality to five kinds:

The first is the felicity of the Hereafter, which is an abiding without annihilation, a joy without sorrow therein, a knowledge with which no ignorance coexists, and a wealth with which no poverty intermingles. It will never be reached except through God, nor is it perfected except through the second kind — namely, the psychic virtues (al-faḍāʾil al-nafsiyyah), whose totality we have already enumerated in four matters: intellect, whose perfection is knowledge; chastity, whose perfection is scrupulous piety (al-waraʿ); courage, whose perfection is striving (al-mujāhadah); and justice, whose perfection is equity. These are, in truth, the roots of religion. These virtues are only perfected through the third kind — namely, the bodily virtues, confined to four matters: health, strength, beauty, and longevity of life. These are completed by the fourth kind — namely, the virtues encompassing the human being, confined to four matters: wealth, family, honor, and the nobility of one's clan. And no benefit from any of this is attained except through the fifth kind — namely, the virtues of divine succor (al-faḍāʾil al-tawfīqiyyah), which are four: God's guidance (hidāyah), His direction (rushd), His straightening (tasdīd), and His reinforcement (taʾyīd). These felicities, after the felicity of the Hereafter, are sixteen in kind. There is no entry for personal striving (ijtihād) in acquiring any of them except the psychic virtues, in the manner already stated.

You have thus come to know that these goods are five: the otherworldly, the psychic, the bodily, the external, and the succoring. Some of them stand in need of others — either a necessary need, like the psychic virtues, without which there is no aspiration to reach the bliss of the Hereafter, and the health of the body, without which there is no attainment of the psychic virtues; or a beneficial need, like the need for these external virtues, for if wealth, family, and clan are absent, defect creeps into the causes of these virtues.

If you say: "What then is the aspect of the need for the external virtues — wealth, family, honor, and nobility of clan?" — Know that these matters run the course of the wing that conveys, and the instrument that facilitates the intended goal. As for wealth: the poor man in seeking perfection is like one hastening to battle without weapon, and like a falconer hunting without wings. For this reason he — peace be upon him — said: "Excellent is righteous wealth for the righteous man." And he said: "Excellent is the aid upon God-consciousness: wealth." How so? For whoever lacks wealth becomes wholly consumed in his hours seeking sustenance, clothing, shelter, and the necessities of livelihood, so he finds no leisure to acquire knowledge, which is the noblest of the virtues. Then he is deprived of the virtue of pilgrimage, almsgiving, the poor-due, and the outpouring of goods. As for the righteous family and pious offspring, the need for them is manifest. As for the righteous woman, she is the tillage of the man and the fortress of his religion. He — peace be upon him — said: "Excellent is the aid upon religion: the righteous woman." And he said concerning offspring: "When a man dies, his work is cut off except from three: an ongoing charity, or knowledge from which benefit is derived, or a righteous child who supplicates for him." Whenever a man's family and kin are many and they assist him, they are to him in the station of ears, eyes, and hands; and through them there becomes easy for him of worldly matters that which would prolong his occupation were he alone. And whenever the necessary occupations in this world are lightened, the heart becomes free for worship and knowledge — so it is an aid upon religion.

As for honor (al-ʿizz): through it a man repels oppression from himself, and no Muslim is free of need for it, for he is never free from an enemy who harms him or a tyrant who seeks him out, disturbing his time and occupying his heart. Therefore it was said: "Religion and sovereignty are twins." And it was said: "Religion is a foundation and sovereignty is a guard; what has no foundation is demolished, and what has no guard is lost." Therefore God — Exalted be He — said: {«وَلَوْلَا دَفْعُ اللَّهِ النَّاسَ بَعْضَهُم بِبَعْضٍ لَفَسَدَتِ الْأَرْضُ»} ("And were it not for God's repelling of people, some by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted"). In sum, the repelling of harm is indispensable for leisure for worship, and that is not accomplished except through a kind of honor. And just as that which conveys to the good is good, so repelling that which diverts from the good is also good.

As for the nobility of clan and the honor of forefathers — it may be belittled, and it is said: "A man is by himself, and people are the sons of what they do well, and the worth of every man is what he does well." By my life, if the honor of lineage is compared without the honor of the self — against the honor of the self without the honor of lineage — the honor of lineage is deemed contemptible. But when it is joined to it, its virtue is not denied: "Where is the noble one, when he strives, save that the nobler of the two is he?" Lineage has been stipulated in the imamate, and it was said: "The imams are from Quraysh." How not so? For moral traits follow the temperaments, and they transmit from the roots to the branches. Therefore he — peace be upon him — said: "Choose for your seed," and he said: "Beware of the green growth upon dung" — meaning the beautiful woman from a corrupt origin. This too is among the felicities. And by it we do not mean affiliation with the sons of this world, its chiefs, and its princes, but rather affiliation with pure and sanctified souls, adorned with knowledge, worship, and intellect.

If you say: "What then is the benefit of these bodily virtues?" — We say: As for the need for health, strength, and longevity, there is no doubt of it. Only the matter of beauty is deemed contemptible, and it is said: "It suffices that the body be sound from diseases that occupy one from pursuing the virtues." By my life, beauty is of little benefit, but it is among the felicities and goods in general. As for this world, its aspect is not hidden. As for the Hereafter, it is from two aspects: One is that ugliness is blameworthy, and natures recoil from it, while the needs of the beautiful are nearer to being answered — so it is like a conveying wing, the likeness of wealth, and that which aids in fulfilling the needs of this world aids in the Hereafter, since reaching the Hereafter is through these worldly means. The second is that beauty in most cases indicates a virtue of the soul, for when the light of the soul completes its radiance, it manifests upon the body. The outward appearance and the inward reality frequently accompany one another. Therefore the practitioners of physiognomy (al-firāsah) relied upon the states of the body and inferred from them the inner moral traits. The eye and the face are like a mirror for the inward, and therefore the traces of anger and evil appear in them. And it was said: "Cheerfulness of face is the title of what is in the soul; and there is nothing on earth ugly except a face uglier than it." Al-Maʾmūn reviewed an army, and a hideous man was presented before him; he questioned him, and behold, he was tongue-tied, so he struck his name from the rolls. He said: "The spirit, when it radiates upon the outward, produces eloquence — and this one has neither outward nor inward." And he — peace be upon him — said: "Seek your need from those with beautiful faces," and he said: "When you send a messenger, seek beauty of face and beauty of name," and he said: "The jurists — when the ranks of those praying are equal, the most beautiful of them in face is most worthy of the imamate." And God — Exalted be He — said, bestowing it as a favor: {«وَزَادَهُ بَسْطَةً فِي الْعِلْمِ وَالْجِسْمِ»} ("And He increased him in expanse of knowledge and body"). And by beauty we do not mean that which stirs lust, for that is effeminacy; rather, we mean tallness of stature upon uprightness, with moderation in flesh, proportionality of limbs, and symmetry of the facial constitution, such that natures do not recoil from gazing upon it.

If you say: "What then is the meaning of the succoring virtues (al-faḍāʾil al-tawfīqiyyah), which are guidance (hidāyah), direction (rushd), straightening (tasdīd), and reinforcement (taʾyīd)?" — Know that tawfīq is that which the human being cannot do without in every state, and its meaning is the concordance of the human will and act with the decree and determination of God — Exalted be He. It is fit for use in both good and evil, but it has become conventionally applied to good and felicity. The aspect of the need for tawfīq is evident. Therefore it was said:

"When there is no aid from God for the youth, then the most that his striving brings upon him is harm."

As for guidance (hidāyah): there is no way for anyone to seek the virtues except through it, for it is the beginning of goods, as God — Exalted be He — said: {«أَعْطَىٰ كُلَّ خَلْقِهِ ثُمَّ هَدَىٰ»} ("He gave everything its creation, then guided"). And He said: {«وَلَوْلَا فَضْلُ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكُمْ وَرَحْمَتُهُ مَا زَكَىٰ مِنكُم مِّنْ أَحَدٍ أَبَدًا وَلَٰكِنَّ اللَّهَ يُزَكِّي مَن يَشَاءُ»} ("And were it not for God's bounty upon you and His mercy, none of you would ever be purified; but God purifies whom He wills"). And he — peace be upon him — said: "None enters Paradise except by the mercy of God" — that is, by His guidance. It was said: "Not even you, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Not even I."

Guidance has three stations: The first is the definition of the path of good and evil, indicated by His saying — Mighty and Majestic be He: {«وَهَدَيْنَاهُ النَّجْدَيْنِ»} ("And We guided him to the two highroads"). God has bestowed this upon all His servants — some by intellect, and some upon the tongues of His messengers. Therefore He said — Exalted be He: {«وَأَمَّا ثَمُودُ فَهَدَيْنَاهُمْ فَاسْتَحَبُّوا الْعَمَىٰ عَلَى الْهُدَىٰ»} ("And as for Thamūd, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance"). The second is that with which the servant is supplied state after state, according to his ascent in the sciences and his increase in righteous works. It is this that He meant by His saying — Exalted be He: {«وَالَّذِينَ اهْتَدَوْا زَادَهُمْ هُدًى وَآتَاهُمْ تَقْوَاهُمْ»} ("And those who are guided — He increases them in guidance and gives them their God-consciousness"). The third is the light that radiates in the world of sainthood (al-wilāyah) and prophethood, by which one is guided to what one would not be guided to by the merchandise of intellect through which obligation (al-taklīf) and the possibility of learning are attained. It is this that He meant by His saying — Exalted be He: {«قُلْ إِنَّ هُدَى اللَّهِ هُوَ الْهُدَىٰ»} ("Say: Indeed, the guidance of God — that is the guidance") — for He attributed it to Himself and named it absolute guidance. It is that which is called life in His saying: {«أَوَمَن كَانَ مَيْتًا فَأَحْيَيْنَاهُ وَجَعَلْنَا لَهُ نُورًا يَمْشِي بِهِ فِي النَّاسِ»} ("Is he who was dead, and We gave him life and made for him a light by which he walks among the people..."), and His saying — Exalted be He: {«أَفَمَن شَرَحَ اللَّهُ صَدْرَهُ لِلْإِسْلَامِ فَهُوَ عَلَىٰ نُورٍ مِّن رَّبِّهِ»} ("Is he whose breast God has expanded for Islam, so he is upon a light from his Lord...").

As for direction (al-rushd), we mean by it the divine care (al-ʿināyah al-ilāhiyyah) that aids the human being in his orientation toward his aims, directing him to what is his welfare and restraining him from what is his corruption — and this is from within, as God — Exalted be He — said: {«وَلَقَدْ آتَيْنَا إِبْرَاهِيمَ رُشْدَهُ مِن قَبْلُ وَكُنَّا بِهِ عَالِمِينَ»} ("And We had already given Abraham his direction before, and We knew him well").

As for straightening (al-tasdīd): it is that His will and movements be set aright toward the sought aim, so that he descends upon it in the swiftest time. Thus rushd is an awakening by definition, while tasdīd is an aid and victory by movement. As for reinforcement (al-taʾyīd): it is the strengthening of his affair by insight (al-baṣīrah) from within, and the strengthening of his force from without. It is what is meant by His saying — Exalted be He: {«إِذْ أَيَّدتُّكَ بِرُوحِ الْقُدُسِ»} ("When I reinforced you with the Holy Spirit"). Near to it is protection (al-ʿiṣmah), which is a divine influx by which the human being is strengthened upon pursuing the good and avoiding evil, until he becomes like one prevented from within, imperceptibly. It is this that He meant by His saying: {«وَلَقَدْ هَمَّتْ بِهِ وَهَمَّ بِهَا لَوْلَا أَن رَّأَىٰ بُرْهَانَ رَبِّهِ»} ("And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her, had he not seen the proof of his Lord"). These matters will not be set in order except through what God supplies to His servant of penetrating and pure understanding, attentive and heedful hearing, a seeing and watchful heart, a sincere teacher, and wealth in excess of what the necessities require — for the deficiency of the deficient one — not wealth that occupies one from religion by its abundance — and a clan and honor that protect from the folly of the foolish and repel the oppression of enemies. Through these causes the felicities are completed.

chapters.title_en: Exposition of the Ultimate End of Felicities and Their Ranks
chapters.arabic_text: ### | بيان غاية السعادات ومراتبها
chapters.anchors:
- Root: غ-ي-ا (gh-y-ā)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The endpoint, limit, or ultimate objective toward which something tends; the terminal boundary of a course.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, the final purpose (ghāyah) of rational action—distinct from mere inclination—aligned with the divine order of ends.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for spatial or temporal terminus; metaphorical (majāz) for the ultimate moral aim, as here.
- Root: س-ع-د (s-ʿ-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Prosperity, good fortune, and enduring well-being; the opposite of misery (shaqāwah).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): True felicity (saʿādah) is the soul’s attainment of its perfection through knowledge and virtuous action—not transient pleasure.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for worldly luck; metaphorical for the soul’s ultimate beatitude, which is the intended sense here.
- Root: ر-ت-ب (r-t-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Order, gradation, and hierarchical arrangement; a rank or station in a sequence.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The ordered degrees of perfection, each higher rank being a means to the next until the final end.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical arrangement; metaphorical for the graded hierarchy of spiritual stations.
- Sībawayh Rule: **Al-ʿAṭf wa al-Tabyīn** (Coordination and Clarification) — The genitive construction (iḍāfah) “ghāyat al-saʿādāt” binds the ultimate end to the plural of felicities, while “marātibihā” (their ranks) is coordinated to indicate that the exposition covers both the final goal and the ordered degrees leading to it.
chapters.translation: I say: Now let us set forth the exposition of the ultimate end of the felicities and the ordered ranks belonging to them.

chapters.title_en: The True Felicity and the Fourfold Division of Goods and Pleasures
chapters.arabic_text:
اعلم أن السعادة الحقيقية هي الآخروية، وما عداها سميت سعادة إما مجازا
أو غلطا، كالسعادة الدنيوية التي لا تعين على الآخرة، وإما صدقا ولكن الاسم
على الآخروية أصدق. وذلك كل ما يوصل إلى السعادة الآخروية ويعين عليه. فإن
الموصل
إلى الخير والسعادة، قد يسمى خيرا وسعادة.
والأسباب النافعة المعينة، تشرحها تقسيمات أربعة: الأول منها ما هو نافع
في كل حال، وهي الفضائل النفسية، ومنها ما ينفع في حال دون حال، ونفعها
أكثر كالمال القليل. ومنها ما ضرره أكثر في حق أكثر الخلق، وذلك بعض أنواع
العلوم والصناعات. ولما كثر الالتباس في هذا، وجب على العاقل الاستظهار
بمعرفة حقائق هذه الأمور، حتى لا يؤثر الضار على النافع، بل النافع على
الرفيع، والرفيع على النفيس الأهم، فيطول عليه الطريق. فكم من ناظر يحسب
الشحم فيمن شحمه ورم! وكم من طالب حبلا ليتمنطق به، فيأخذ حية فيظنها حبلا
فتلدغه! والعلم الحقيقي هو الذي يكشف عن هذه الأمور.
التقسيم الثاني: إن الخيرات بوجه آخر تنقسم إلى مؤثرة لذاتها، وإلى مؤثرة
لغيرها، وإلى مؤثرة تارة لذاتها وتارة لغيرها. فينبغي أن يعرف مراتبها،
ليعطي كل رتبة حقها.
فالمؤثرة لذاتها السعادة الآخروية، فليس وراء تلك الغاية غاية أخرى.
والمؤثرة لغيرها من المال، كالدراهم والدنانير. فلولا أن الحاجات تنقضي بها
لكانت كالحصباء، وسائر الجواهر الخسيسة. والمؤثرة تارة لذاتها وتارة
لغيرها، كصحة الجسم. فإن الإنسان وإن استغنى عن المشي الذي  يراد سلامة
الرجل له، فيريد أيضا سلامة الرجل م حيث هي سلامة.
التقسيم الثالث: إن الخيرات تنقسم من وجه آخر إلى نافع وجميل ولذيذ.
والشرور ثلاثة ضار وقبيح ومؤلم. فكل واحد ضربان، أحدهما مطلق، وهو الذي
يجمع الأوصاف الثلاثة في الخير، كالحكمة، فإنها نافعة وجميلة ولذيذة، وفي
الشر، كالجهل، فإنه ضار وقبيح ومؤلم. والثاني مقيد، وهو الذي جمع بعض هذه
الأوصاف دون بعض. فرب نافع مؤلم، كقطع الأصبع الزائدة، والسلعة الخارجة،
ورب نافع قبيح كالحمق، فإنه راحة حيث قيل: استراح من لا عقل له، أي لا يغتم
للعواقب، فيستريح في الحال،
ورب نافع من وجه، ضار من وجه، كإلقاء المال في البحر، عند خوف الغرق فإنه
ضار للمال، ونافع في نجاة النفس، والنافع قسمان: قسم ضروري، كالفضائل
النفسية، والاتصال إلى سعادة الآخرة، وقسم قد يقوم غير مقامه، فلا يكون
ضروريا، كالسكنجبين في تسكين الصفراء.
التقسيم الرابع: إن اللذات بحسب القوى الثلاث والمشتهيات الثلاثة ثلاث،
إذ اللذة هي عبارة عن إدراك المشتهى، والشهوة عبارة عن انبعاث النفس لنيل
ما تتشوقه، لذة عقلية أو بدنية مشتركة مع جميع الحيوانات، وبدنية مشتركة مع
بعض الحيوانات. أما العقليات، كلذة العلم والحكمة، وهي أقلها وجودا
وأشرفها. أما قتلها، فلأن الحكمة لا يستلذها إلا الحكيم، وقصور الرضيع عن
إدراك لذة العسل والطيور السمان والحلاوات الطيبة لا يدل على أنها ليست
لذيذة، واستطابته للبن لا تدل على أنه أطيب الأشياء. والناس كلهم إلا
النادر ممنون في صبا الجهل بالعنة في رتبة العلم. فلذلك يستلذون الجهل،
وقال الشاعر:
ومن يك ذا فم مر مريض ... يجد مرا به الماء الزلالا
وأما أشرفيتها، فلأنها لازمة لا تزول، ودائمة لا تحول،
وباقية لذاتها، وثمرها في الدار الآخرة إلى غير نهاية. والقادر على
الشريف الباقي، إذا رضي بالخسيس الفاني، كان مصابا في عقله، محروما بشقاوته
وإدباره. وأقل أمر فيه أن الفضائل النفسية، لا سيما العلم والعقل، لا تحتاج
إلى أعوان وحفظة، بخلاف المال. فإن العلم يحرسك وأنت تحرس المال. والعلم
يزيد بالإنفاق،  والمال ينقص به، والعلم نافع في كل حال ومطلقا وأبدا،
والمال يجذب إلى الرذيلة وتارة إلى الفضيلة. ولذلك ذم في القرآن في مواضع،
وإن سمي خيرا في مواضع.
الثانية هي اللذة المشتركة بين الإنسان وبين سائر الحيوانات، كلذة المأكل
والمشرب والمنكح، وهي أكثرها وجودا. الثالثة التي يشارك فيها الإنسان بعض
الحيوانات، وهي لذة الرياسة والغلبة، وهي أشد التصاقا بالعقلاء، ولذلك قيل:
" آخر ما يخرج من رؤوس الصديقين حب الرياسة ". وكيف تكون لذة الجماع والأكل
لذة مطلقة، وهي من وجه إزالة ألم؟ ولذلك قال الحسن: " الإنسان صريع جوع
وقتيل شبع ". وجميع لذات الدنيا سبع: مأكل ومشرب ومنكح
وملبس ومسكن ومشموم ومسموع ومبصرز وهي بجملتها خسيسة، كما روي عن علي كرم
الله وجهه، إذ قال لعمار بن ياسر، وقد رآه يتنفس كالحزين: " يا عمار، إن
كان تنفسك على الآخرة فقد ربحت تجارتك، وإن كان على الدنيا فقد خسرت صفقتك.
فإن وجدت لذاتها المأكولات والمشروبات والمنكوحات والملبوسات والمسكونات
والمشمومات المسموعات والمبصرات. فأما المأكولات، فأفضلها العسل، وهو صنعة
ذباب. والمشروبات أفضلها الماء، وهو أهون موجود، وأعز مفقود. وأما
المنكوحات، فمبال في مبال، وحسبك أن المرأة تزين أحسن شيء منها، ويراد أقبح
شيء منها. وأما الملبوسات فأفضلها الديباج وهو نسج دودة. والمشمومات
فأفضلها المسك، وهو دم فارة، والمسموعات، فريح هابة في الهواء، والمبصرات
فخيالات صائرة إلى فناء ". هذا كلامه.
ومن آفاتها أن كل واحدة منها يتبرم بها بعد استيفائها في لحظة. فليعتبر
حالة الفراغ عن الجماع والأكل بما قبله، ولينظر كيف ينقلب المطلوب مهروبا
عنه في الحال، فأين يوازي هذا ما تدوم لذته، ولا تفنى أبد الآباد راحته؟
وهو الابتهاج بكمال النفس بالفضائل النفسية، خصوصا الاستيلاء على الكل
بالعلم والعقل.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: س-ع-د (sa-ʿa-da)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of ease, prosperity, and good fortune; felicity as enduring well-being.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): True felicity (al-saʿādah) is the ultimate good of the afterlife; worldly felicity is either metaphorical (majāz) or erroneous.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal felicity is the eternal bliss of the Hereafter; worldly uses are figurative extensions.
- Root: ف-ض-ل (fa-ḍa-la)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Excess, superiority, and virtue; moral excellences as surplus of good.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Virtues (al-faḍāʾil) are the soul's perfections, intrinsically beneficial in all states.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal virtue is intrinsic good; metaphorical when applied to transient utilities.
- Root: ل-ذ-ذ (la-dh-dha)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Sweetness and pleasure; sensory gratification.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Pleasure (al-ladhdhah) is the perception of the desired; intellectual pleasure is noblest and most enduring.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal pleasure is sensory; metaphorical when applied to intellectual joy, which is the truest form.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — For parsing complex sentences with "either...or" (immā...aw) and exceptions (illā), ensuring precise logical distinctions in the divisions.
chapters.translation:
Know that true felicity (al-saʿādah al-ḥaqīqiyyah) is that of the Hereafter; whatever is other than it is called felicity either metaphorically (majāzan) or erroneously (ghalaṭan), like worldly felicity that does not aid one toward the Hereafter—or truthfully, but the name is more veracious for the Hereafter. And that is everything which leads to and assists in attaining the felicity of the Hereafter. For that which leads to good and felicity may itself be called good and felicity.

The beneficial and assisting causes are expounded by four divisions. The first of them: what is beneficial in every state—these are the soul's virtues (al-faḍāʾil al-nafsiyyah). Among them is what benefits in one state but not another, and its benefit is greater, like a little wealth. Among them is what is more harmful than beneficial for most creatures—these are certain types of sciences and crafts. And since confusion abounds in this matter, it is incumbent upon the intelligent person to fortify himself by knowing the realities of these things, so that he does not prefer the harmful over the beneficial, but rather the beneficial over the lofty, and the lofty over the precious and most important—lest the path become prolonged for him. How many a viewer reckons fat in one whose fat is a tumor! And how many a seeker of a rope to gird himself with takes a serpent, thinking it a rope, and it stings him! True knowledge (al-ʿilm al-ḥaqīqī) is that which unveils these matters.

The second division: Goods, from another aspect, are divided into what is effective for its own sake, what is effective for something other than itself, and what is effective sometimes for its own sake and sometimes for another. One ought to know their ranks, so as to give each rank its due.

What is effective for its own sake is the felicity of the Hereafter—there is no other end beyond that end. What is effective for something other than itself is wealth, like dirhams and dinars. Were it not that needs are fulfilled by them, they would be like pebbles and other base stones. What is effective sometimes for its own sake and sometimes for another is bodily health. For a man, though he may dispense with walking for which the soundness of the leg is intended, still desires the soundness of the leg in itself, insofar as it is soundness.

The third division: Goods, from yet another aspect, are divided into the beneficial (nāfiʿ), the beautiful (jamīl), and the pleasant (ladhīdh). Evils are three: the harmful (ḍārr), the ugly (qabīḥ), and the painful (muʾlim). Each of these is of two kinds. One is absolute (muṭlaq)—that which combines the three attributes in good, like wisdom (al-ḥikmah), for it is beneficial, beautiful, and pleasant; and in evil, like ignorance (al-jahl), for it is harmful, ugly, and painful. The second is restricted (muqayyad)—that which combines some of these attributes but not others. For there is a beneficial yet painful thing, like cutting off a supernumerary finger or an external tumor; and a beneficial yet ugly thing, like foolishness (al-ḥumq), for it is a relief, as it is said: "He who has no intellect rests"—that is, he does not grieve over consequences, so he rests in the present moment. And there is what is beneficial in one respect and harmful in another, like casting wealth into the sea when fearing drowning—it is harmful to the wealth, but beneficial in the salvation of the soul. The beneficial is of two kinds: a kind that is necessary (ḍarūrī), like the soul's virtues and the attainment of the felicity of the Hereafter; and a kind that something else may stand in its place, so it is not necessary, like oxymel (sikanjabīn) in calming yellow bile.

The fourth division: Pleasures (al-ladhdhāt), according to the three faculties and the three appetites, are three—for pleasure is the expression for the perception of the desired, and appetite (al-shahwah) is the expression for the soul's impulse to attain what it yearns for: an intellectual pleasure, a bodily pleasure shared with all animals, and a bodily pleasure shared with some animals. As for the intellectual ones, like the pleasure of knowledge and wisdom, they are the least in existence and the noblest. As for their being few—because wisdom is not relished except by the wise. The infant's incapacity to perceive the pleasure of honey, fat birds, and sweet delicacies does not indicate that they are not pleasant; and his finding milk agreeable does not indicate that it is the most pleasant of things. All people, save the rare, are afflicted in the infancy of ignorance with impotence regarding the rank of knowledge. Therefore they relish ignorance. The poet said:
"Whoever has a bitter, sickly mouth—even clear water tastes bitter to him."

As for their being noblest—because they are enduring, not vanishing; perpetual, not changing; their pleasure abides, and their fruit in the abode of the Hereafter is without end. And one who is capable of the noble and enduring, yet is content with the base and perishing, is afflicted in his intellect and deprived by his misery and decline. The least matter in this is that the soul's virtues, especially knowledge and intellect, need no helpers or guardians, unlike wealth. For knowledge guards you while you guard wealth. Knowledge increases with expenditure, while wealth decreases by it. Knowledge is beneficial in every state, absolutely and forever; wealth draws one toward vice at times and toward virtue at others. Therefore it is blamed in the Qurʾān in some places, though called good in others.

The second is the pleasure shared between man and all other animals, like the pleasure of eating, drinking, and copulation—and it is the most abundant in existence. The third is that in which man shares with some animals—the pleasure of leadership (al-riyāsah) and dominance (al-ghalabah)—and it is the most firmly attached to the intelligent. Therefore it is said: "The last thing to leave the heads of the veracious is love of leadership." How could the pleasure of copulation and eating be an absolute pleasure, when in one respect it is the removal of pain? Therefore al-Ḥasan said: "Man is a victim of hunger and a corpse of satiety." All the pleasures of this world are seven: eating, drinking, copulation, clothing, dwelling, smelling, hearing, and seeing—and in their entirety they are base, as is related from ʿAlī, may God honor his face, when he said to ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, having seen him breathing like one grieving: "O ʿAmmār, if your breathing is for the Hereafter, then your trade has profited; but if it is for this world, then your bargain has lost. For you find its pleasures in edibles, drinkables, copulables, wearables, dwellables, smellables, hearables, and seeables. As for edibles, the best of them is honey, and it is the craft of a fly. As for drinkables, the best is water, and it is the cheapest of existing things and the most precious of missing ones. As for copulables—it is urine in urine; suffice it that a woman adorns the best part of her, while the worst part of her is sought. As for wearables, the best is silk brocade, and it is the weaving of a worm. As for smellables, the best is musk, and it is the blood of a mouse. As for hearables—it is a wind passing through the air. And as for seeables—they are phantasms hastening to annihilation." This is his speech.

Among its afflictions is that each one of them becomes wearisome after fully partaking of it in a moment. Let one consider the state after the completion of copulation and eating in comparison to what preceded it, and let him see how the desired is transformed into the shunned in that very instant. Where does this compare to that whose pleasure endures and whose ease never perishes for all eternity? And that is the rejoicing in the soul's perfection through the soul's virtues, especially the mastery over all things through knowledge and intellect.

chapters.title_en: Exposition of What Is Praised and Blamed Among the Acts of the Belly’s Appetite, the Genitals, and Anger
chapters.arabic_text:
### | بيان ما يحمد ويذم من أفعال شهوة البطن

### | والفرج والغضب:
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح-م-د (ḥ-m-d) & ذ-م-م (dh-m-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: ḥamd = commendation with intentional praise; dhamm = censure with explicit blame.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): ḥamd is tied to voluntary acts deserving reward; dhamm to acts deserving punishment in the scale of sharīʿah.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for speech-based praise/blame; metaphorical (majāz) when applied to acts as indirect causes.
- Root: ش-ه-و-ة (sh-h-w-t) — appetite/desire
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: shahwah = innate craving for what pleases the senses.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In ethical discourse, shahwah is the lower faculty (quwwah shahwāniyyah) that must be disciplined by ʿaql (intellect) and sharʿ (law).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical craving; metaphorical for the soul’s inclination toward excess.
- Root: غ-ض-ب (gh-d-b) — anger
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: ghaḍab = boiling of the blood in the heart seeking vengeance.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Anger is a natural faculty (quwwah ghaḍabiyyah) — praiseworthy when used for defending truth, blameworthy when it oversteps into fury.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the emotion; metaphorical for the action that results from it (e.g., striking, killing).
- Sībawayh Rule: **Bāb al-ʿAṭf ʿalā al-Maʿnā** (Coordination by meaning) — The three nouns (shahwat al-baṭn, al-farj, al-ghaḍab) are coordinated under a single semantic category of “lower appetitive faculties,” allowing the subsequent exposition to treat them as one moral domain.
chapters.translation: I say: Know that the acts proceeding from the appetite of the belly, the genitals, and anger are not, in themselves, either praiseworthy or blameworthy in the absolute sense. Rather, they are rendered so by their relation to the intellect and the revealed law (al-sharʿ). For the belly’s appetite, when it seeks merely what sustains the body and preserves health, is praiseworthy — nay, it is a necessary instrument for the attainment of the soul’s perfection. But when it exceeds the bounds of necessity and inclines toward gluttony and luxury, it becomes blameworthy, for it turns the soul toward the animal and away from the angelic. Likewise, the appetite of the genitals: if it seeks lawful procreation and the preservation of lineage, it is praiseworthy; but if it pursues mere lust and transgression, it is blameworthy. And anger: if it arises in defense of the truth, in repelling injustice, and in commanding the good and forbidding the evil, it is praiseworthy — indeed, it is the very weapon of religion. But if it erupts from personal vanity, vengeance, or worldly rivalry, it is blameworthy, for it blinds the eye of discernment and deafens the ear of guidance. Thus, the criterion (al-mīzān) in all these is the balance of the intellect and the measure of the law — not the bare existence of the appetite, nor its total annihilation, but its disciplined subordination to the higher ends for which man was created.

chapters.title_en: The Criterion of Moral Action — Section 30: On the Governance of the Appetites of the Belly and the Loins, and the Branches of Anger
chapters.arabic_text:
أما شهوة البطن فداعية إلى الغذاء، والمطعم ضربان: ضروري وغير ضروري. أما
الضروري، فهو الذي لا يستغني عنه في قوام البدن، كالطعام الذي يتغذى به،
والماء الذي يرتوي به، وهو ينقسم إلى محمود ومكروه، ومذموم  ومحظور. أما
المحمود، فأن يقتصر على تناول ما لا يمكنه الاشتغال والتقوى على العلم
والعمل إلا به، ولو اقتصر عنه لتحللت قواه واختل بدنه، فهذا المقدار، إذا
تناوله من حيث يجب كما يجب، فهو
معذور، بل مشكور ومأجور، إذ البدن مركب النفس، لتقطع به منازلها إلى الله
تعالى. وكما أن الجهاد عبادة، فإمداد فرس المجاهدة بما يقويه على السير
بالمجاهد أيضا عبادة، ولذلك قال عليه السلام: " عند أكل الصالحين تنزل
الرحمة "، وذلك إذا تناوله تناول من اضطر إلى شيء، يود لو استغنى عنه.
وإدخال الطعام البطن وإخراجه قريب. ولذلك قيل: من كان همه ما يدخل في بطنه،
كانت قيمته ما يخرج منه. وليعلم الآكل أنه في تناول فضلات الأشجار والنبات
كالخنزير في تناول عذرة الإنسان وفضلته، وكالجعل في تناول فضلة الحيوان.
ولو كان للأشجار ألسنة، لناطقت متناول فضلاتها بالتشبيه بهذا المتناول
لفضلة الحيوان.
وأما المكروه، فهو الإسراف والإمعان من الحلال والزيادة على قدرة البلغة.
قال عليه السلام:
" ما من وعاء أبغض إلى الله تعالى من بطن مليء من حلال "، وهو أيضا مضر
من جهة الطب، فإنه أصل كل داء. قال عليه السلام: " البطنة أصل الداء
والحمية أصل الدواء، وعودوا كل جسد ما اعتاد ". فقال محققو الطب: لم يدع
عليه السلام شيئا من الطب إلا وأدرجه تحت هذه الكلمات الثلاث.
ولا ينبغي أن يستهين طالب السعادة بهذه الزيادة، وإن سميناها مكروها لا
محظورا، فإنه مكروه سريع السياقة إلى المحظورات، بل إلى أكثر المحظورات.
فإن مثار الشرور قوة الشهوات، ومقوي الشهوات هي الأغذية. فامتلاء البطن
مقوي للشهوب، وتقوي الشهوة داعية للهوى، والهوى أعظم جند الشيطان، الذي إذا
تسلط سباه عن ربه وصرفه عن بابه. وإمداد جنود الأعداء بالمقويات يكاد ينزل
منزلة عين العداوة. فلهذا يكاد تكون الكراهية فيه حضرا. ولذلك قيل لبعضهم:
" ما بالك مع كبرك لا تتعهد بدنك وقد أنهك ".
فقال: " لأنه سريع المرح فاحش الأشر فأخاف أن يجمع بي فيورطني. ولئن
أحمله على الشدائد أحب إلي من أن يحملني على  الفواحش ". فإن قلت: فما
المقدار المحمود؟ فعلم أنه نبه عليه السلام على التقدير بخبرين، أحدهما
قوله: " حسب ابن آدم لقيمات يقمن صلبه، فإن كان لا بد فثلث للطعام، وثلث
للشراب، وثلث للنفس "، فأما اللقيمات فهي دون العشرة ويقرب منه قوله عليه
السلام: " المؤمن يأكل في معي واحد، والمنافق يأكل في سبعة أمعاء "، والأحب
الأكل في سبع البطن، فإن غلب النهم ففي الثلث. وأظن أن الحد ثلث في حق
الأكثر، وإن كان ذلك قد يختلف باختلاف الأشخاص. وعلى الجملة فلا بد أن يكون
دون الشبع، حتى يخف البدن للعبادة والتهجد باليل، وتضعف القوى عن الانبعاث
إلى الشهوات.
وأما المحظور فهو التناول مما حرم الله عز وجل من مال الغير أو المحرمات.
وأفحشها شرب المسكر، فإنه أعظم آلات الشيطان في إزالة العقل، الذي هو من
حزب الله، وأوليائه، وآثار الشهوة والقوى السبعية التي هي من أحزاب الشيطان
وأوليائه. وهذا حكم المطاعم على الإجمال. ولا يطمعن أحد في سلوك طريق
السعادة، قبل أن يراعي أمر المطعم في مقداره ووجه حله، فإن المعدة منبع
القوى، فكأنه الباب والمفتاح إلى الخير والشر جميعا. ولذا عظم في الشرع أمر
الصوم لأنه على الخصوص يتوجه إلى قهر أعداء الله تعالى كما روي: " إن الصوم
لي وأنا الذي أجزي به "، إلى غير ذلك مما ورد فيه.
وأما شهوة الفرج، فأفعالها تنقسم إلى محمود ومكروه ومحظور. أما المحمود
فهو المقدار الذي لا بد منه لحفظ النوع، فإن النكاح ضروري لبقاء نوع
الإنسان باتصال نسله، كما أن الغذاء ضروري لبقاء شخصه إلى حين أجله.
والشهوة خلقت باعثة على إبقاء النسل، بطريق الوطء، كما
خلق الجوع باعثا على إبقاء الشخص بالأكل، ولذلك قال: " تناكحوا، تناسلوا
تكثروا، فإني مباه بكم الأمم ". فمن كان قصده في النكاح أمرين: أحدهما
النسل لكثرة المباهاة، وأن يلحقه بعده ولد صالح يدعو له، والثاني أن يدفع
عن نفسه فضلة المني، التي إذا اجتمعت كانت كالمرة، والدم إذا اجتمع عظمت
نكايته في البدن بإثارة المرض، وفي الدين بالدعوة  إلى الفجور، فالنكاح على
هذا الوجه محمود وسنة وداخل تحت قوله: " من احب فطرتي فليستسن بسنتي ". ومن
نكح فقد حصن نصف دينه. ولا بأس بغرض ثالث، وهو أن يكون في بيته من يدبر أمر
منزله، ليتفرغ هو للعلم والعبادة، فيصير النكاح على هذا الوجه من جملة
العبادات، فإن الأعمال بالنيات. وإمارة هذا أن لا يطلب من المرأة إلا
الجمال للتحصن، وحسن الخلق في تدبير المنزل، والديانة للصيانة والنسب
الديني فقط. فإنه إمارة الديانة وحسن الخلق، فإن
العرق نزاع، ولذلك قال عليه السلام: " عليك بذات الدين، تربت يداك،
وإياكم وخضراك الدمن ". وقال: " تخيروا لنطفكم ". وليطلب صحة البدن وأن لا
يكون عقيما لأجل الولد فإنه المقصود. ولذلك كره العزل، وإتيان المرأة من
ورائها، فإنه إهمال للحراثة، ونساؤكم حرث لكم. ولا بأس بطلب الأبكار،
لتستحكم الألفة، وقد ندب الشرع إليها.
وأما المكروه فأن يقصد التمتع بقضاء الشهوة فقط، ثم يمعن فيه ويواظب
عليه، وربما يتناول ما يزيد في شهوته، وذلك مضر شرعا، ولا كراهية فيه في
نفسه، فإنه مباح،
ولكنه انصراف عن الله إلى اتباع الهوى وتشبه بالثيران والحمر. وإثارة
لشهوة بالمطعومات القوية والأسباب الباعثة تضاهي إثارة سراسباع ضارية،
وبهائم عادية، ثم الانتهاض بعدها للخلاص منها.
وأما المحظور، فعلى وجهين: أحدهما أن يقضي الشهوة في محل الحرث، ولكن
بغير عقد شرعي، ولا على الوجه المأمور، وهو الزنا. وقد قرن ذلك بالشرك حيث
قال: (الزاني لا ينكح إلا زانية أو مشركة) . والثاني تعاطيه في غير محل
الحرث، وهو أفحش من الزنا لأن الزاني لم يضيع الماء، بل وضعه في محل الحرث
على غير الوجه المأمور. وهذا قد ضيع، وكان ممن قال الله تعالى: (ويهلك
الحرث والنسل) . ولذلك سميت اللواطة الإسراف، فقال تعالى: (إنكم لتأتون
الرجال شهوة من دون النساء بل أنتم قوم مسرفون) . فهذه مراتب الناس في شهوة
الفرج.
وقد ينتهي بعض الضلال إلى العشق، وهو عين الحماقة وغاية الجهل بما وضع
الجماع له،
ومجاوزة لحد البهائم في تملك النفس، وضبطها لها، لأن المتعشق  لم يقنع
بإرادة شهوة الجماع، وهي أقبح الشهوات وأجدرها بأن يستحي منها، حتى اعتقد
أن لا تنقضي إلا في محل واحد، والبهيمة تقضي الشهوة أنى اتفق فتكتفي به.
وهذا لا يكتفي إلا من معشوقته، حتى ازداد به ذلا إلى ذل وعبودية إلى
عبودية. واستسخر العقل لخدمة الشهوة، وقد خلق ليكون آمرا مطاعا لا يكون
خادما للشهوة، محتانا لأجلها، وهو مرض نفس فارغة لا همة لها. وإنما يجب
الاحتراز من أوائلها، وهو معاودة النظر والفكر، وإلا فبعد الاستحكام يعسر
دفعها. وكذلك عشق الجاه والمال والعقار والأولاد، حتى حب اللعب بالطيور
والنرد والشطرنج، فإن هذه الأمور تستولي على طائفة ينقضي عليهم الدين
والدنيا، ولا يصبرون عنها. ومثال رد الشهوة في أول انبعاثها صرف عنان
الدابة عن توجهها إلى باب دار تدخله، فما أهون منعها وصرف عنانها. ومثال
علاجها بعد استحكامها أن تترك الدابة، حتى تدخل وتجاوز الباب، ثم تأخذ
بذنبها جارا لها إلى وراء، وما أعظم التفاوت بين الأمرين! فليكن الاحتياط
في بدايات الأمور، فأما أواخرها فلا تقبل الإصلاح في الأكثر، إلا بجهد شديد
يوازي نزع الروح.
وأما أفعال الغضب فتنقسم إلى محمود ومكروه ومحظور. أما المحمود ففي
موضعين: أحدهما المسمى غيرة، وهو أن يقصد حريم الرجل ويتعرض لمحارمه.
فالغضب له ولدفعه محمود، وقلة التأثر به خنوثة وركاكة، ولذلك قال عليه
السلام: " إن سعدا لغيور، وإن الله أغير منه "، وقد وضع الله الغيرة في
الرجال، لحفظ الأنساب. فإن النفوس لو تسامحت بالتزاحم على النساء لاختلطت
الأنساب. ولذلك قيل: كل أمة وضعت الغيرة في رجالها، وضعت الصيانة في
نسائها. والثاني الغضب عند مشاهدة المنكرات والفواحش، غيرة على الدين،
وطلبا للانتقام، ولذلك مدحوا بكونهم أشداء على الكفار رحماء بينهم. ولذلك
قال عليه السلام: " خير أمتي أحداؤها "،
فالمراد به الحدة لحمية الدين. ولذلك قال تعالى: (ولا تأخذكم بهما رأفة
في دين الله) . ومع هذه فالسلطان إذا غضب عند جناية جان، فينبغي أن يحبسه
ولا يبادر إلى عقوبته حتى يجدد النظر فيه، فإن الغضب غول العقل،  فربما
يحمله على مجاوزة حد الواجب في الانتقام. وأما المكروه فغضبه عند فوات
حظوظه المباحة نيلها، كغضبه على خادمه وعبده عند كسر آنيته، أو توانيه في
خدمته، بحكم تغافل يمكن الاحتزاز عنه. فهذا لا ينتهي إلى حد المذموم، ولكن
العفو والتجاوز أولى وأحب. ولذلك قيل لواحد حكيم: لا تصفح عن عبدك وهو يقصر
في خدمتك، فيفسد باحتمالك. فقال: " لأن يفسد عبدي في صلاح نفسي خير من أن
تفسد نفسي في صلاح عبدي ". فإن احتمال ذلك إصلاح للنفس والانتقام إصلاح
للعبد.
وأما المذموم فهو الاستشاطة عن الفخر والتكبر والمباهاة والمنافسة والحقد
والحسد، وعن أمور واهية تتعلق بالحظوظ البدنية، من غير أن يكون في الانتقام
مصلحة في المستقبل دينا ودنيا، وهو الغالب على أكثر الخلق، وهو انقياد
للخلق الذي يضاد الحلم والتحلم. فإن الحلم عبارة عن إمساك النفس عن هيجان
الغضب، والتحلم عن إمساكها عن قضاء الوطر منه، إذا هاج، والكمال في الحلم،
ولكن التحلم صبر على المكروه، وفيه أيضا خير كثير. فهذه مراتب أفعال الغضب.
والناس في الغضب يختلفون، فبعضهم كالحلفاء، سريع التوقد، سريع الخمود،
وبعضهم كالقطا بطيء الخمود، وبعضهم بطيء التوقد سريع الخمود، وهو الأحمد،
ما لم ينته إلى فتور الحمية والغيرة. وأسباب الغضب أما من جهة المزاج،
فالحرارة واليبوسة، يدل عليهما تعريف الغضب، فإن الغضب معناه غليان دم
القلب، فإن كان على من فوقك في القدرة على الانتقام، تولد منه
انقباض الدم من ظاهر الجلد إلى القلب، وكان حزنا، ولأجله يصفر الوجه. وإن
كان على من دونك تولد منه ثوران دم القلب، لا انقباضه، فيكون منه الغضب
الحقيقي وطلب الانتقام. وإن كان على نظيرك في القدرة على الانتقام، تولد
منه تردد الدم بين انقباض وانبساط، ويختلف به لون الوجه فيحمر ويصفر
ويضطرب. وبالجملة قوة الغضب محلها القلب، ومعناه حركة الدم وغليانه. وأما
ما وراء المزاج، فالاعتياد، فإن من يعاشر جماعة يباهون بالغضب والطباع
السبعية انطبع ذلك فيه. وإن من خالط أهل الهدوء والوقار أثرت العادة أيضا
فيه. وأما سببه  المخرج له من القوة إلى الفعل في الحال، فهو العجب
والافتخار والمراء واللجاج والمزاح والتيه والاستهزاء والضيم وطلب ما فيه
التنافس والتحاسد وشهوة الانتقام، وكل ذلك مذموم. وحق من اعتراه الغضب أن
يتفكر فيما قاله بعض الحكماء لبعض السلاطين وقد سأله حيلة في دفع الغضب،
فقال: " ينبغي أن تذكر أنه يجب
أن تطيع لا أن تطاع فقط، وأن تخدم لا أن تخدم فقط، وأن تحتمل لا أن تحتمل
فقط، وأن تعلم أن الله يراك دائما، فإذا فعلت ذلك لم تغضب ".
واعلم أن الغضب له فروع كما سبق، ومن جملتها الشجاعة والتهور والمنافسة
والغبطة والحسد على ما سبق، ولكن نزيدها شرحا. أما الشجاعة فخلق بين التهور
والجبن، فإن اعتبر إضافتها إلى النفس فهي صرامة القلب في الأهوال وربط
الجأش عند المخاوف، وإن اعتبر بالفعل فالإقدام على موضع الفرصة وتولدها من
الغضب وحسن الأمل وبها يصابر الإنسان الشدائد، بل بها يصبر عن المعاصي، فإن
الغضب إذا سلط على الشهوة زجرها. ولما كان الدين شطره رغبة في الخير، وشطره
تركا للشر قال عليه السلام: " الصبر نصف الإيمان "، ولما كان بعض الشرور في
شهوة الفرج والبطن،
وبعضها في غيرهما قال: " الصوم نصف الصبر ". والصبر صبران، صبر جسمي وهو
تحمل المشاق بالمدن، أما فعلا كتعاطي الأعمال الشاقة، وأما انفعالا كاحتمال
الضرب الشديد والمرض العظيم. والمحمود التام هو الضرب الثاني وهو الصبر
النفسي. فإن عن تناول المشتهيات، سمي عفة، وإن كان على احتمال مكروه،
اختلفت أسماؤه بحسب اختلاف المكروه، فإن كان في مصيبة، اقتصر على اسم
الصبر، ويضاده الجزع والهلع، وإن كان في احتمال غني سمي ضبط النفس ويضاده
البطر، وإن كان في حرب سمي شجاعة، ويضاده الجبن، وإن كان في كظم الغيظ
والغضب، سمي حلما، ويضاده التذمر، وإن كان في نائبة مضجرة سمي سعة الصدر،
ويضاده الضجر والتبرم وضيق الصدر، وإن كان في إخفاء كلام سمي كتم السر،
وإن كان على فضول العيش سمي زهد وقناعة، ويضاده الحرص والشره، ولذلك قال
تعالى: (والصابرين في البأساء)  أي المصيبة والضراء، أي الفقر وحين البأس،
أي المحاربة، (أولئك الذين صدقوا وأولئك هم المتقون)
وأما الغبطة والمنافسة والحسد التي هي من جملة الفروع أيضا، فالغبطة
محمودة والحسد مذموم. قال عليه السلام: " المؤمن يغبط والمنافق يحسد ".
والمنافسة محمودة قال تعالى: (وفي ذلك فليتنافس المتنافسون) . والغبطة تمني
الإنسان أن ينال كل ما ناله أمثاله، من غير أن يغتنم لنيل غيره. فإذا انضم
إليه الجد والتشمير في الوصول إلى مثله أو خير منه، فهو منافسة. والحسد هو
تمني زوال النعمة عن مستحقيها، وربما كان مع سعي في إزالتها. والخبيث
الحسود من يكون ساعيا في الإزالة من غير أن يطلبها لنفسه. والحسد غاية
البخل، إذ البخيل يبخل بمال نفسه، والحسود يبخل بمال الله على غيره.
وقيل: الحسد والحرص هما ركنا الذنوب ولهما ضرب المثل بآدم وإبليس، إذ حسد
إبليس آدم فصار لعينا، وحرص آدم على ما نهي عنه فأخرج من الجنة. فهما شجران
يثمران الهموم والغموم والخسران، فمن قطع عروقها نجا، وبالجملة فالحسد عين
الحماقة، لأن من لا يغنم بخير يصل إلى أهل المغرب، مع أنه لا يناله بوجه،
فلم يغتم بخير يصل إلأى عشيرته وشركائه وجيرانه وأهل بلده، وربما بوجه، فلم
يغتم بخير يصل إلى عشيرته وشركائه وجيرانه وأهل بلده، وربما ينال منه حظا.
وقوله عليه السلام: " لا حسد إلا في اثنين: رجل أتاه الله مالا فجعله في حق
ورجل آتاه الله حكمة فهو يقضي بها "، إنما أراد به الغبطة، فإن الحسد قد
يطلق لإرادتها.
فهذا هو القول في ضبط أفعال هذه الصفات. فإن قلت: فمن ضبط أفعال هذه
القوى حتى حدث في نفسه، من أفعاله أخلاق راسخة يتيسر بها هذه الأفعال، فهل
يكون عفيفا؟ فاعلم أن العفة لا تتم بهذا القدر ما لم ينضم إليه عفة اليد
واللسان والسمع والبصر، وحدها
في اللسان الكف عن السخرية والغيبة والنميمة والكذب والهمز والتنابذ
بالألقاب، وفي السمع ترك الإصغاء إلى قبائح اللسان من الغيبة وغيرها، وإلى
استماع الأصوات المحرمة وكذلك في جميع الجوارح والقوى.  وعماد عفة الجوارح
كلها ألا يطلقها في شيء مما يختص بها، إلا فيما يسوغه العقل والشرع، وعلى
الحد الذي يسوغه ثم لا تتم بذلك، ما لم يكن قصده في الإقدام والإحجام تحري
الفضيلة وطلب التقرب إلى الله عز وجل ونيل مرضاته. فأما إن كان قصده بعفته
انتظارا لما هو أكثر، أو لأنه لا يوافق مزاجه أو لخمود شهوته، أو لاستشعار
خوف في عاقبته، كسقوط حشمته أو لأنه ممنوع من تناوله، فكل ذلك ليس بعفة،
وإنما كل ذلك تجارة وترك حظ لحظ يماثله. وكل ذلك غير كاف في تحصيل العفة،
فليعلم ذلك، ولنخض بعد ذلك في تعريف التعلم والتعليم وتهذيب القوة العقلية.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ش-ه-و (Sh-H-W)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Desire, craving, longing of the soul for a thing; the inclination of nature toward what pleases it.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The appetitive faculty (al-quwwah al-shahwāniyyah) — a divinely-instilled impulse in the animal soul for the preservation of the individual and the species.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — the innate craving; metaphorical (majāz) — the soul's yearning for what is unlawful, as in "shahawāt al-nafs" (the lusts of the soul) in the Quranic idiom.
- Root: غ-ض-ب (Gh-D-B)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Boiling, ebullition; anger as the surging of the blood of the heart seeking vengeance.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The irascible faculty (al-quwwah al-ghaḍabiyyah) — created for repelling harm and defending the sacred; its excess is blameworthy, its deficiency is effeminacy.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — the physical boiling of the blood; metaphorical — the soul's resolve to repel what opposes it.
- Root: ع-ف-ف (ʿ-F-F)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Abstention from what is unlawful; contentment with what suffices.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The virtue of temperance (ʿiffah) — the mean of the appetitive faculty, restraining it from excess and deficiency.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — refraining; metaphorical — the comprehensive virtue governing all faculties, as al-Ghazālī extends it to the hand, tongue, ear, and eye.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of Condition and Qualification (al-sharṭ wa al-waṣf) — in sentences like "إذا تناوله من حيث يجب كما يجب" (if he partakes of it as it ought, in the manner it ought), the conditional particle governs the protasis, and the apodosis is qualified by the dual restriction of manner and quantity, requiring the reader to parse the nested adverbial clauses (ẓarf) as coordinated restrictions on the act.
chapters.translation:
I say: As for the appetite of the belly, it is a summoner to nourishment; and the edible is of two kinds: the necessary and the non-necessary. As for the necessary, it is that without which the constitution of the body cannot dispense — such as the food by which one is nourished and the water by which one is quenched. And it divides into the praiseworthy (maḥmūd), the disapproved (makrūh), the blameworthy (madhmūm), and the prohibited (maḥẓūr).

As for the praiseworthy, it is that one restrict himself to partaking of only that amount without which he cannot engage in knowledge and works, nor be steadfast upon them. Were he to abstain from it, his powers would dissolve and his body would become disordered. This measure, if he partakes of it as it ought, in the manner it ought, he is excused — nay, he is thanked and rewarded; for the body is the mount of the soul, by which it traverses its stations unto God Most High. And just as jihad is an act of worship, so too is the provisioning of the horse of the mujāhid with what strengthens it for the journey — by the mujāhid as well — an act of worship. For this reason, peace be upon him, said: «At the eating of the righteous, mercy descends.» That is, when he partakes as one who is compelled to a thing, wishing he could dispense with it. And the bringing of food into the belly and its expulsion are near akin. Therefore it was said: "Whosoever's concern is what enters his belly, his worth is what exits from him." And let the eater know that in partaking of the refuse of trees and plants, he is like the pig in partaking of the excrement of man and his waste, and like the dung-beetle in partaking of the waste of animals. Were trees to have tongues, they would reproach the partaker of their refuse by likening him to this partaker of animal waste.

As for the disapproved, it is extravagance (isrāf) and excess in the lawful, and the increase beyond the measure of sufficiency. He, peace be upon him, said: «There is no vessel more hateful to God Most High than a belly filled with the lawful.» And it is also harmful from the perspective of medicine, for it is the root of every disease. He, peace be upon him, said: «Gluttony is the root of disease, and dieting is the root of the cure; and accustom every body to what it is habituated.» The verifiers among the physicians said: "He, peace be upon him, left nothing of medicine unmentioned, but encompassed it under these three words."

And the seeker of felicity should not hold this increase in contempt, even though we have called it disapproved and not prohibited; for it is a disapproval swift in leading to the prohibited — nay, to most of the prohibited. For the source of evils is the strength of the appetites, and the strengthener of the appetites is food. The filling of the belly strengthens the appetites, and the strengthening of appetite summons caprice (hawā), and caprice is the greatest army of Satan, which, when it dominates, captivates him from his Lord and turns him from His door. And the provisioning of the armies of the enemies with strengtheners almost descends to the station of outright enmity. For this reason, the disapproval in it almost becomes a prohibition. Therefore it was said to one of them: "What is the matter with you, despite your age, that you do not tend to your body, and it has become emaciated?" He said: "Because it is swift in exultation, gross in insolence; I fear it will gather me and ensnare me. And if I carry it upon hardships, that is dearer to me than that it carry me upon indecencies."

If you say: What then is the praiseworthy measure? Know that he, peace be upon him, indicated the measure in two reports. One of them is his saying: «Sufficient for the son of Adam are a few morsels to keep his spine erect; but if it must be, then a third for food, a third for drink, and a third for breath.» As for the morsels, they are fewer than ten. And near to it is his saying, peace be upon him: «The believer eats in one intestine, and the hypocrite eats in seven intestines.» And the most beloved is eating in a seventh of the belly; but if voracity prevails, then in a third. And I hold that the limit is a third for most people, though that may vary with the variation of persons. And in sum, it must be less than satiety, so that the body becomes light for worship and night-vigil (tahajjud), and the powers weaken from surging toward the appetites.

As for the prohibited, it is the partaking of what God Mighty and Majestic has forbidden — whether from the wealth of another or the unlawful things. And the most heinous of these is the drinking of intoxicants, for it is the greatest instrument of Satan in removing the intellect, which is of the party of God and His friends; and it is a manifestation of appetite and the bestial powers, which are of the parties of Satan and his friends. This is the ruling on edibles in sum. And let no one aspire to traverse the path of felicity before he observes the matter of food in its measure and in the manner of its lawfulness; for the stomach is the spring of the powers — it is as if it were the door and the key to both good and evil. For this reason, the matter of fasting is magnified in the Sacred Law, because it is specifically directed to the subjugation of the enemies of God Most High, as was narrated: «Fasting is for Me, and I shall reward it» — and other such reports concerning it.

As for the appetite of the loins, its acts divide into the praiseworthy, the disapproved, and the prohibited. As for the praiseworthy, it is the measure that is indispensable for the preservation of the species; for marriage is necessary for the survival of the human species through the continuity of its progeny, just as nourishment is necessary for the survival of the individual until his appointed term. And the appetite was created as an impeller toward the preservation of offspring, by way of coition, just as hunger was created as an impeller toward the preservation of the individual by eating. For this reason, he said: «Marry, beget, and multiply, for I shall boast of you before the nations.» So whoever's intention in marriage is two things — one, the progeny for the abundance of boasting, and that a righteous child should follow him who prays for him; and two, that he repel from himself the excess of semen, which, when it accumulates, becomes like bile, and blood, when it accumulates, its harm becomes great in the body by arousing disease, and in religion by summoning to lewdness — then marriage on this face is praiseworthy, a Sunnah, and included under his saying: «Whosoever loves my nature (fiṭrah), let him follow my Sunnah.» And "whosoever marries has fortified half his religion." And there is no harm in a third purpose: that he have in his house one who manages the affairs of his home, so that he may devote himself to knowledge and worship; thus marriage on this face becomes part of the acts of worship, for deeds are by intentions. And the sign of this is that he seek from the woman only beauty for fortification, good character in managing the home, religiosity for protection, and religious lineage only — for it is the sign of religiosity and good character, since lineage is a puller. Therefore he, peace be upon him, said: «Upon you is the one of religion — may your hands be dusted — and beware of the green growth upon dung.» And he said: «Choose for your seed.» And let him seek soundness of body and that she be not barren, for the sake of offspring, for that is the intended purpose. Therefore coitus interruptus (ʿazl) was disapproved, and the approaching of the woman from behind, for it is neglect of the tillage; and «your women are a tillage for you.» And there is no harm in seeking virgins, that affection may be firmly established, and the Sacred Law has urged it.

As for the disapproved, it is that one intend merely the enjoyment of satisfying the appetite, then persist in it and be constant upon it, and perhaps partake of what increases his appetite. This is harmful in the Sacred Law, though there is no disapproval in it in itself, for it is permissible; but it is a turning away from God toward the following of caprice, and a likening to bulls and donkeys; and an arousal of appetite by strong foods and inciting causes, resembling the arousal of predatory beasts and rabid animals, then the rising up afterward to be delivered from them.

As for the prohibited, it is in two faces: One is that he satisfy the appetite in the place of tillage, but without a lawful contract, and not in the commanded manner — and that is fornication (zinā). God has coupled it with polytheism where He said: «The fornicator does not marry but a fornicatress or a polytheist» {al-Nūr 24:3}. The second is his engaging in it in other than the place of tillage — and that is more heinous than fornication; for the fornicator did not waste the seed, but placed it in the place of tillage in other than the commanded manner, whereas this one has wasted it, and was of those of whom God Most High said: «And He destroys the tillage and the progeny» {al-Baqarah 2:205}. For this reason, sodomy (liwāṭah) was named "extravagance" (isrāf), for He Most High said: «Indeed, you come to men with desire instead of women — nay, you are a people extravagant» {al-Aʿrāf 7:81}. These are the ranks of people in the appetite of the loins.

And some of the misguided may reach the point of passionate love (ʿishq) — and it is the very essence of folly and the extreme of ignorance concerning that for which coition was instituted, and a transgression of the limit of beasts in the soul's possession of itself and its restraint of it. For the passionate lover is not content with willing the satisfaction of the sexual appetite — which is the ugliest of appetites and the most deserving of being shamed — until he believes it cannot be fulfilled except in one particular place; whereas the beast satisfies its appetite wherever it happens and is content with that. But this one is not content except with his beloved, until he increases in humiliation upon humiliation and servitude upon servitude. And he has subjugated the intellect to the service of the appetite, though it was created to be an obeyed commander, not a servant of appetite, degraded for its sake. And it is a disease of an empty soul with no aspiration. And one must guard against its beginnings — which are the repetition of gazing and reflection — for otherwise, after it becomes entrenched, its repulsion becomes difficult. Likewise the love of prestige, wealth, property, and children — even the love of playing with birds, backgammon, and chess — for these things overpower a group upon whom religion and this world pass away, and they cannot bear to be without them. And the example of repelling the appetite at its first surging is the turning of the reins of a mount from its direction toward the door of a house it would enter — how easy is its prevention and the turning of its reins! And the example of treating it after its entrenchment is to leave the mount until it enters and passes beyond the door, then take hold of its tail, dragging it backward — and how great is the difference between the two matters! So let caution be in the beginnings of things; as for their ends, they do not admit of reform in most cases, except with a severe effort that rivals the extraction of the soul.

As for the acts of anger, they divide into the praiseworthy, the disapproved, and the prohibited. As for the praiseworthy, it is in two places: One is what is called jealousy (ghayrah) — that one intend the sanctity of a man and the exposure of his inviolables. So anger for that and for repelling it is praiseworthy; and the lack of being affected by it is effeminacy and weakness. Therefore he, peace be upon him, said: «Indeed, Saʿd is jealous, and God is more jealous than him.» And God has placed jealousy in men for the preservation of lineages; for were souls to be lax in crowding upon women, lineages would become mixed. Therefore it was said: "Every nation that placed jealousy in its men, God placed protection in its women." The second is anger upon witnessing abominations and indecencies — jealousy for religion and seeking vengeance. Therefore they were praised for being «harsh against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves» {al-Fatḥ 48:29}. And therefore he, peace be upon him, said: «The best of my community are its sharp-tempered ones» — meaning by it the sharpness for the zeal of religion. And therefore He Most High said: «And let not pity for them seize you in the religion of God» {al-Nūr 24:2}. Yet with all this, if a ruler becomes angry at the crime of a criminal, he should detain him and not hasten to punish him until he renews his examination of the matter; for anger is the destroyer of the intellect, and perhaps it will carry him to exceed the limit of the obligatory in vengeance.

As for the disapproved, it is his anger at the loss of his permissible shares — like his anger at his servant or slave upon the breaking of his vessel, or his negligence in his service, by way of an oversight that could be guarded against. This does not reach the limit of the blameworthy, but pardon and forbearance are more fitting and more beloved. Therefore it was said to a wise man: "Do not overlook your slave when he falls short in your service, lest he be corrupted by your tolerance." He said: "That my slave be corrupted in the soundness of my soul is better than that my soul be corrupted in the soundness of my slave." For tolerating that is the reform of the soul, and vengeance is the reform of the slave.

As for the blameworthy, it is the raging from pride, arrogance, vainglory, rivalry, rancor, and envy — and from trivial matters pertaining to bodily shares — without there being in the vengeance any benefit for the future, in religion or this world. And this is what prevails over most of creation, and it is submission to the creature that opposes forbearance (ḥilm) and self-restraint (taḥallum). For forbearance is the expression of the soul's restraint from the surging of anger; and self-restraint is its restraint from fulfilling its desire from it, when it surges. And perfection is in forbearance; but self-restraint is patience upon the disliked, and in it also is much good. These are the ranks of the acts of anger.

And people differ in anger: some are like the dry herb — quick to ignite, quick to extinguish; some are like the sandgrouse — slow to extinguish; and some are slow to ignite and quick to extinguish — and this is the most praiseworthy, so long as it does not reach the point of the slackening of zeal and jealousy. As for the causes of anger — from the side of temperament, they are heat and dryness, indicated by the definition of anger; for the meaning of anger is the boiling of the blood of the heart. If it is against one above you in power of vengeance, there is generated from it a contraction of the blood from the surface of the skin to the heart, and it becomes grief, and for that reason the face yellows. If it is against one below you, there is generated from it a surging of the blood of the heart, not its contraction, and from it arises true anger and the seeking of vengeance. If it is against your equal in power of vengeance, there is generated from it a fluctuation of the blood between contraction and expansion, and by it the color of the face varies — it reddens, yellows, and becomes agitated. And in sum, the seat of the power of anger is the heart, and its meaning is the movement and boiling of the blood. As for what is beyond temperament, it is habituation; for whoever associates with a people who boast of anger and bestial natures becomes imprinted with that. And whoever mixes with the people of calm and dignity, habit also affects him. As for its cause that brings it out from potentiality to actuality at the moment, it is self-admiration (ʿujb), pride, disputation, obstinacy, jesting, haughtiness, mockery, oppression, and the seeking of what involves rivalry, envy, and the appetite for vengeance — and all of that is blameworthy. And it behooves the one overtaken by anger to reflect upon what one of the sages said to one of the kings, when he asked him for a stratagem to repel anger. He said: "You should remember that you must obey, not merely be obeyed; and serve, not merely be served; and bear, not merely be borne; and know that God sees you always. If you do that, you will not become angry."

Know that anger has branches, as has preceded; and among them are courage (shajāʿah), recklessness (tahawwur), rivalry (munāfasah), emulation (ghibṭah), and envy (ḥasad), as has preceded — but we shall add explanation to them. As for courage, it is a character between recklessness and cowardice. If it is considered in relation to the soul, it is the firmness of the heart in terrors and the tying of the composure at fears; and if considered by act, it is the advance upon the place of opportunity. And it is generated from anger and good hope; and by it a man endures hardships — nay, by it he refrains from sins, for anger, when it is given authority over the appetite, rebukes it. And since religion is half of it a desire for good and half of it an abandonment of evil, he, peace be upon him, said: «Patience is half of faith.» And since some evils are in the appetite of the loins and the belly, and some are in other than them, he said: «Fasting is half of patience.» And patience is of two kinds: bodily patience — which is the bearing of hardships by the body, whether actively, like engaging in arduous works, or passively, like enduring severe beating and great illness. And the complete praiseworthy one is the second kind — and it is soul-patience. If it is concerning the partaking of desired things, it is called temperance (ʿiffah); and if it is upon bearing a disliked thing, its names differ according to the difference of the disliked.
